metadata.title: Top 5 Prediction Market APIs in 2026 (Polymarket, Kalshi & More)
metadata.author: OngPredicts
metadata.shortDescription:
I compared 5 prediction market APIs in 2026 to see how they stack up for cross-venue builders  from onchain data and wallet analytics to sports odds, AI agents, normalized market data, live feeds and execution.

Best Prediction Market API: https://predictefy.com/en/prediction-market-api

00:00 Best Prediction Market APIs in 2026
00:23 #5 Bitquery – Onchain Prediction Market Data
00:58 #4 Nansen API – Polymarket Wallet & Trader Analytics
01:53 #3 Monid – Prediction Market Tools for AI Agents
03:03 #2 SportsGameOdds – Sportsbook & Prediction Market Data
03:39 #1 Predictefy – Cross-Venue Prediction Market API
06:25 Final Thoughts & Resources

This ranking looks at three key areas: prediction market venue coverage, what developers can do with the data, and how much additional infrastructure you need to build yourself.

I compare Bitquery, Nansen, Monid, SportsGameOdds and Predictefy for developers building prediction market products, trading tools, aggregators, screeners and analytics platforms.

Predictefy provides one normalized prediction market API across 16 served venues, with market catalogs, order books, trades, historical candles, live streams, cross-venue market matching and execution workflows where supported.

Instead of maintaining separate integrations and schemas for every prediction market, developers can discover markets, compare equivalent markets across venues, analyze historical data, monitor live activity and build toward execution from one connected toolkit.

Whether you're building a prediction market aggregator, cross-venue screener, trading bot, arbitrage scanner, analytics platform or automated trading system, this video breaks down five different approaches to prediction market infrastructure in 2026.

Tools & resources mentioned:

Predictefy
Bitquery
Nansen
Monid
SportsGameOdds

#PredictionMarkets #PredictionMarketAPI #Polymarket #Kalshi #TradingAPI #DeveloperTools

Whether you're building a prediction market aggregator, trading bot, arbitrage scanner, analytics platform or automated trading system, this video breaks down the best APIs available in 2026.

metadata.title: Prediction Market Assistant with Perplexity Sonar API and Kalshi API
metadata.author: Part Time Larry
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video we explore how to build an AI assistant for prediction markets. We write code in Python that uses the Kalshi API to fetch prediction market odds, then use the Perplexity Sonar Reasoning API to evaluate those odds. We use structured outputs support to extract the bid price, a side, whether the contract was under/overpriced, and a confidence score. This gives us the ability to programmatically place an order for an underpriced contract. We use Streamlit for the UI.

Source Code: https://github.com/hackingthemarkets/prediction-market-assistant

0:00 Demo of the App
2:16 Perplexity Sonar API with DeepSeek and Structured Output
3:36 Kalshi API and events as context
4:13 Grok3 has pretty good analysis of prediction markets
6:56 These models are more willing to speculate
7:21 Testing responses in Perplexity Sonar Reasoning playground
8:23 Going beyond an assistant to an agent
9:07 Getting the code from my Github
10:09 Python code walkthrough, dependencies, environment
11:32 Running the Streamlit app, caching Kalshi event data
12:40 Events vs. Markets, my Super Bowl and Kendrick Lamar bets
14:55 Event and category json, pagination, caching for speed
17:23 Quick Streamlit UI component review
18:33 Matching search term, capturing markdown for context
19:53 Evaluate Bet button, callback function, odds markdown as context
20:47 Evaluate bet function, Perplexity payload, system prompt
21:57 Pydantic model for contract data
22:49 Perplexity JSON output is in beta, not 100% reliable
23:47 Displaying the analysis in a dialog
24:58 Language models are not deterministic, not 100% reliable
26:05 Why I called it an assistant and not an agent
26:45 Wrapping up: do you want more prediction market content?

Prediction markets have gone from niche curiosity to core infrastructure for traders, quants, and consumer fintech apps. In this Codex session, we break down the top 5 prediction market APIs for powering real-time odds dashboards and trading frontends.

You’ll learn:
- Why your API choice defines latency, UX, and trust in your product
- The four key ranking criteria: latency & real-time UX, resolution accuracy, liquidity & venue coverage, and regulatory posture
- How developer ergonomics and data breadth impact time-to-first-query
- Which APIs are best for multi-venue dashboards vs single-venue frontends

We walk through Codex, Polymarket, Kalshi, Syve, and TVDatafeed, and explain where each one shines for web3, fintech, and quant teams that need production-grade reliability at scale.

If you’re building trading UIs, odds apps, or consumer products that surface implied probabilities and real-money prediction markets, this deep dive will help you choose the right data layer.

Watch to understand how Codex consolidates multi-venue prediction market data into one trading-grade API, and when you might use venue-native or analytics-only feeds alongside it.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro and evaluation criteria
2:13 Codex as cross-venue default
4:54 Polymarket’s venue-native API
6:51 Kalshi for US-regulated markets
8:53 Syve for DeFi and analytics
10:45 TVDatafeed for historical data
11:50 How teams should choose among APIs

segments.text: Today, we're diving into the wild world
of prediction markets, and more
specifically, the APIs that power
real-time odds dashboards and trading
front ends.
If you're building a trading UI or an
odds app, your data feed basically
decides how fast and trustworthy your
product feels. So, we're going to walk
through the top five prediction market
APIs you should be thinking about.
>> Yeah, prediction markets have moved from
being this nerdy side project to serious
infrastructure for traders, quants, and
consumer fintech apps. And choosing the
wrong API can your latency, your
accuracy, and even your legal reach,
especially in the US.
>> So, before we get into the list, what
were the criteria for ranking these
APIs? Because there are a lot of data
providers out there.
>> The core lens here is can this API
actually power a production-grade,
high-traffic trading or analytics UI?
We looked at four big things, latency
and real-time UX, resolution accuracy
and transparency, liquidity and venue
coverage, and regulatory posture,
especially whether US users can legally
access the venue.
>> On top of that, we also weighed
developer ergonomics, breadth of data
like events and order books, and whether
the API works better for multi-venue
dashboards or single-venue front ends.
>> So, this is really aimed at teams that
need reliability and scale, not just
hobby projects.
>> Exactly. The audience is Web3 and
fintech product teams, quant and trading
desks, and consumer apps that want to
show odds, implied probabilities, or
real money prediction markets without
building their own data plumbing.
>> All right, let's hit the headline first.
What's the quick summary of the top five
and what each is best at?
>> The short version is Codex is the best
cross-venue API for multi-venue odds and
trading. Polymarket is the best native
DeFi API. Kalshi is the best US
regulated centralized API. Sive is an
analytics layer complement, and TV data
feed is mainly useful for bootstrapping
charts, not full production feeds.
>> Got it. So Codex is sitting in that
number one spot. Why does it stand out
as the default choice for odds
dashboards and trading front ends?
>> Codex is basically a high performance
on-chain data API that spans more than
80 networks and hundreds of millions of
wallets, and it's battle tested by big
names like Coinbase, TradingView,
Uniswap, Magic Eden, and others. For
Prediction Market specifically, it gives
you a unified schema for events,
markets, order books, trades, volume,
liquidity, open interest, and even
trader positions and holdings across
venues like Polymarket and Kalshi.
It exposes all of this via a GraphQL
style API plus websockets and live
subscriptions, so it's built for trading
terminals and real-time dashboards, not
just background analytics.
>> So instead of wiring up three different
APIs and normalizing everything
yourself, you basically plug into Codex
once and get that cross-venue view?
>> That's the big value prop. Codex
eliminates the need to stitch together a
bunch of venue native APIs and then
maintain all those integrations over
time.
It normalizes symbols, IDs, and
resolution statuses so you get
consistent objects, and it's low latency
enough to feel snappy in a trading UI
with sub-second responses and streaming
that's been proven at scale for over 50
million users via TradingView.
For a head of product or CTO, this means
one integration, less custom ETL, fewer
edge cases, and a much faster path to
shipping a multi-venue dashboard or
trading front end.
>> Who's the ideal kind of team for Codex?
Because it sounds powerful, but maybe
not for everyone.
>> It's perfect if you're building
multi-venue odds dashboards that show
Polymarket and Kelsi side by side,
cross-venue trading front ends that want
best price routing, or token-aware apps
that mix portfolios and prediction
markets.
Enterprise fintech products, especially
at Series A and beyond, benefit because
Codex gives them reliability, latency,
and correctness without building a data
team from scratch.
>> And what are the catches? Where does
Codex not quite fit?
>> It's not the cheapest option, and it's
probably overkill if you just want a
basic odds widget for a side project on
a single venue.
Also, because it's an abstraction layer,
it might not expose every esoteric field
or brand-new feature that a venue-native
API offers, especially for experimental
order types or beta markets.
>> All right, let's move to number two,
Polymarket. What makes Polymarket's own
API so compelling, especially for
crypto-native teams?
>> Polymarket is the leading crypto-native
prediction market platform, and as of
November 5th, 2026, it has a huge
catalog, over 17,000 live markets just
in 2026, plus thousands more across
categories like statistics and hourly
markets.
Their API is venue-native and tuned for
their order book with WebSocket
streaming for snapshots, price changes,
trades, and lifecycle events like
creation, pauses, and resolution.
Resolution is done on-chain via Yuma's
optimistic oracle with a short challenge
window, and contracts trade from 0 to
100 cents, which maps directly to
implied probability percentages.
>> So if I'm building a Polymarket-focused
trading UI, I'm probably going straight
to their API rather than through an
aggregator?
>> Exactly. If your product is Polymarket
first, say a dedicated terminal or
analytics dashboard, their native API
gives you the lowest latency and the
richest access to venue specific
features. You get deep liquidity,
real-time order book feeds, and
transparent on-chain resolution logic,
which you can explain fairly clearly in
your UI once you translate the UMA
mechanics.
>> And where does Polymarket fall short
compared to something like Codex?
>> First, it's single venue. So if you want
Kalshi or other venues in your app,
you'll need additional integrations.
Second, there are US access constraints.
Polymarket geoblocks and has a separate
US regulated product, so global and US
users don't see the same catalog.
Finally, the on-chain resolution flow
with challenge windows can feel
confusing for mainstream users unless
you invest in explaining it in the UX.
>> Let's talk about number three, Kalshi.
This one's interesting because it's very
much positioned as the US regulated
player.
>> Kalshi is a centralized, federally
regulated prediction market exchange in
the US, and it's built to give both
retail and institutional traders a
compliant way to trade event outcomes.
Beyond the regulatory angle, they've
reported big institutional momentum with
a massive Series G and annualized
trading volume over a trillion dollars,
plus a big uptick in institutional flow.
>> Their public API gives unauthenticated
market data, listings, quotes, price
history, and they also support web
sockets for live price and order book
updates.
>> You mentioned resolution via official
sources. Why does that matter for
product teams?
>> For US-facing apps, being able to say
this market settles based on data from
official agencies is huge for
compliance, user trust, and internal
risk teams.
Kalshi resolves markets based on
authoritative sources, but the tradeoff
is timing. Depending on when official
data is released, settlement can take
from about an hour to more than 12 hours
after a market closes.
>> So who should be prioritizing Kalshi's
API?
>> US consumer
>> apps and fintech products that need a
clear compliance story should have
Kaishi on their shortlist.
It's also a strong fit for institutional
and professional macro traders who want
event exposure tied to official economic
data and government releases.
>> And the limitations sound similar to
Polymarket in some ways. Is it mainly
about being single venue?
>> Right. It only covers Kaishi's own
markets, so you still need another
provider for multi-venue dashboards. And
the centralized structure won't appeal
to teams that want on-chain
composability.
Plus, the resolution lag means you can't
always offer instant settlement even
when the outcome feels obvious because
you're waiting on the official data
feed.
>> Let's move down the list to number four,
Sieve. This one isn't really a
prediction market API per se, right?
>> Sieve is primarily a blockchain
analytics and token data provider, not a
dedicated prediction market engine.
It focuses on low latency token prices,
DEX trades, pool TVL and liquidity, and
wallet analytics with batch endpoints
for thousands of tokens and pools and
websockets for real-time updates. In the
public docs that were reviewed, there
aren't obvious prediction market
specific endpoints like events, markets,
or dedicated prediction order books.
>> So why does it make the top five list at
all if it doesn't speak prediction
markets natively?
>> Because it's a strong complement to a
prediction market stack, especially if
your app is as much about DeFi and
tokens as it is about odds. You can use
Sieve for contextual analytics like
correlating wallet activity, token
flows, and DEX volume with movements in
prediction markets while another
provider handles the markets themselves.
>> Who's the ideal user of Sieve in this
context?
>> Analytics heavy products and quant teams
who want to overlay prediction markets
on top of broader DeFi data benefit the
most.
It's also attractive if you already use
Sieve for token data and want to extend
that infra alongside a separate
prediction market API.
>> And the obvious tradeoff is that it's
not a one-stop prediction market shop.
>> Exactly. Sieve doesn't give you native
events, market structures, or resolution
semantics for prediction markets, so you
cannot rely on it as your primary odds
feed.
It only makes sense when paired with
something like Codex, Polymarket, or
Kelsi. And by itself, it adds
integration overhead if your only goal
is prediction markets.
>> That brings us to number five, TV data
feed, which sounds very different from
the others. What is it actually?
>> TV data feed is essentially a
TradingView historical data downloader.
It's designed to pull OHLC bars for
symbols that TradingView supports, often
used in Python scripts or backtesting.
It lets you download up to 5,000 bars
per time frame and may require a
TradingView login for full symbol
access, so it's more of a chart
bootstrapper than a real-time
venue-native prediction market feed.
>> So if I see TV data feed in GitHub and
think, great, prediction market API, I'm
misunderstanding what it's for?
>> Exactly. It doesn't talk directly to
prediction venues like Polymarket or
Kelsi. It doesn't handle order books or
market lifecycle events, and it's not
built for trading-grade latency.
It's useful for prototypes, backtesting,
and internal research dashboards, but
not for production odds dashboards or
trading front ends that need robust
real-time data.
>> All right. So we've gone through the top
five. How should teams actually choose
between these APIs based on their
product model?
>> It helps to think in terms of
archetypes. If you're building a
multi-venue odds dashboard or trading
front end that aggregates Polymarket and
Kelsi, you want a unified schema,
WebSockets, and cross-venue coverage.
And Codex is the default fit there.
If you're laser focused on a single
crypto-native venue, like a Polymarket
only trading UI, you probably go
straight to the Polymarket API and
optionally add a data provider for token
analytics.
>> And what about teams that are US first
or highly regulated?
>> For US-focused consumer apps and
fintechs with strict compliance
requirements, Kaushi's regulated status
and official source resolution make it a
natural primary venue.
You can always pair it with a
cross-venue layer later if you expand
internationally, but Kaushi gives you
the legal clarity to ship in the US now.
>> Then you've got analytics-heavy tools
and people who just want a prototype.
How do they fit in?
>> For analytics-heavy tools that want to
mix DeFi and prediction markets, a
sensible combo is Codex or a
venue-native API for the markets plus
Sieve for token prices, pools, and
wallet activity.
If you're just experimenting, you can
get away with TV data feed plus a
venue-native API like Polymarket or
Kaushi to get basic time series and odds
without building a full infra stack.
>> Let's hit a few common questions
quickly. First, if someone asks, what's
the best prediction market API for
real-time odds dashboards, how do you
answer?
>> For multi-venue dashboards, Codex is
generally the best starting point
because it aggregates venues like
Polymarket and Kaushi into a single
trading-grade API with normalized data.
If you only care about one venue, then
Polymarket's native API or Kaushi's
market data API will be enough,
depending on whether you're
crypto-native or US-regulated first.

metadata.title: Why Kalshi Bettors Lose (72 Million Trades Analyzed)
metadata.author: Part Time Larry
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, we discuss Jonathan Becker's blog post entitled "The Microstructure of Wealth Transfer", which analyzed over 72 million Kalshi trades.

Blog Post: https://www.jbecker.dev/research/prediction-market-microstructure
Github: https://github.com/jon-becker/prediction-market-analysis
My writeup / mailing list: https://hackingthemarkets.com/why-kalshi-takers-lose-money-72m-trades-analyzed/

0:00 Becker Blog post
1:22 Longshot Bias
5:37 Makers and Takers
7:51 Yogi Berra Bias: “It Ain’t Over Til it’s Over”
10:43 The Optimism Tax / Default Bias
12:01 Emotional Categories
13:13 Black Swans and the occasional longshot
14:17 The “Nothing Ever Happens” Strategy

segments.text: So, a few days ago I was scrolling
through the site Hacker News and I came
across this article called the
microstructure of wealth transfer in
prediction markets.
Love the title there, so I decided to
dive in. And what we have here is a
senior software engineer at Coinbase,
where I used to work, some of you may
know. His name is Jonathan Becker and
what he did was create a huge data set
of Kalshi trades, 72 million of them.
And what he found is that there are a
number of well-known biases that have
been uh documented in research for
decades now that apply to Kalshi markets
and are causing retail traders to lose
uh lots of money on these prediction
markets. So, uh in this tutorial, what I
want to do is discuss uh what some of
these biases are and how you might write
code to actually uh take advantage of
some of these biases or at least to
avoid them. And one nice thing about
this paper is that he released an
open-source repository here, complete
with Python scripts, and we know Python
here, right? And what you can do here is
actually build the data set, the
historical data set of 72 million Kalshi
trades, and study it for uh these
inefficiencies. And what this does is uh
build these parquet files and allows you
to run these DuckDB queries in order to
analyze the data. And I'll show you how
to do that. But first, let's go over
some of the biases that he outlines in
the paper. The first of those is long
shot bias. And what he does here is
reference a paper by Thaler and Ziemba.
It's a well-known paper uh written in
1988 that studies a horse race bettors.
And what they found is that uh bettors
are willing to overpay on long shot. So,
maybe a horse only has a 5% uh chance of
winning, but you'll pay uh 6 cents per
contract. So, you'll pay as if they have
a 6% chance of win- winning. And you
might say, well, that is horse racing
and this is from 1988. What does that
have to do with the current uh
environments or prediction markets in
2026? And what you find is that uh this
psychology actually holds up over time.
And it makes sense when you think about
something like uh WallStreetBets, for
instance. You see people uh buying these
YOLO options and they want to show I
called it, I made this huge gain, I I
won 20 20x my money in one day. And a
lot of this long shot bias happens in
sports markets in particular. You can
see I'm guilty of this. I Here's a bet I
placed at the beginning of the NBA
season. Uh I was originally born in the
Houston area, so I bought that the
Houston Rockets would be the NBA
champion. And I bought that with a 7% uh
chance of happening at the beginning of
the of the season. Uh and I was going to
show everybody, haha, I called it at the
beginning of the year, uh 15x gains or
whatever. Uh what you see has actually
happened over time is that now the
Rockets only have a 4% chance of winning
the NBA finals and you can see my $43 is
now worth uh $24 and I've lost nearly
half of my money. And this is because I
was biased. I want my team to win so
much that I'm willing to pay a little
bit too much to have a contract that
says the Rockets are going to win uh the
championship. Now, in the article on the
website hackingthemarkets.com, uh link
below, I've placed some code that you
can use to analyze these trades on the
GitHub repository. And so, he has a
GitHub repo um that is linked in the
article. So, with a command make analyze
win by price, I ran that and you see he
has these different scripts that are
prepared and you can write your own. And
so, we have one called uh win rate by
price here.
And if you look at that, you see that it
has all the code you need in order to
analyze the resolved markets. And so,
the way this works, this will actually
uh execute an analysis script called uh
win rate by price. And what this does is
actually uh build a data set, so you see

segments.text: High iGaming affiliate programs rarely fail because of one catastrophic mistake. They
lose margins slowly through operational gaps that never trip a single alarm on
their own. A program can hit its growth targets, clear its reporting checks, and
still be quietly leaking money through attribution fraud, commission logic, or
payouts. In this vertical, the biggest risks are usually invisible until they've
already gotten expensive. After working with operators running these programs at
scale, the pattern repeats itself. It's rarely one big mistake. It's a handful of
operational areas that never get fully locked in, and each one quietly compounds
the others. They show up as margin you can't account for, affiliates you can't
trust, and a program that looks healthy on the dashboard but isn't performing the way
the numbers suggest it should. These are the 8 operational pillars we'd review
first if we inherited a program tomorrow. Not because the concepts are unfamiliar to
you, but because most experienced operators have one or two of these only partially
dialed in, and that's exactly where the margin disappears. If you already run a
tight operation, this tells you where to pressure test it. And if something feels
off but you haven't been able to name it, this is where you'll find it. Let's get
into it. Pillar 1 is your commission model, and specifically how it connects directly
to your fraud exposure. Many treat the commission structure as a financial
decision. It's actually a risk management decision. If you're running CPA deals on
FTDs in a market with heavy bonus activity, you've built a financial incentive for
affiliates to drive players who deposit once, collect a bonus, and disappear. The
commission model you choose determines what kind of affiliate behavior your
program rewards. Revshare on NGR aligns affiliates with your actual business
outcomes. CPA can still work, but only when the deal terms are tight enough to filter
out behavior before the payout fires. Loose CPA terms attract exactly the wrong type
of affiliate, and by the time that shows up in the numbers, you've already paid for it.
Pillar 2 is the number that should actually be driving your payouts, and it's
NGR, not gross revenue. This sounds obvious until you look at how many programs are
still calculating commissions on gross. Many discover this the expensive way:
after a strong deposit month gets quietly erased by withdrawals, the commission engine
never accounted for it. Paying affiliates on gross means paying them before you know
whether those players were actually profitable. If your platform doesn't
support NGR-based commission calculation natively, that's an infrastructure problem
that gets more expensive the faster you grow. Pillar 3 is FTD tracking, and it's the
point where attribution breaks down most often. The gap between a click and a
completed deposit is wider than most assume, and it's rarely one obvious failure.
Delayed tracking, session drops, device switching, and browser privacy changes each
chip away at attribution quietly. Your dashboard still shows the conversion, but
the affiliate who actually drove that player doesn't get credited, or worse, the
wrong affiliate does. At scale, those misattributions add up to real money
leaving the program without anyone noticing. Programs that integrate tracking
directly with their payment provider catch far fewer of these gaps than ones relying
on pixel fires or last-click cookies across a journey that can span days.
Pillar 4 is your multi-brand and multi-geo setup, and why it needs its own dedicated
infrastructure: not filters or naming conventions, but actual separate tracking
environments that report independently. Here's what happens when operators rely on
workarounds instead: affiliate agreements built for one brand start bleeding into
reporting for another, and commission structures built for one market get
applied incorrectly in a different geo because the environment was never properly
separated. When an audit comes or an affiliate disputes a payout, you're
untangling months of mixed data under pressure. Mature programs treat their
infrastructure as multi-brand from day one, not something retrofitted later.
Pillar 5 and this is the one that catches even experienced operators, is that fraud in
iGaming doesn't look like fraud. Fraud in other verticals is usually detectable
because it looks abnormal: bot traffic, suspiciously round numbers, conversion
rates no legitimate affiliate actually achieves. In iGaming, sophisticated fraud
looks like performance: high click volume, solid FTD numbers,
conversions that clear your initial review without raising a single flag. What you
don't see until later is the player quality underneath: players who deposit
once, trigger a bonus, generate negative NGR, and never come back. By the time the data
tells you the truth, you've already paid out. That's a lesson most only need to
learn once. The fix isn't a fraud detection tool bolted on after the fact. It's a
review window built into your conversion workflow before any commission is approved.
Pillar 6 is compliance, and why it's really a payout problem wearing a different hat.
The legal side, license requirements, responsible gambling standards, and marketing
restrictions by market, matters and most operators have that covered. The compliance
issue that actually hits your margin is operational. Different affiliates in
different markets carry different tax situations, payment preferences, and
documentation requirements. When your payout process can't handle that cleanly
and automatically, your finance team ends up managing exceptions by hand every month.
Someone gets paid the wrong amount because a tax rate wasn't applied correctly, and
that affiliate's trust takes a hit while your team investigates and reprocesses.
The affiliates who matter most have options, and getting paid feeling like a second job
is reason enough to leave. Build payout infrastructure that handles compliance
automatically across every market you operate in, and this entire category of
problem disappears. Pillar 7 is conversion on-hold buffering, and it's one of the most
underused tools in any iGaming program. Most operators know conversion statuses
exist. Fewer use them strategically. The on-hold status lets you delay the point at
which a conversion becomes visible and payable to an affiliate, giving your team
time to verify the quality of the underlying player behavior before any
commission locks in. In iGaming, where the difference between a valuable long-term
player and a bonus chaser can take days or weeks to reveal itself, that buffer isn't
optional. A player deposits, the conversion fires, and instead of immediately entering
your approval queue, it sits on hold while your team monitors the player's activity
over a defined window. Did they keep playing after the bonus cleared? Did they
generate positive NGR? Only when the answers point to a real player does the
conversion move forward. Build it into your standard workflow, and you'll catch a
meaningful percentage of low-quality conversions before they ever hit your
payout queue. And Pillar 8, the last one, is payout automation and why at scale it
stops being a convenience feature and becomes core infrastructure. Manual payouts
work when you have 20 affiliates, and they stop working long before you have 200. At
scale, operating across multiple markets with different payment preferences and
varying minimum thresholds, manual payouts aren't just slow; they're a consistent
source of errors, disputes, and affiliate churn. The operators we've seen scale large
iGaming programs efficiently automated their entire payout workflow early:
settlements generated automatically,
payments processed through integrated providers, taxes handled without manual
exports, and affiliates paid on time without anyone touching a spreadsheet.
When your payout infrastructure is built correctly, your team's attention goes where
it should: to the relationships, the deals. Those are the 8 pillars, and if even 2 or 3
of them aren't fully locked in yet, you already know where to start. Every pillar
in this list connects back to the same thing: a program that pays for real
performance, tracks it accurately, and doesn't let margin disappear quietly in
the background. That's what a well-run iGaming affiliate program actually looks
like. If you're looking for a platform to handle this kind of complexity natively
Trackdesk does exactly that. Multi-brand setups, NGR-based commission logic, payout
automation built in, fraud controls, and a team that understands how iGaming programs
actually operate. Book a demo with our team using the first link in the description
below. And if this video was helpful, I highly recommend that you check out the
next video on your screen right now. Inside, we break down how top operators actually
structure CPA, rev share, and hybrid payouts across their affiliate rosters. So if
commission strategy is where you want to go deeper, that's your next watch. Also,
don't forget to hit like, subscribe, and turn on the bell so you don't miss what we
put out next. I'll see you there.

metadata.title: How a Casino Affiliate Program Actually Works – With Numbers
metadata.author: 15M iGaming Media & Dealflow Platform
metadata.shortDescription:
A casino affiliate can earn a fixed payment for bringing in a qualified player – or receive a percentage of the revenue that player generates over time.

But the headline commission rarely tells the whole story.

In this video, we follow the money through a casino affiliate program and explain how the business actually works – from the first tracked click to registration, first-time deposit, qualification, and ultimately affiliate commission.

We break down the three main payment models in iGaming: CPA, RevShare, and Hybrid, using published industry benchmarks and practical examples to show how each structure works and where the real differences appear.

We also explain why a headline like 35% RevShare does not necessarily mean the affiliate receives 35% of everything a referred player generates. The actual payment depends on how the contract defines NGR, which deductions apply, and whether conditions such as negative carryover or administrative charges are included.

And to show how large the affiliate business can become, we look at Better Collective and why major affiliate companies operate less like simple referral websites and more like full-scale media businesses built around content, technology, acquisition, and long-term commercial relationships.

⏱️ Key Moments

00:00 – How casino affiliate programs make money  
00:40 – How the affiliate tracking chain works  
02:21 – CPA, RevShare and Hybrid explained  
04:24 – Why 35% RevShare isn’t really 35%  
06:05 – How large affiliate businesses can become  
07:28 – What the economics mean for affiliates and operators  
08:34 – Resources and the next episode

depend on the market, traffic quality,
and individual agreements. Now, imagine
an affiliate delivers 20 qualified
players under a $250
CPA agreement. That's $5,000 in gross
commission. The affiliate knows the
payment per approved acquisition, but
not necessarily their final margin after
expenses. The second model is revenue
share, or rev share. Instead of a fixed
acquisition payment, the affiliate
receives a percentage of net gaming
revenue generated by referred players.
The same benchmark provides a reference
range of 25 to 45% with a reported
median of 30%. Unlike CPA, the payment
depends on customer activity and the
operator's revenue calculations. A
customer generating no positive
commissionable revenue may generate no
rev share payment. The third model
combines both approaches. It's called
hybrid. The benchmark estimates that
roughly 45% of new tier one agreements
use hybrid structures. It describes
combinations such as $75 to $150 in CPA
plus 15%
revenue share. For example, 10 qualified
customers at $100 each would generate
$1,000 up front if their combined
commissionable net gaming revenue later
reached $2,000. A 20% share would add
$400. Total commission, $1,400. That's a
hypothetical calculation, not a real
affiliate's earnings. Hybrid
arrangements spread compensation between
acquisition and ongoing player activity,
but there is one number every affiliate
must understand before signing a revenue
share agreement.
35% sounds straightforward. If a casino
generates $1,000, an affiliate might
assume they're receiving 350, but that's
not necessarily how the contract works.
First, we need to distinguish gross
gaming revenue from net gaming revenue.
Gross gaming revenue, or GGR, is
generally calculated as stakes minus
player winnings. It isn't the same as
customer deposits, and it isn't company
profit. Revenue share agreements
commonly use a narrower figure, NGR. The
precise definition depends on the
operator's contract. Let's build a
hypothetical example. Suppose a referred
group of customers generates $1,000 in
gross gaming revenue over a month. Under
our example contract, the operator
deducts $150 in bonuses and promotional
costs. Another hundred goes toward
gaming taxes. Payment processing and
other agreed charges account for $50.
That leaves $700 in commissionable net
gaming revenue. Now, apply the 35% rev
share rate. The affiliate receives $245,
not 350, and certainly not 35% of
everything players deposited or wagered.
In this example, the effective
commission equals 24.5%
of the original gross gaming revenue.
Different contracts may define NGR
differently. They can also include
negative balance carryover,
administration charges, or other
conditions that affect future payments.
This is why comparing revshare offers by
percentage alone can be misleading. A
30% agreement with fewer deductions
could potentially outperform a 35%
agreement with a less favorable revenue
definition. The headline rate is only
half the calculation. The contract
determines the rest.
To understand the scale of this
industry, consider Better Collective.
It's a publicly listed digital sports
media group whose business includes
affiliate-driven customer acquisition.
In the second quarter of 2026, Better
Collective reported approximately 89.1
million euros in revenue. Over the same
quarter, it reported 373,000
new depositing customers. That's a 24%
increase in new depositing customers
compared with the same quarter a year
earlier. According to the company's
interim report, 70% of those new
depositing customers came through
revenue share agreements. But there's a
crucial distinction. The 89 million
euros represents company revenue across
multiple business activities. It isn't
simply a commission total from those new
customers. Better Collective also
operates media brands and generates
revenue through activities beyond
traditional casino affiliate deals. And
the reported customer figure isn't a
count of people each receiving a fixed
CPA payment. Some customers contribute
to revenue share arrangements whose
commercial value develops over time. So,
dividing quarterly revenue by new
customers wouldn't give us a reliable
CPA rate. What the figures demonstrate
is something different. At scale,
affiliate marketing isn't just a website
collecting referral fees. It can become
an entire media business built around
audiences, content, technology,
acquisition, and long-term commercial
relationships.
For an affiliate evaluating a deal, the
biggest number on the rate card isn't
necessarily the most important. A high
CPA is useful only when customers
qualify and acquisition costs remain
manageable. A high rev share percentage
matters only when the revenue
definition, deductions, and player
activity support it. And a hybrid
agreement only makes sense when both
components are evaluated together. For
operators, the equation works in
reverse. They need to compare
acquisition commissions with the
expected value of customers while
accounting for operating costs,
retention, and regulatory obligations.
In regulated markets, affiliate
relationships also create compliance
responsibilities. The UK's Gambling
Commission, for example, makes clear
that gambling operators remain
responsible for relevant breaches
involving third-party marketing. That
means traffic quality and responsible
marketing are part of the economics,
too. The basic lesson is simple.
Affiliate marketing is a business of
measurable acquisition costs and
uncertain future customer value. The
winning commercial arrangement isn't
automatically the one with the highest
advertised commission. It's the one
whose actual terms make financial sense.

segments.text: Prediction markets and sports books can
look similar at first. Both are
connected to future outcomes. Both can
involve sports and both can make you
think about the chance of something
happening before it actually happens.
But the way they work is very different.
With a sports book, you are usually
placing a bet on odds offered by the
operator. With a prediction market, you
are buying and selling event contracts
against other traders. That difference
changes how prices are set, how risk
works, and how users should think about
each market. Sports books use odds. At a
sports book, the main language is odds.
You might see odds on a team winning a
game, a player scoring, or a total going
over or under a certain number. The
sports book creates the market, sets the
odds, and accepts the bet. Those odds
also usually include a betting margin,
which is part of how sports books manage
risk and generate revenue. So when you
place a bet at a sports book, you are
generally betting into a price created
by the sports book itself. That is the
traditional sports betting model.
Prediction markets use contracts.
Prediction markets work differently.
Instead of betting on sports book odds,
users trade contracts based on
real-world events. Those contracts
usually ask a yes or no question. For
example, will a team win tonight? Will
Bitcoin reach a certain price? Will a
political event happen before a
deadline? A yes contract might trade at
60 cents while the no side trades around
40 cents. If the yes side is correct
when the market settles, that contract
usually resolves at $1. If it is wrong,
it resolves at zero. So instead of
saying what are the odds, prediction
market users are really asking, what is
this event contract worth right now? Who
sets the price? This is one of the
biggest differences. In a sports book,
the operator sets and adjusts the odds.
In a prediction market, the price is
shaped by traders. If more people buy
yes, the yes price can rise. If more
people move toward no, the no price can
rise. That means prediction markets are
usually more peer-to-peer. You are not
just taking a price from one central
sports book. You are trading in a market
where other users are buying and selling
contracts. This is why prediction market
prices can also act like a live signal
of public expectations, but that signal
is not perfect. Prices can still be
wrong, emotional, or affected by [music]
low liquidity. The language is
different. The terminology is also
different. Sports books talk about bets,
wagers, odds, and payouts. Prediction
markets talk about trades, contracts,
probabilities, and settlement. That may
sound like a small difference, but it
affects how users [music] think. In
sports betting, the focus is usually on
picking the outcome and taking the odds.
In prediction markets, the focus is also
on price movement. You may buy a
contract, sell it before the event ends,
or hold it until settlement. That
trading element is what makes prediction
markets feel closer to a financial
market than a traditional sports book.
The types of markets. Sports books are
mostly built around sports. They may
include pregame bets, live betting,
player props, parlays, and futures.
Prediction markets can include sports,
too, but they are usually broader. You
may find markets on politics, crypto,
economics, entertainment, technology,
weather, culture, and major news events.
So, the category range can be much
wider. This is one reason prediction
markets have grown quickly. They turn
many real-world events into tradeable
questions. Regulation and availability.
Another major difference is regulation.
Sports books are regulated as gambling
operators and availability depends
heavily on state or local betting laws.
Prediction markets can be regulated
differently because they are structured
around event contracts instead of
traditional bets. For example, some
platforms operate under financial or
commodities regulation rather than
[music] standard gambling regulation,
but this area is still changing quickly.
Availability can vary by platform,
state, country, and event category. So,
users should always check whether a
platform is legally available where they
live before signing up or trading. The
main risk difference. The risk also
feels different. At a sports book, your
bet either wins or loses based on the
outcome and the odds you accepted. In a
prediction market, the contract value
can move before the event settles. That
means you may be able to sell early if
the price moves in your favor, but you
can also lose value before the final
result if the market moves against you.
So, prediction markets add another
layer, timing. You are not only thinking
about who wins or what happens. also
thinking about whether the current
contract price makes sense. Common
beginner mistake. The biggest mistake is
treating prediction markets like sports
books with different branding. They are
not the same thing. If you come from
sports betting, you may be used to
looking for odds, but in prediction
markets, the key number is the contract
price. That price reflects implied
probability, possible upside, downside
risk, liquidity, and trader sentiment.
So, the better question is not just who
will win. It is, is this contract price
correctly for the risk? Conclusion. So,
prediction markets versus sports books,
what is the real difference?
>> [music]
>> Sports books offer odds for bets,
usually set by the operator. Prediction
markets offer event contracts with
prices shaped by traders. Sports books
are mainly built around sports betting.
Prediction markets can cover sports,
politics, crypto, economics, culture,
and much more. And while sports books
focus on placing a bet, prediction
markets add the ability to trade in and
out of positions before settlement.
prediction markets more flexible, but
also more complex. So, before using
either one, understand the structure,
the risks, the rules, and whether the
platform is available in your location.

future of prediction markets. For more

metadata.title: Prediction Markets vs Sports Betting: What is the difference?
metadata.author: Simple Betting Guides
metadata.shortDescription:
This beginner-friendly video explains the difference between prediction markets and sports betting in simple terms. You will learn how sports betting usually works through sportsbook odds, while prediction markets often work more like trading event contracts based on future outcomes.

We cover the basic difference between betting odds and Yes/No contracts, how probability is shown in each system, how payouts work, and why prediction market prices can suggest the market’s current estimate without guaranteeing what will happen.

0:00 - Introduction
0:24 - Betting odds vs Event contracts
0:42 - Odds example
0:58 - Event contract example
1:16 - Prices
1:34 - Usual events
1:52 - Probability
2:11 - Payout structure
2:30 - Risks
2:49 - Beginner mistake
3:08 - Recap

segments.text: Prediction markets and sports betting
can look similar at first.
In both cases, people place money on
something that may or may not happen.
But, the structure is not exactly the
same.
Sports betting is usually built around
betting odds from a sports book, while
prediction markets often work more like
trading contracts on future events.
Prediction markets versus sports
betting.
In sports betting, the sports book
usually offers odds on a match, and the
better chooses which side to bet on.
In a prediction market, traders usually
buy and sell contracts tied to a
specific event outcome, often yes or no.
So, instead of just taking odds, you are
trading an event contract. In a simple
sports bet, you might bet $10 on team A
at odds of two.
If team A wins, your bet returns $20
total.
If team A loses, you lose your stake.
The odds show both the possible payout
and the implied chance. In a prediction
market, the same idea might appear as a
question, will team A win?
If the yes contract costs 60 cents, the
market is roughly suggesting a 60%
chance.
If the event happens, a correct contract
usually settles at $1. If it does not
happen, it usually settles at zero. One
major difference is how prices are
formed.
In sports betting, the sports book sets
and adjusts the odds. In many prediction
markets, prices are shaped by traders
buying and selling contracts.
The platform may provide the market, but
the price is influenced by supply,
demand, and trader opinion. Sports
betting usually focuses on sports
events, who wins, how many points are
scored, or what happens during a game.
Prediction markets can include sports,
too, but they can also cover many other
future events like elections, economic
data, weather outcomes, or policy
decisions, depending on the platform.
Both systems can suggest probability,
but they show it differently.
Sports betting uses odds, so you usually
need to convert the odds into implied
probability.
Prediction markets often show prices
between zero and $1, so the price can be
easier to read as the market's rough
probability estimate. The payout
structure also feels different.
In sports betting, your return depends
on the odds and your stake.
In prediction markets, a contract often
has a fixed settlement value.
If you buy at 60 cents and it settles at
$1, your profit is the difference before
fees. If it settles at zero, you lose
what you paid. But, the risks are still
very real in both.
You can be wrong, you can overpay, you
can follow hype, and fees or spreads can
reduce your result.
Neither sports betting nor prediction
markets guarantee profit.
Both require careful thinking, risk
control, and realistic expectations. A
common beginner mistake is saying
prediction markets are just sports
betting with a different name.
They can overlap, especially when the
event is sports-related, but the
mechanics are different.
Sports betting is usually sports book
odds.
Prediction markets are usually tradable
event contracts. So, in simple terms,
sports betting usually means placing
bets through a sports book using odds.
Prediction markets usually mean trading
contracts based on future events.
They can both involve probability and
risk, but they are structured
differently, priced differently, and
sometimes cover very different kinds of
events. If this helped you understand
prediction markets versus sports
betting, like the video and subscribe
for more simple betting guides and
market explanations.

metadata.author: 🎓Profeissor.com🚀Digital Assets, AI & FinTech
metadata.shortDescription:
🔮#Prediction #Markets: 𝗖𝗙𝗧𝗖 🎯𝙀𝙫𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝘾𝙤𝙣𝙩𝙧𝙖𝙘𝙩𝙨 𝕡𝕦𝕓𝕝𝕚𝕔 𝕚𝕟𝕥𝕖𝕣𝕖𝕤𝕥 𝕒𝕟𝕒𝕝𝕪𝕤𝕚𝕤 🗝️Key takeaways from the 267‑page proposed rule👇
 
🧠𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘀?
Binary derivatives🎲  
✅ If a future event happens → you get paid
❌ If not → you get nothing
Event contracts are futures or swaps which fall within the CFTC's jurisdiction. A platform that offers event contracts to the public must generally register with the CFTC as a designated contract market (𝗗𝗖𝗠)
 
⚖️“𝗣𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁” 𝕊𝕡𝕖𝕔𝕚𝕒𝕝 ℙ𝕣𝕠𝕧𝕚𝕤𝕚𝕠𝕟
Under the Commodity Exchange Act, certain event contracts can be banned on DCMs if they "involve" the following "𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀" and are "contrary to the public interest”:
🚫Unlawful activity  
🚫Terrorism / assassination / war  
🚫Gaming
🚫Similar harmful activities
 
But what does “𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲” actually mean?🧐
👉CFTC says focus on the 𝗿𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝙉𝙊𝙏 the event contract itself or related trading activity
💡Examples:
❌Contract on whether a 𝕔𝕣𝕚𝕞𝕖 is committed = involves unlawful activity  
✅Contract on whether someone is convicted by a 𝕔𝕠𝕦𝕣𝕥 ≠ involve unlawful activity because court judgment is a lawful judicial act
 
🧩𝗖𝗙𝗧𝗖’𝘀 𝟯-𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁
1️⃣ Is it an event contract?  
2️⃣ Does it involve an enumerated activity?  
3️⃣ Is it contrary to public interest? (multi-factor, case-by-case analysis)
 
🏀𝗚𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 vs🎖️𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 
🎮𝗚𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 = sports, poker🍀  
🏆𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀 = elections, Nobel Prize, Oscars (𝙣𝙤𝙩 enumerated activities)
 
🌍𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁’𝘀 𝗢𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝗰𝗼𝗽𝗲?
CFTC says many event contracts fall outside the “public interest” Special Provision because they do 𝙣𝙤𝙩 "involve" enumerated activities.  E.g., event contracts referencing: 
✅ CPI / GDP  
✅ Interest rates  
✅ FX / currencies  
✅ Elections & political outcomes
 
👉But these are still subject to other CEA/CFTC requirements
 
📊 𝗣𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁 = 𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗝𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗛𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴
CFTC acknowledges that event contracts can:
📊 Aggregate market sentiment  
📊 Provide signals for decision-making  
📊 Support pricing even without direct #hedging use
E.g., trading volume on sports-based event contracts can generate useful economic signals (e.g. for nearby hotels)
 
⚙️𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀
CFTC will closely look at:
🔍 Objective & verifiable settlement data  
🛡️ Anti-manipulation safeguards  
🏗️ Exchange #compliance infrastructure  
📉 Risk of #insider trading
 
🔮𝗕𝗶𝗴 𝗣𝗶𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲
CFTC proposal is not just about event contracts. It’s about:
⚖️ Where #regulation draws the line
🧠 How markets price future uncertainty
🌐 Whether prediction markets go mainstream
 
And ultimately:
👉 Can regulated markets harness the “wisdom of crowds”?
👉 Without creating perverse incentives or social harm?
 
#CFTC #Derivatives #Regulation #FinReg #DigitalAssets #Markets #Risk #Innovation #Law🚀

segments.text: So, today we're going to take a look at
the US CFTC's recent 267-page proposed
rule on event contracts. The proposal
relates to how the CFTC will decide
whether certain event contracts are
contrary to the public interest and
therefore should not be listed on
CFTC-regulated prediction markets. This
is a very important topic because
prediction markets have gained
significant popularity in the United
States, and event contracts are now
being used by retail investors,
financial institutions, media
organizations, and other market
participants to express views about
future events,
and to aggregate information.
Now, by way of background, the CFTC
stands for the Commodity Futures Trading
Commission. It is the US federal agency
responsible for regulating the US
derivatives markets, including futures,
swaps, and certain listed options.
Now, the reason the CFTC is involved in
prediction markets is that many event
contracts that trade on these markets
are swaps or futures, which fall within
the CFTC's jurisdiction. Now, you can
take a look at one of my earlier videos
on prediction markets for some further
background information.
Now, event contracts are essentially
derivative contracts where the
settlement depends on whether or not a
future event occurs.
These contracts are often structured as
binary contracts. So, if the reference
event occurs, you receive a payment, and
if the reference event does not occur,
then you do not receive any payment.
Now, prediction markets are the markets
where event contracts are traded. In the
United States, a prediction market which
offers event contracts to the public
generally needs to be registered with
the CFTC as a designated contract market
or DCM.
A DCM is essentially a CFTC-regulated
exchange that offers trading of futures
[snorts] or swaps, including event
contracts. So, the CFTC's jurisdiction
over prediction markets comes from its
jurisdiction over futures and swaps
traded on CFTC registered DCMs.
Now, the particular statutory provision
that forms the basis of the CFTC's
proposal is section 5c subparagraph C5c
of the Commodity Exchange Act. The CFTC
refers to this provision as the special
rule.
The special rule states that the CFTC
may determine that certain event
contracts which involve certain
enumerated activities are contrary to
the public interest, which means that
they cannot be listed or made available
for clearing or trading on CFTC
regulated prediction markets.
These enumerated activities include any
activity that is unlawful under any US
federal or state law, terrorism,
assassination, war, gaming, or other
similar activity that the CFTC
determines to be contrary to the public
interest.
Now, the special provision has
historically raised many difficult
questions. For example, what does it
mean for an event contract to involve an
enumerated activity, such as gaming?
Does an election outcome-based event
contract involve gaming simply because
people are staking money on an uncertain
future outcome?
Does a contract linked to oil prices
involve war simply because oil prices
are sensitive to global armed conflict?
Now, the CFTC's proposed rule is
designed to answer these types of
questions.
At a high level, the proposal does two
main things.
First, it clarifies the scope of the
enumerated activities. Second, the
proposal sets out the factors that the
CFTC intends to consider in deciding
whether an in-scope event contract is
contrary to the public interest.
According to the CFTC, the special rule
requires a three-step analysis. Step one
is to ask whether the contract in
question is an event contract in the
first place. In other words, is it an
agreement, contract, transaction, or
swap in an excluded commodity that is
based upon an occurrence, the extent of
an occurrence, or a contingency. Now,
excluded commodity has a precise
definition in the Commodity Exchange
Act.
If the answer to the first question is
no, then the special rule does not
apply.
Step two is to ask whether the event
contract involves one of the enumerated
activities. So, the question is whether
the reference event is an unlawful
activity, terrorism, assassination, war,
gaming, or other similar activity. If
the answer is no, then again, the
special rule does not apply.
The third step is whether the contract
in question is contrary to the public
interest, and this will require a
case-by-case multi-factor analysis. Now,
one of the most important points in the
CFTC's proposal is how the CFTC
interprets the word involve as used in
the special provision.
The CFTC's focus is on whether the
reference event in the event contract is
an enumerated activity. Importantly, the
focus is not on whether the event
contract itself or the trading of the
event contract constitutes the
enumerated activity. This distinction is
very important. Take gaming as an
example. If you define gaming as staking
something of value on a contingent
outcome, then virtually every event
contract would constitute gaming because
every event contract involves staking
value on whether a future event happens.
That would make the gaming category
limitless and would make the other
categories of enumerated activities
effectively useless.
The CFTC says that that cannot be the
right way to interpret or read the law.
According to the CFTC, the correct
approach is to ask whether the
underlying reference event is itself a
gaming activity. This distinction is
central to the CFTC's proposal and its
proposed framework.
So, having provided a high-level
overview of the CFTC's overall
analytical framework, we can now go
through each of the enumerated
activities and discuss whether the
proposal provides any additional clarity
about its scope of application. And
after dealing with the scoping question,
we can then look at the public interest
factors set out in the CFTC's proposal.
So, let's start with the first
enumerated activity, which is unlawful
activity.
Here, the CFTC says that it is not
necessary to define the phrase "activity
that is unlawful under any federal or
state law."
Instead, the CFTC says that it will
focus on whether the reference event
itself is the unlawful activity.
For example, an event contract that
settles on whether a particular person
commits a crime would involve unlawful
activity. And this is because the
reference event is the crime itself.
In contrast, an event contract that
settles on whether a person is convicted
of securities fraud by a specific date
does not involve unlawful activity
because the reference event is the
court's conviction judgment, which is a
lawful judicial act and not an unlawful
activity. So, now let's turn to
terrorism, assassination, and war.
The CFTC proposes to interpret these
terms broadly.
For terrorism, the proposal focuses on
violent or destructive activities
occurring outside the United States with
an element of coercion or intimidation
and some relationship to political or
social groups or ideologies.
The CFTC also says terrorism can include
cyberterrorism and other non-physical
attacks that cause substantial
disruption or disruption as long as they
have the necessary coercive or
ideological element. For war, the CFTC
says that it does not require a formal
declaration of war. Instead, war can
include belligerent military activities
and violent activities by organized
groups. It may include missile strikes,
drone strikes, and civil wars. Again,
the reference event itself must
constitute war.
For example, an event contract that
settles on whether oil futures close
above a certain price does not involve
war, even though oil prices are
sensitive to military actions. This is
because movement of oil price itself is
not war.
The proposal also deals with facially
neutral contracts that can be satisfied
through multiple causal pathways.
For example, suppose an event contract
settles on whether a foreign government
facility remains functional as of a
certain date. On its face, the event
sounds neutral, but one pathway by which
the facility may cease from a functional
is war. So, under the CFTC's proposed
approach, that contract would involve
war unless the contract terms expressly
exclude the war pathway. So, now let's
turn to gaming. The CFTC proposes to
define gaming as an activity that has
three key elements. First, participants
engage in the activity for recreation or
to entertain others. Second, the
activity is governed by rules. And
third, the activity includes measurable
outcomes that depend on luck, skill, or
athletic ability.
So, gaming includes sports, e-sports,
chess, poker, and roulette. It also
includes games of pure chance, games of
skill, and games involving both chance
and skill.
But, the CFTC also draws a distinction
between games and contests. A contest is
an activity where participants compete
for a prize, award, or position based on
qualifications or merit displayed in
general or over an extended period.
The CFTC says that contests are not
gaming. So, political elections are not
gaming because an election's outcome
depends on voters' judgment about who
should hold office, not on luck, skill,
or athletic ability during a
recreational activity.
Similarly, the Nobel Prize and the
Academy Awards are contests, not games.
Having clarified the scope of enumerated
activities, the CFTC gives examples of
event contracts that generally fall
outside the special rule altogether
because they do not involve any
enumerated activity. Examples of these
out-of-scope event contracts include
contracts that are based on economic
indicators,
financial indicators, and foreign
exchange rates or currencies.
Out-of-scope event contracts also
include those that are based on
political election results or other
political outcomes such as legislative
votes or political appointments. It's
important to note that these contracts
may still be subject to other Commodity
Exchange Act and CFTC regulatory
requirements, but they do not trigger
the public interest analysis under the
special rule. So now that we have dealt
with the scoping issue, we can move to
the final part of the CFTC's three-step
analysis, which is the public interest
analysis.
The CFTC proposes a multi-factor
approach. And the general public
interest factors set out in the CFTC's
proposal apply to all event contracts
that involve enumerated activities.
The first general factor is whether the
contract provides meaningful hedging or
price basing utility, yields
economically, financially, or
commercially useful information, or
promotes innovation and fair
competition. Importantly, the CFTC is
not saying that an event contract must
be used for hedging in order to pass the
public interest test. The CFTC instead
recognizes that prediction markets can
have information aggregation value and
[clears throat] can help reveal market
sentiment. That information may be
useful in commercial decision-making
even if the contract itself is not
directly used as a hedge.
The second general factor is whether
meaningful information about the
underlying event is available to the
broader market. If meaningful insight is
concentrated in one person or a very
small group of insiders who are legally
prohibited from trading, then the
contract may not benefit from the wisdom
of the crowds. The third general factor
is market integrity. And here, the CFTC
will consider whether the contract
presents a particular risk of
manipulation or market disruption.
Another general factor is whether the
prediction market has the compliance and
self-regulatory infrastructure to
administer the event contract properly.
Now, in addition to these general public
interest factors, the CFTC also proposes
some specific factors for particular
enumerated activities.
For the unlawful activity enumerated
activity, the basic approach is that if
a contract settles on whether a specific
person commits a specific crime, then
that may incentivize wrongdoing and to
raise manipulation concerns. Having said
this, the CFTC also notes that contracts
based on aggregate crime rates may have
information utility for insurance,
demographic analysis, or economic
planning.
Now, in terms of terrorism,
assassination, or war, the CFTC's
approach is much stricter. The specific
public interest factors relate to
national security risk, inside
information, and facilitation of harmful
conduct. The CFTC is concerned that
trading in these contracts may create
misleading market signals, distract law
enforcement efforts, or may be
manipulated by bad actors.
It is also concerned that people with
genuine insight into the event are often
insiders with legal duties of
confidentiality or duties to report the
information to authorities. These people
should not be trading on that
information. Finally, for gaming, the
CFTC takes a more nuanced approach. The
CFTC says that event contracts involving
games that depend entirely on random
chance are highly likely to be contrary
to the public interest.
For sports, the CFTC identifies factors
that support a positive public interest
finding.
Contracts based on aggregate outcomes of
professional or collegiate sports are
generally less concerning from a public
interest perspective. And if the
contract settles by reference to a
publicly reported, league verified, or
other objectively determinable data,
then that is helpful as well.
The CFTC also likes sports that have
established integrity frameworks, such
as recognized governing bodies,
published rules, and disciplinary
procedures.
The CFTC's proposal identifies several
sports-related contracts that are likely
to give rise to public interest
concerns, such as contracts that are
based on player injuries or physical
altercations during a game.
Contracts based on a referee's judgment
call or a player's discreet actions are
also problematic. The CFTC's concern
here is that a single player or official
may have too much ability to affect the
settlement outcome of the event
contract.

This is a very important topic because prediction markets have gained significant popularity in the United States, and event contracts are now being used by retail investors, financial institutions, media organizations, and other market participants to express views about future events, and to aggregate information. Now, by way of background, the CFTC stands for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. It is the US federal agency responsible for regulating the US derivatives markets, including futures, swaps, and certain listed options. Now, the reason the CFTC is involved in prediction markets is that many event contracts that trade on these markets are swaps or futures, which fall within the CFTC's jurisdiction. Now, you can take a look at one of my earlier videos on prediction markets for some further background information. Now, event contracts are essentially derivative contracts where the settlement depends on whether or not a future event occurs. These contracts are often structured as binary contracts. So, if the reference event occurs, you receive a payment, and if the reference event does not occur, then you do not receive any payment. Now, prediction markets are the markets where event contracts are traded. In the United States, a prediction market which offers event contracts to the public generally needs to be registered with the CFTC as a designated contract market or DCM. A DCM is essentially a CFTC-regulated exchange that offers trading of futures [snorts] or swaps, including event contracts. So, the CFTC's jurisdiction over prediction markets comes from its jurisdiction over futures and swaps traded on CFTC registered DCMs. Now, the particular statutory provision that forms the basis of the CFTC's proposal is section 5c subparagraph C5c of the Commodity Exchange Act. The CFTC refers to this provision as the special rule. The special rule states that the CFTC may determine that certain event contracts which involve certain enumerated activities are contrary to the public interest, which means that they cannot be listed or made available for clearing or trading on CFTC regulated prediction markets. Does an election outcome-based event contract involve gaming simply because people are staking money on an uncertain future outcome? Does a contract linked to oil prices involve war simply because oil prices are sensitive to global armed conflict? Now, the CFTC's proposed rule is designed to answer these types of questions. Second, the proposal sets out the factors that the CFTC intends to consider in deciding whether an in-scope event contract is contrary to the public interest. Now, excluded commodity has a precise definition in the Commodity Exchange Act. If the answer to the first question is no, then the special rule does not apply. Step two is to ask whether the event contract involves one of the enumerated activities. So, the question is whether the reference event is an unlawful activity, terrorism, assassination, war, gaming, or other similar activity. If the answer is no, then again, the special rule does not apply. The third step is whether the contract in question is contrary to the public interest, and this will require a case-by-case multi-factor analysis. Now, one of the most important points in the CFTC's proposal is how the CFTC interprets the word involve as used in the special provision. The CFTC's focus is on whether the reference event in the event contract is an enumerated activity. Importantly, the focus is not on whether the event contract itself or the trading of the event contract constitutes the enumerated activity. This distinction is very important. Take gaming as an example. If you define gaming as staking something of value on a contingent outcome, then virtually every event contract would constitute gaming because every event contract involves staking value on whether a future event happens. That would make the gaming category limitless and would make the other categories of enumerated activities effectively useless. The CFTC says that that cannot be the right way to interpret or read the law. According to the CFTC, the correct approach is to ask whether the underlying reference event is itself a gaming activity. This distinction is central to the CFTC's proposal and its proposed framework. So, having provided a high-level overview of the CFTC's overall analytical framework, we can now go through each of the enumerated activities and discuss whether the proposal provides any additional clarity about its scope of application.
