segments.text: A few days ago, the US CFTC made two
very important announcements on
prediction markets.
Today, we're going to take a look at
what they are and consider their
implications.
First of all, what are prediction
markets? Essentially, prediction markets
are regulated derivatives markets where
event contracts are listed and traded.
And who is the CFTC? Well, the CFTC
stands for Commodity Futures Trading
Commission. It is essentially a US
federal agency that is in charge with
regulating the US futures market, the US
market, and also certain listed options.
The CFTC recently issued an advanced
notice of proposed rulemaking, ANPR, in
relation to prediction markets. On the
same day, the CFTC also published a
staff advisory on prediction markets.
These two announcements are important
because they reaffirm the CFTC's
exclusive jurisdiction over prediction
markets and signals regulatory
recalibration in the future. What
exactly are prediction markets? Well,
prediction markets are essentially
markets whereby participants buy and
sell event contracts based on whether a
future event occurs. The CFTC describes
prediction markets as functioning as
information aggregation vehicles because
the contract prices on these markets
essentially reflect the market's
collective view of the probability of a
particular event. And this information
can be used for price discovery,
information aggregation, and also risk
transfer. In other words, somebody with
exposure to that particular event can
purchase event contracts on a prediction
market for hedging purposes. The
prediction markets are markets on which
event contracts are traded. So, what are
event contracts? Basically, event
contracts are derivative contracts
whereby the settlement is dependent on
whether or not a future outcome occurs.
In other words, the payoff under the
contract depends on whether or not a
future event takes place. And these are
often structured as binary yes or no
outcomes, which means that the payoff is
either a fixed amount if the future
event occurs or zero if the future event
does not occur. So, why is the CFTC
paying so much attention to prediction
markets? One reason is because these
markets are very large and also growing
at an accelerating rate. For example,
the aggregate trading volume in 2025 was
$64 billion
and the aggregate trading volume in 2026
is projected to grow to over 300 billion
US dollars. The US CFTC has also noticed
rapid growth in the following metrics:
trading volumes, the diversity of
underlying event contracts, and also
lots more applications to the CFTC to
operate prediction markets. The CFTC
regulates prediction markets pursuant to
the US Commodity Exchange Act, CEA.
According to this law, platforms that
offer event contracts to the public must
register with the CFTC as designated
contract markets or DCMs. And more
specifically, the CFTC has exclusive
jurisdiction over futures and swaps
traded on DCMs. What is the specific
legal basis for the CFTC's jurisdiction
over event contracts? Well, as I
mentioned before, the CFTC has
jurisdiction over swaps and futures. And
depending on how it is structured, an
event contract can either constitute a
swap or a futures contract as defined in
the Commodity Exchange Act. I've set out
the definitions here on the screen. As
you can see, the term swaps is very
broadly defined to include any agreement
that provides for payment which depends
on the occurrence or non-occurrence of
an event or contingency that has
potential financial, economic, or
commercial consequence. This is a broad
definition which can capture quite a lot
of event contracts. Similarly, the CFTC
also has jurisdiction over futures
contracts on excluded commodities. And
the term excluded commodities is also
very broadly defined to include any
contingency that is beyond the control
of the parties, which also has
financial, commercial, or economic
consequence. So, one of the reasons why
prediction markets have attracted quite
a bit of controversy in the United
States is because lots of event
contracts are in fact based on the
outcomes of sports events or political
events. So, a real question exists as to
whether there is an actual distinction
between event contracts on the one hand
and gambling on the other. Now,
according to the CFTC, it is important
to distinguish between the two, and
here's why. The CFTC explains that event
contracts serve price discovery and risk
management purposes, and that the
market-based probability implied in the
pricing of these contracts provide
useful economic data. In addition, event
contracts are traded on CFTC-regulated
centralized exchanges.
In contrast, gambling focuses on
entertainment. It is for speculative
purposes only with no real economic
purpose. In addition, gambling is
typically regulated in the United States
by the various US states. So, as you can
see from this quote by the CFTC
chairman, the CFTC believes that event
contracts have important economic
purposes and also fall squarely within
the CFTC's exclusive jurisdiction, which
means that only the CFTC can regulate
prediction markets and event contracts,
and it is not for the US states to
regulate them as gambling contracts.
As I mentioned earlier, prediction
markets in the United States must
generally register with the CFTC as
designated contract markets or DCMs.
Now, DCMs are CFTC-regulated exchanges
that's available to both retail and
institutional traders.
Now, under the CEA, DCMs must comply
with 23 statutory core principles, and
these core principles reflect the role
that DCMs play in promoting the
integrity of the US derivatives market,
and they essentially require DCMs to
establish and enforce trading rules, to
monitor trading activity, and also to
serve as frontline self-regulatory
organizations.
In addition, whenever a DCM wants to
list a new contract, such as an event
contract, it must either go through a
self-certification process or seek the
CFTC's approval. The 23 DCM core
principles touch on quite a broad range
of topics relating to market integrity,
manipulation prevention, position
limits, transparent trading, governance,
conflicts management, dispute
resolution, financial resources, system
safeguards, and many other topics. And
all of these are designed to ensure the
integrity of the US derivatives market.
In addition to these general core
principles, the CA contains a provision
that specifically relates to event
contracts. And this provision basically
allows the CFTC to prohibit the listing
or trading of any event contract that
the CFTC considers to be contrary to the
public interest. And here, the statute
specifically calls out certain types of
activities that could potentially be
contrary to the public interest, such as
activities that are unlawful, that
relate to terrorism, assassination, war,
gaming, or other similar activities. So,
now let's take a look at the CFTC's
advance notice of proposed rulemaking,
AMPR, on prediction markets. Now, AMPR
is essentially a preliminary document
that US federal regulators sometimes
publish before formal rulemaking. And
its purpose is to gather input and data
from the public before the regulator
puts pen to paper.
Now, by way of background, back in 2024,
under the previous US administration,
the CFTC at that time proposed some
rules in relation to prediction markets
already. And under those proposed rules,
the CFTC actually wanted to prohibit
certain sports and political event-based
event contracts because the CFTC at the
time considered them to be inconsistent
with the public interest. Now, under the
new administration, the CFTC has in fact
withdrawn those proposals, and it is now
taking a fresh look at prediction
markets and looking at how the statute
and its its existing rulebook should
apply to prediction markets. Now, given
the fact that the purpose of the AMPR is
for the CFTC to gather data and
information from the public before
commencing any formal rulemaking, it's
not surprising that the CFTC has raised
14 questions on how to regulate
prediction markets. A lot of these
questions relate to how the DCM core
principles should apply to prediction
markets. They also relate to which types
of event contracts are contrary to the
public interest. And in this context,
the CFTC specifically mentions the
statutory provision which refers to
event contracts based on war and
terrorism. And here, the CFTC asked some
specific questions. For example, the
CFTC asked whether terrorism should
include cyberterrorism, and if so, how
to distinguish between cyberterrorism on
the one hand and other types of
cyberattacks on the other. The CFTC also
asked the question about the scope of
the concept of war. Does war include all
types of military actions, or are there
certain types of military actions that
do not constitute war? And how to
distinguish between war on the one hand
and civil unrest on the other? So, these
are all very important questions for the
CFTC and for members of the public to
consider. Interestingly, in the AMPR,
the CFTC also asked a number of
questions in relation to
blockchain-based prediction markets. And
this is definitely a trend we are seeing
whereby a lot of crypto firms are
entering into the prediction market
space. So, now let's turn to the second
important document published by the CFTC
on prediction markets. And this is the
staff advisory published by the Division
of Market Oversight. Now, unlike the
AMPR, which really signals a future
potential direction of CFTC rule-making,
the staff advisory is really about
communicating the CFTC staff's current
views on the listing and trading of
event contracts. And importantly, it is
not intended to create any binding rules
or regulations or to amend any existing
rules or regulations, but rather convey
how the staff is currently thinking
about event contracts and the
application of existing rules and
regulations to these contracts.
One of the purposes of the staff
advisory is to reiterate the importance
of compliance and to communicate the
CFTC staff's regulatory and supervisory
expectations for DCMs in relation to a
number of core principles, which are
particularly relevant to prediction
markets and event contracts, and these
are listed on the slide. The CFTC staff
also communicated their expectations in
terms of new product procedures that
DCMs would follow in relation to event
contracts. And also, the staff advisory
urges DCMs to be proactive frontline
regulators when it comes to event
contracts and to engage the CFTC staff
early in relation to any new types of
event contracts that they are
considering listing on their exchanges.
The CFTC staff advisory specifically
calls out sports-related events
contracts as something that warrants
special attention by DCMs. They explain
that there's heightened manipulation and
integrity risks associated with
sports-related events contracts because
often a small group of athletes can have
concentrated control over outcomes and
thereby assert insider influence. So,
it's very important for DCMs to ensure
that the outcomes of these
sports-related event contracts are
objectively determinable and not easily
manipulated or influenced. It's
therefore important for DCMs to engage
in active monitoring and to work with
sports leagues and other governing
bodies to understand their integrity
frameworks and also any information
asymmetries. So, what are some of the
big picture takeaways from the CFTC's
recent announcements on prediction
markets?
First of all, the fact that the CFTC is
paying so much attention to this area is
an indication that prediction markets
are becoming mainstream.
The CFTC, under the current
administration, is open to innovation
and it is open to developing
fit-for-purpose rules and regulations on
prediction markets and event contracts.
These rules will likely reassert the
CFTC's exclusive jurisdiction over these
markets and also focus on the proper
application of the DCM core principles
to prediction markets and event
contracts.
The next phase of CFTC rulemaking will
likely be shaped by industry input and
data. Therefore, it's important for
market participants to communicate their
views to the CFTC.

metadata.title: View from the CFTC ft. CFTC Director of Enforcement David Miller & CNN | NEXTPredict NYC 2026
metadata.author: NEXTPredict
metadata.shortDescription:
A direct conversation with the regulator on the evolving framework for event contracts. This session will explore the CFTC's enforcement priorities, how existing laws are being applied to prediction markets, and where the lines are being drawn around insider trading and market manipulation. What are the regulator's key concerns, what is the current state of play, and how much regulatory activity is happening behind the scenes? What should the industry expect next?

Speakers:
• Marshall Cohen, Senior Reporter, CNN (moderator)
• David Miller, Director of Enforcement, CFTC

Recorded live at NEXTPredict Summit New York 2026, Day 1 (Thursday, October 22), The Summit (Main Stage), Convene at 30 Hudson Yards.

The World's Prediction Markets Summit lands in New York, over two days with 2,500 business leaders from across the world who decide the future of this emerging industry. Conveniently placed two weeks before the US midterm elections, the next big moment for the prediction markets industry will be broadcast from Convene Hudson Yards on October 22-23.

More from NEXTPredict: https://nextpredict.io

segments.text: All right, hello everybody.
Thrilled that you are all with us today.
I'm Marshall Cohen, I'm a senior
reporter at CNN. I cover prediction
markets.
Uh right here at Hudson Yards actually,
CNN offices are just upstairs. Uh with
me is David Miller from the CFTC. Uh let
me tell the crowd a little bit about
your background. David Miller, the
director of enforcement at the Commodity
Futures Trading Commission.
Of course, we all know that's the
federal agency that regulates prediction
markets.
He was appointed earlier this year by
CFTC Chairman Mike Selig. Before joining
the agency, David was a federal
prosecutor at Main Justice, at the DOJ,
and at SDNY here in Manhattan. And
before [snorts] that, he also was
assistant general counsel at the CIA.
David, very happy to have you here.
Uh we got 30 minutes. We got so much to
cover. It's been a huge year for the
CFTC when it comes to prediction
markets.
As we get toward the end of the year
here, what do you think is the single
most important action that the agency
has taken this year under Trump, under
Chairman Selig, when it comes to this
industry?

conference for having me here. Thank
you, Marshall, for moderating this. Um
just as a disclaimer, uh my views are my
own and don't necessarily represent that
of the commission or its staff. Um this
is obviously been a huge year for
prediction markets, and we at the CFTC
are very pro-innovation. Um we
appreciate everything that our

So to the extent that something's not violating insider trading law, it could still be market manipulation, and we've brought cases in that area. So I think if you sort of look at what we have done in the last 6 to 8 months since I was appointed, and and obviously this year since you know, Chairman Selig has taken the role, is we're doing our job. We're policing fraud, abuse, manipulation in all of our markets, including the prediction markets. >> Okay. Those cases of course still pending. Both guys there have pleaded not guilty and totally deny wrongdoing, but notable enforcement actions there. You know, I wanted to ask you about your background a little bit. A lot of people in this space they're tech guys, they're data nerds. Very few of them prosecuted terrorists >> [laughter] >> before getting into the prediction space. So what from that part of your career what lessons from that part of your career have you carried over into this new role? >> Yeah, so I started my career as a lawyer actually as a securities fraud lawyer, a securities litigator, and and then I wound up in the national security world at CIA and then at DOJ headquarters as a terrorism prosecutor. But when I moved back up to New York to join the Southern District of New York, I actually spent most of my time in that office in the securities and commodities fraud unit. So I actually prosecuted a ton of case insider trading case. I've been prosecuting and defending insider trading cases for 15 20 years. And and so when I left that office, I immediately got into crypto. And I was a partner at two global law firms before I rejoined the government. And and so I've been representing financial institutions, crypto exchanges, funds, individuals in the crypto enforcement space now for a decade. So it wasn't a big step for me to be involved in this. >> Oh, of course. >> Yeah. >> It's it's a interesting wrinkle in the realm. >> But I I didn't answer your question. To answer the question about what what lessons? I mean, terrorism cases, especially the international terrorism cases that I was involved in prosecuting many years ago, are highly complex, detailed cases, much more complex than most federal criminal cases. And so being able to sort of understand from a prosecutor's standpoint how things play out down the road, especially if you're dealing with national security and classified information, takes a certain skill and something you learn. And I think look, you know, I brought that skill set over to when I was a prosecutor and as a defense lawyer in the securities and commodities fraud sphere, be it for crypto or any other kind of technology. >> So you said a few moments ago and you've said this before that you feel like there are misconceptions out there about insider trading. So what what do you think are the myths? >> Yeah. >> And who's who's promoting those myths? >> Well, I don't know that anybody any group is necessarily promoting it. To answer the last part of that question first. I just think there's a misunderstanding, and so bear with me as I explain. Um so, insider trading law essentially is as a general matter a judicially interpreted offense, um court-made law essentially. There's no statute federal statute that says this is these are the elements of insider trading and this is how you can prosecute. It doesn't exist. What there is, however, are anti-fraud anti-manipulation statutes under the securities laws and the commodities laws. And so, the securities laws have been around for a while, and there's something called Section 10b and SEC Rule 10b-5 that basically say you can't engage in fraud and manipulation in connection with the purchase or sale of a security. And courts have said insider trading is fraud, okay? The under Dodd-Frank and the Commodity Exchange Act, which governs the commodities and derivatives markets, basically adopted a new statute that reads exactly like the securities statute, essentially importing that law for >> for derivatives. >> for derivatives and commodities, exactly. >> And the of course the event contracts that we all know so well. >> All right, and and and so, as you know, our view is that most event contracts are swaps. Swaps are a derivative, they're under what's called Section 6c and Rule 181, which are basically the same as 10b and 10b-5 in the securities realm. Therefore, insider trading law applies. Now, what people don't get is that insider trading basically is about a breach of duty. So, whether it's under what's called the classical theory, you're an insider at a company and you have material nonpublic information. So, you have duty to shareholders not to trade against them, okay? Or, as courts have said, the misappropriation theory, which is what applies in our markets into the prediction markets, which is you have a duty to the source of whatever material nonpublic information you're imparted with. That could be your employer, could be if you're a government employee, the government or the people of the United States. And if you breach that duty by misappropriating that material nonpublic information and trading or tipping on it, you're not supposed to do that. It's a confidential information, right? Then and you do that in connection with whether it's a commodity or some kind of derivative then contract IE a swap, you are violating the misappropriation theory of insider trading. Now, one caveat that I always like to give when I talk about insider trading, >> [snorts] >> especially in our markets. Our markets really started right as the commodity futures trading commission has its roots in agriculture, right? That's where the markets start in agricultural markets. And we as the law has said and as we believe, you know, we want people to hedge with their own information, okay? So, if you were an agricultural farming collective and you were concerned about your crop for the season, as we have for decades now, we want you to be able to hedge against that thing. >> That's your own secret. >> It's Well, it could be it could be your own your own material nonpublic >> Or it could be something publicly observable. >> Could be publicly, but it could be your own and so you're not you're not breaching a duty yourself by trading on that information. Now, even if though you have no insider trading cuz you're not breaching a duty to yourself, you could still have market manipulation. So, if I know something and I'm allowed for whatever reason to trade on it cuz it's my own information, but I go out into the marketplace and I start making public statements that are misrepresentations or otherwise lies and then I move the market and create artificial forces of supply and demand by doing so, that's market manipulation. So, even if it's not insider trading, it's still be market exactly. >> Let me ask you a hypothetical here. This is a question that people in my newsroom have asked me >> Okay. >> ever since I started covering these markets cuz we're getting to the the breach of duty the and the duty of confidentiality. Everyone understands that if you're a member of the military and you're on that helicopter hovering above Nicolas Maduro compound in Venezuela, you cannot open up your phone, go on Polymarket and trade on his ouster because you're a member of the military, it's classified information, you have a duty of confidentiality to the US government, right? >> As a general matter, of course. >> Yes. >> Without talking about any specific case. >> Of course. Of course. But flip the script. What if you are Nicolas Maduro in the compound looking up and publicly observing, "Holy crap, these helicopters, I think they're coming for me. Let me quickly get out my phone and bet that I'm going to be out as president of Venezuela." Based off the publicly observable stuff. >> Is this money to pay your lawyers? Is that legal? >> With that He does He In that case, he wouldn't have a duty to anybody. >> No. >> So I know it's kind of crazy, but it it's a serious question about where those lines are. How would that How would that go? >> No, it's a good It's a good question, Mark. There's two parts to this. One is putting aside the Commodity Exchange Act, exchanges as registered entities with us have certain responsibilities and obligations in matching up what's called the core principles, okay, which are set out in statute and regulation. And um exchanges consistent with that have rules. And some exchanges do have rules that if you possess the information that is critical for that event contract, you know, because it's your knowledge, you're the subject of it, you're not supposed to trade. Now, that doesn't mean that you're breaking federal law by doing that. >> It's an agent's It's a rule of a company. >> Exactly. Exactly. Now, they can bring, you know, they can fine you and all that, but in terms of >> do it. >> Maybe. Um uh so, again, as long as he's not manipulating the market in any way, >> possibly. Very fascinating. Okay, >> we are less than 2 weeks away from the midterm elections. We have seen this year already scandals involving political candidates betting on their own races uh on prediction markets and being punished by the prediction market companies for doing so. Uh are there I know you can't speak about specific investigations that I would never ask you to do that, but big picture, is the agency investigating any midterms related activity for potential manipulation or insider trading? >> Well, I'm not going to go specific on the midterms, but I will say that um we do investigate and have investigated um and may have open investigations about some candidates who have um uh you know, placed trades on contracts that are based on their own elections because those particular candidates have made statements um uh that are inconsistent with the truth. And it doesn't have to be even just a candidate for office, right? I mean, we brought an action this summer against a former congressman >> Right. George Santos. >> for making misrepresentations um with respect to his appearance >> at a particular hearing. Right. So, but so, what about political candidates campaign staff? Is that something that the agency's looking at because we've already seen examples from the prediction market companies saying, "Hey, this is happening." >> I'll I'll say this. We have seen um coverage about that exact scenario that you talked about, including um campaign staff with knowledge of internal polling, for example, um trading on event contracts. I can't speak to any particular investigations. I'll say this, going back to what Like said a few minutes ago. If you're an employee, be it a campaign staffer or working for a company or whatever it is, odds are that you signed some kind of employment agreement at some point that provides a duty of confidentiality. If you go and you take that information and go and trade on an event contract that's premised upon your job, your candidate's role, odds are you're misappropriating that information and you're committing insider trading and we're going to look at that and we'll come after you if that's the case. >> Okay, so the message to all campaign staff and candidates, don't bet on your races. >> I mean, look, again, I I it's hard to for me to speak in abstract. I'll just say that I've been pretty clear in my public statements about what's in bounds and what's not, of course. >> Any special plans for election night, November 3rd? I mean, thousands, maybe tens of thousands of markets are going to be settled that day on the on the prediction companies. Uh results will be pouring in. There's tons of opportunities for manipulation, things Are you guys the on the enforcement team going to be up all night watching the results and policing the markets or >> We're watching. We have a robust surveillance capability at the agency and not only internally, but obviously working with the exchanges and other entities and we are keenly aware of these issues. So, we're watching. >> Okay, November 3rd, look out. So, got to ask you about this big Bloomberg story that came out last week. Uh really made some waves and it was it was talking about your own division, the enforcement division. So, I don't want to make sure I get this right, too. Bloomberg's story said that there was a CFTC investigation into suspicious oil futures trading that happened right before President Trump made some market-moving announcements about Iran. This was earlier this year. I'm sure everybody in this room knows what I'm talking about because it was a huge story. People were stunned by that with potentially many, many millions of dollars changing hands right before those announcements from the president about Iran and oil. Bloomberg reported that in a quote highly unusual move, a senior political appointee and an advisor to chairman Mike Selig asked career staff at the agency to retract a referral that called for a more robust investigation into those futures trades. Now, I saw Mike Selig last week on Fox pushing back very aggressively against this. I don't care so much about the tit-for-tat between the CFTC and Bloomberg. We just want to know what happened. >> Well, look, there's only so so much I can say, especially about an open investigation, but let me say this. And And some of this is consistent with what Chairman Selig did say on CNBC. First, there are factual inaccuracies in that Bloomberg article. >> Um such as? >> I'm not going to get into details. There are There are factual inaccuracies. Number one. Number two is we have a robust investigation, and it's not necessarily the norm for us to acknowledge that. Chairman Selig has said that. Um I'm reiterating it. And number three, that we've had an investigation regarding this issue from the beginning. And um you know, the Bloomberg article talks about events that took place I I I think it may have been in April or whatever. I'll just say that we had an investigation in the division of enforcement from the beginning. Um we are here to do our job, uh which includes policing insider trading in the markets, including the energy and oil markets. And to the extent that um people think that uh the division of enforcement or myself are shrinking violets and we're not doing their job, they are sorely mistaken. >> Okay. Investigation's underway into the oil futures trades. >> We [clears throat] have open investigations. >> All right. Let's talk about another investigation that's not open, closed. Uh the teleprompter guy, I'm sure everybody knows what I'm referring to here, the former White House teleprompter operator Gabriel Perez, a long-time aid to President Trump. He uh was caught uh on Kalshi trading on mentioned markets for the president's speeches. Uh I should point out just for full disclosure, I work for CNN. CNN has a partnership with Kalshi. Uh we use their data to cover some major events, but they don't influence our coverage and we don't trade on prediction platforms. So, the CFTC said in its settlement with Perez that he owed a duty of trust and confidentiality to the United States government and that he breached those duties. That's the words of the agency. Uh and he did so 50 times with these trades, according to the settlement. So, for those egregious actions, breaching your duty of trust to the US government, he paid a 60,000 65,000 dollar fine. I know he cooperated with the investigation and months before this all came out, you guys updated the rules for the types of uh benefits you can get from cooperating, but I want you to defend this deal. Why do you think 65,000 dollars for breaching your duty of confidence to the government, insider trading and manipulation from inside the White House, why is that only uh 65,000 dollar fine? >> Well, let me >> And no apparent Justice Department prosecution. >> Well, first on the last part, I can't speak for the Department of Justice, of course, full stop. Um >> No apparent investigation though, as far as >> Again, I can't I can't speak >> know, but why why 65K here? >> So, let let me there's a lot there to unpack. Um so, first, as we set forth in the order, it was serious conduct um and and he did breach his duties to the US government, to the people of the United States under what's called the STOCK Act as well as something called the Eddie Murphy rule which we we call it affectionately which generates from Trading Places, yeah. Um and and again it's about as I said earlier with respect to the misappropriation theory it's about a breach of duty, right? So that lays the foundation for why this is insider trading and material nonpublic information. Um before I get to sort of the details of the cooperation I want to say this. This action shows that we are serious about policing insider trading regardless of who you are. And I know there is a lot of stories out there. There's a narrative that gets pushed. Look at this case and look what we did, okay? >> Because he works for the for President Trump. >> He was >> Because he works for the Trump White House. >> He he was a relatively senior person within the White House, okay? And he had been as we pointed out uh in the order with campaigns and the president for a long time. So I'll just say that. Um with respect to the the terms of the settlement. So my recollection is Mr. Perez gained approximately 100 and I don't want to say 107,000 or something like that. >> Yeah, over right around 100K. >> Yeah. Um so so there was disgorgement obviously had to pay it back, okay? >> Right. >> Um hold on. I'll get to the panel. >> unlawful trades. >> Yeah, hold on. I'm getting to it. >> business making that money in the first place. >> I'm getting to it. >> Okay. >> So then there's the penalty, the monetary penalty, right? And so the monetary penalty was premised on a what we call a one-time penalty, okay? So that's basically the value of the gain, all right? But discounted under our new cooperation policy. So in May um one of my sort of first priorities was to issue a new cooperation advisory because frankly the prior ones were extremely confusing. um Um, last year there was like a 12 cell matrix and nobody could figure it out. So, I wanted this to be clear and transparent consistent with the chairman's views, my views on the way the enforcement division is supposed to interact with the public uh in being transparent and pro-innovation, but also being tough in policing fraud. And there is different tiers within that cooperation policy and it's actually consistent with the Department of Justice policy uh in many ways. Um, but one of the you know, the tiers is a path for what's called a declination. There's a near miss category and there's a third category. Mr. Perez was in the third category, okay, which provides as a general matter that if you cooperate and remediate and self-report or not self-report, cooperate and remediate, excuse me, then you can have up to a >> said. How she said they caught him and they reported to you. >> he did not self-report. So, up to a 25% discount >> Yeah. >> absent extenuating circumstances. As we set forth and there's a footnote in that cooperation advisory, Mr. Perez's cooperation was exemplary for many reasons including admissions and things and pointing to certain places and assisting the commission in resolving the action. >> that that that that makes sense to some. To others, I've spoken to some former CFTC commissioners that said they just don't think that's enough deterrents. But anyway, we've we've got uh more topics to get to. Quickly though, did the White House approve that deal? >> Uh, you look, I'm not going to speak to in internal discussions with the White House or anything. I'll just say this. We have a commission process internally that involves um getting approval from the commission and there's internal deliberations and memo writing that's required okay. Um, and settlements are done with respect to the commission. >> So, the CFTC approved a license switching gears here for Polymarket US uh to operate in the United States. They acquired a company that had a US license and now Polymarket operates in the US with oversight from the CFTC, but obviously Polymarket also has its enormous offshore platform that has all kinds of markets on there that could never fly in the US. Markets on war, markets on Iran. It's on their offshore site for a reason. I assume that they'd get their license pulled if they tried to put those on the US platform, but just from a big picture perspective, how is the CFTC okay with licensing a company that has its sort of clean US version over here, but we all know that it has its offshore site on the outside where they have markets that are illegal under federal law. How How does that work? >> That's a leading question if I've ever heard one. So >> it's a fair question. >> So uh >> Because it's like, yes, you know, you're wearing your US uniform today and I'm dealing with the regulator here, but after our meeting, I'm going to put on my international uniform and there are very popular markets, but those are not permissible markets. >> So let me let me say a few things about Polymarket. Um number one, obviously, they have a registered entity um that is an entity with respect that largely relates to sports event contracts within the United States. >> Yeah. >> Um they do have the dot com international platform. Uh I don't want to get into particulars about what's right and what's wrong. There's been a lot of reporting about potential investigations that we may or may not have with respect to Polymarket. But I will point to this. Um in the Van Dyke case that you mentioned and also the Spang Nulo >> trader and the Google guy. >> Um you know, the the trading as alleged occurred on the Polymarket international platform for both of those cases. If you look at our complaints, you will see that we established jurisdiction venue in the Southern District of New York. >> Right. >> Notwithstanding the fact that um those trades took place on the polymarket.com platform. I will leave it at that. >> Understood. Uh a lot of people saw last week that on the Polymarket international site for a couple weeks they had a market on whether any of the people uh at the fraternity in Cornell would be charged with rape. Have you heard about these markets on >> Yeah. They're It was taken down. Um it's the offshore site, so it's not really on the US entity, but was that something that has been of any discussion at the agency? Have you Did you guys ask Polymarket to take those down? >> I mean, I can't get into internal discussions that we have. I'll just say as a as a general matter, we have issued advisories uh in the last few months um uh concerning various types of event contracts that we have concerns over that either would if for registered entities would violate what's called the special rule, um that are readily susceptible to manipulation. So, think for example in the sports world, injury type contracts which were discussed in one of the advisories. And, you know, look, but to the extent that an entity is operating outside the United States um with contracts that would never be approved in the United States, that that's you know, it's outside the United States, it's not subject to our jurisdiction necessarily, depending upon the facts and circumstances. Um all of that being said, part of the reason why we are not doing regulation by enforcement, and we have encouraged people to come into the United States to register with us, whether that be in crypto or prediction markets or otherwise, is because not only because we're obviously pro-innovation, but still policing fraud robustly, is that we want to make sure that the FTX's don't happen again. And so, to the extent that there are large platforms outside the United States that aren't registered here, um that are in it some way touching into the United States or registering or excuse me or operating in some way in the United States, we want to try to >> Bring it in. >> Bring those people in so that they can be registered, they can be monitored, they can comply with statutes and regulations to prevent fraud and manipulation from happening. >> Gotcha. All right, last question cuz we have about 1 minute left, but I did see the advisory last week or 2 weeks ago about uh the mention markets that are very popular. It seems like uh the agency is telling companies that they need to rein this in because they are so susceptible to manipulation. That's of course what tripped up the teleprompter operator. So, are mention markets on their way out? >> I Look, I I I wouldn't be so bold as to profess whether a certain market is on the way out or not. I'll say that the advisory was pretty specific about the risks associated with mention markets. We are concerned. Um we have been concerned about them. Um and obviously to the extent that, you know, any market that um we oversee involves a derivative and van contracts primarily are swaps, we are concerned about fraud and manipulation, and that's why the advisory was issued. So, I I can't say whether they're on the way out or not. I just say that obviously our advisory was clear with respect to the concerns that we have, and we're watching. >> All right, so are we. David Miller, thank you so much. Great to have you here today, and thanks to all of you for coming out. >> [applause] >> Thank you.

This is the story of Kalshi’s founders, its federally regulated event-contract exchange, and the legal fight over what the Commodity Exchange Act allows. We explain how yes-or-no contracts work, what the court decisions actually covered, and why regulatory compliance can become a business moat—without treating one ruling as blanket approval for every kind of event betting.

0:00 - The CFTC Order
0:21 - What Is an Event Contract?
1:17 - The Ballerina and the Quant

3:34 - The Lawsuit

segments.text: In September of 2023, the federal
government sent a direct order to two
20-something entrepreneurs, "Shut this
down immediately or face federal
prosecution."
Most founders would have folded.
Instead, they took the regulator to
federal court, won a historic showdown,
and unlocked a multi-billion dollar
financial gold rush.
For more than a century, betting on the
future of the American government was
strictly illegal.
If you tried to trade cash on who would
become the next president or which party
would control the Senate, Washington
labeled it illicit gambling.
Wall Street had options for oil, gold,
and tech stocks.
But when it came to the single biggest
variable driving the global economy,
government policy and elections, there
was no direct market.
Then came Kalshi.
Founded by two young MIT graduates, this
platform didn't just want to create a
betting app.
They wanted to build a regulated
financial exchange where you could trade
yes or no contracts on real-world
events.
From Federal Reserve interest rate cuts
to election outcomes, everything had a
price between 1 cent and 99 cents.
And when Washington tried to crush them,
they didn't run offshore.
They fought back and changed the rules
of American finance forever.
To understand this multi-billion dollar
war, you have to look at the founders.
Tarek Mansour was a Lebanese-American
math prodigy who interned at Goldman
Sachs and traded at Citadel.
His co-founder, Luana Lopes Lara, grew
up in Brazil, spent 8 years training at
the Bolshoi Ballet Academy, and then
pivoted into quantitative trading at
Bridgewater Associates, the world's
largest hedge fund.
While working in finance, they noticed a
massive, systemic flaw.
If a hedge fund wanted to hedge against
a recession, they had to buy complex
baskets of bonds or short tech stocks.
If a farmer wanted to protect against a
hurricane, traditional insurance was
slow, expensive, and filled with
loopholes.
Why wasn't there a clean, simple
contract that paid out based on raw
reality?
A binary option, either an event happens
or it doesn't.
They called the company Kalshi, an
Arabic word meaning everything.
Most Silicon Valley tech founders
operate under the motto, "Move fast and
break things."
In financial markets, if you move fast
and break rules, you end up in federal
prison.
Competitors like Polymarket set up shop
offshore, leaning on cryptocurrency to
stay outside American borders.
But Tarek and Luana chose a painfully
slow, high-risk strategy. They went
straight to Washington.
They spent years knocking on the doors
of the Commodity Futures Trading
Commission.
In late 2020, they pulled off what many
thought was impossible. Kalshi became an
officially registered designated
contract market.
They could legally offer contracts on
inflation, the weather, and Central Bank
decisions.
Retail traders flooded in.
But the founders had their eyes on the
real crown jewel, US elections.
In 2023, Kalshi submitted contracts to
allow Americans to trade control of
Congress.
The CFTC slammed the door shut.
Regulators issued an official ban,
claiming political trading was gaming, a
legal term for gambling, and argued that
putting money on elections would
undermine democracy and invite market
manipulation.
For Kalshi, this was an existential
moment.
If they backed down, their vision of the
everything exchange was dead.
So, in November 2023, Kalshi filed a
lawsuit against their own federal
regulator.
Imagine suing the very government agency
that holds the legal authority to shut
down your business overnight.
That wasn't just bold.
It was a bet-the-company legal suicide
mission.
For months, Kalshi bled cash on legal
fees while federal lawyers tried to
dismiss the case.
The CFTC argued that election contracts
serve no public interest and violated
state anti-gambling statutes.
Then came September 2024.
US District Judge G.I.M. Cobb delivered
a shocking ruling.
The court rejected the CFTC's reasoning,
finding that the agency had exceeded its
statutory authority.
The judge concluded these contracts did
not fall under the statute's definition
of gaming.
The ruling concerned Kalshi's
congressional control contracts, not
every kind of election betting or event
contract.
The CFTC rushed to seek an emergency
stay to stop trading before the November
election.
On October 2nd, 2024, the DC Circuit
Court of Appeals denied the government's
emergency stay request.
That cleared the way for Kalshi to list
its congressional control contracts
while the legal process continued.
For the first time in decades, US
customers could access these election
event contracts on a federally regulated
exchange.
Trading activity surged.
Investors rushed to back prediction
market platforms, and Kalshi's valuation
rose across successive funding rounds.
Those private valuations are
round-specific estimates, not the same
as public company market caps.
The growth also brought controversy.
Critics warned that event contracts
could create incentives for
manipulation, insider trading, or harm
to election integrity.
Supporters argued that prices aggregated
information and provide a way to hedge
uncertainty.
And the legal fight did not settle every
question.
Regulators continued to challenge other
event contracts, and the boundaries of
what can be listed remain subject to law
and further decisions.
This battle between Kalshi and
Washington teaches us three critical
business lessons.
First, regulatory strategy can become a
moat.
While foreign platforms face geographic
restrictions, Kalshi invested years in
federal authorization and litigation.
Compliance is slow and expensive, but a
license and a favorable ruling can
create an advantage competitors cannot
copy overnight.
Second, information has economic value.
Event markets turn clearly defined
outcomes into prices, but a market price
is not a guarantee of truth, and markets
need rules that determine manipulation.
And third, the biggest markets can hide
in plain sight.
Businesses hedge currency and interest
rates.
Kalshi's founders asked whether clearly
defined events could also become useful
financial contracts.
If you enjoyed this story, subscribe for
more business and billionaire insights.

Competitors like Polymarket set up shop offshore, leaning on cryptocurrency to stay outside American borders. But Tarek and Luana chose a painfully slow, high-risk strategy. They went straight to Washington. They spent years knocking on the doors of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. In late 2020, they pulled off what many thought was impossible. Kalshi became an officially registered designated contract market. They could legally offer contracts on inflation, the weather, and Central Bank decisions. Retail traders flooded in. But the founders had their eyes on the real crown jewel, US elections. In 2023, Kalshi submitted contracts to allow Americans to trade control of Congress. The CFTC slammed the door shut. Regulators issued an official ban, claiming political trading was gaming, a legal term for gambling, and argued that putting money on elections would undermine democracy and invite market manipulation. For Kalshi, this was an existential moment. If they backed down, their vision of the everything exchange was dead. So, in November 2023, Kalshi filed a lawsuit against their own federal regulator. Imagine suing the very government agency that holds the legal authority to shut down your business overnight. That wasn't just bold. It was a bet-the-company legal suicide mission. For months, Kalshi bled cash on legal fees while federal lawyers tried to dismiss the case. The CFTC argued that election contracts serve no public interest and violated state anti-gambling statutes. Then came September 2024. US District Judge G.I.M. Cobb delivered a shocking ruling. The court rejected the CFTC's reasoning, finding that the agency had exceeded its statutory authority. The judge concluded these contracts did not fall under the statute's definition of gaming. The ruling concerned Kalshi's congressional control contracts, not every kind of election betting or event contract. The CFTC rushed to seek an emergency stay to stop trading before the November election. On October 2nd, 2024, the DC Circuit Court of Appeals denied the government's emergency stay request. That cleared the way for Kalshi to list its congressional control contracts while the legal process continued. For the first time in decades, US customers could access these election event contracts on a federally regulated exchange. Trading activity surged. Investors rushed to back prediction market platforms, and Kalshi's valuation rose across successive funding rounds. Those private valuations are round-specific estimates, not the same as public company market caps. The growth also brought controversy. Critics warned that event contracts could create incentives for manipulation, insider trading, or harm to election integrity. Supporters argued that prices aggregated information and provide a way to hedge uncertainty. And the legal fight did not settle every question. Regulators continued to challenge other event contracts, and the boundaries of what can be listed remain subject to law and further decisions. This battle between Kalshi and Washington teaches us three critical business lessons. First, regulatory strategy can become a moat. While foreign platforms face geographic restrictions, Kalshi invested years in federal authorization and litigation. Compliance is slow and expensive, but a license and a favorable ruling can create an advantage competitors cannot copy overnight. Second, information has economic value. Event markets turn clearly defined outcomes into prices, but a market price is not a guarantee of truth, and markets need rules that determine manipulation. And third, the biggest markets can hide in plain sight. Businesses hedge currency and interest rates. Kalshi's founders asked whether clearly defined events could also become useful financial contracts. If you enjoyed this story, subscribe for more business and billionaire insights.

metadata.title: The CFTC Explained 2026: Who Polices US Futures, Swaps and Retail Forex
metadata.author: Brokerchampion
metadata.shortDescription:
If you trade futures, options on commodities, swaps or retail forex as a US person, one regulator sits over all of it: the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the CFTC. It's an independent federal agency headquartered in Washington, DC, headed by a five-member commission appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate — and no more than three commissioners may come from the same political party. Its statutory mandate is to "foster open, transparent, competitive, and financially sound markets" in derivatives. The dividing line is easy to remember: if it's a derivative on a commodity — including currencies and certain crypto assets — it's the CFTC's. Stocks, bonds, mutual funds and ETFs belong to the SEC.

The US has regulated commodity futures since 1922, when the Grain Futures Act gave the Department of Agriculture authority over wheat and corn futures. The Commodity Exchange Act of 1936 broadened that authority. By the 1970s, with financial futures about to launch, Congress decided the existing regulator was undersized, and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission Act of 1974 created the CFTC with sole jurisdiction over US futures and options, taking over from the Commodity Exchange Authority. The Act required all futures to trade on designated contract markets, set registration for futures commission merchants, commodity pool operators, commodity trading advisors and introducing brokers, and created a "reparations" remedy for customers harmed by registered intermediaries. The agency began operations on April 21, 1975. Dodd-Frank in 2010 then handed it the swap market — far larger than futures by notional value — with mandatory central clearing of standardised swaps, swap-dealer registration, real-time public reporting and position limits.

For retail traders, a handful of rules show up directly. Regulation 5.30 caps retail forex leverage at 50:1 on the seven major pairs and 20:1 on every other pair — higher than the 30:1 ESMA and ASIC allow on majors, but far below offshore norms of 500:1 and up. The retail forex dealer regime adds a $20 million minimum capital requirement, FIFO order execution, a ban on hedging same-pair longs and shorts, and daily customer-fund segregation reporting — which is why most international forex brokers don't accept US clients at all. Rule 4.41 requires a prominent disclaimer on any hypothetical or back-tested performance: the "hypothetical performance results have many inherent limitations" language at the bottom of almost every US futures newsletter. And Rule 575 prohibits spoofing, banging the close and wash trading — for a retail trader as much as for a high-frequency desk.

Know where the protection stops. The CFTC enforces capital adequacy, customer-fund segregation, conduct and disclosure on registered intermediaries, and since MF Global's collapse in 2011 exposed gaps, FCM customer funds must be reported daily. It does not cover trading losses, and it does not cover unregistered offshore brokers. The agency works alongside the National Futures Association, the industry self-regulator that handles much of the day-to-day registration and examination, and recourse when a registered FCM fails runs through NFA arbitration and bankruptcy-court priority for segregated customer funds.

The practical checklist takes minutes. Search the firm on NFA BASIC at nfa.futures.org for registration status, history and disciplinary actions; check the CFTC's enforcement records on cftc.gov; and for retail forex dealers, read the NFA monthly financial reports. A broker that isn't registered with both the CFTC and the NFA but still accepts your business as a US person is operating illegally — no "tier-1 European licence" changes that. Outside the US the CFTC has no direct authority: UK traders look to the FCA, EU traders to national regulators such as CySEC or BaFin, and Australian traders to ASIC.

segments.text: The CFTC protects US traders, but that
means lower leverage. Is your broker
legal? Here's how to check.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission
is the US regulator for futures,
commodity options, swaps, and retail
forex. If you trade these products from
the United States, its rules determine
which brokers can legally serve you, how
much leverage you receive, and how your
money must be protected. The CFTC was
created by Congress in 1974. That marked
the shift from a narrow agricultural
regulator to a federal agency overseeing
a much broader financial market. Futures
had moved beyond wheat and corn into
currencies, interest rates, energy,
metals, and eventually swaps. The CFTC
regulates the marketplaces where
derivatives trade, the firms that
execute and clear those trades, and
companies that advise or manage customer
money. A futures exchange, such as CME
or ICE, is where contracts are listed
and matched. A futures commission
merchant holds your margin and helps
clear trades. An introducing broker may
be the retail-facing company you sign up
with, even when another firm actually
holds the funds. The CFTC also
supervises commodity pool operators,
trading advisors, swap dealers, and
retail foreign exchange dealers. A
retail foreign exchange dealer, or RFED,
is a US-licensed broker offering
off-exchange forex to American
customers. That structure creates an
important distinction. The broker brand
on your screen is not always the entity
holding your money or carrying the
trade. The key question is which
registered legal entity is responsible
for your account. Stocks, bonds, mutual
funds, and ETFs generally belong to the
Securities and Exchange Commission, or
SEC. Futures on commodities, futures on
currencies, and many swaps fall under
the CFTC. The product matters more than
the marketing label. The CFTC's
strongest retail impact appears in US
forex rules. A firm offering
off-exchange forex to US retail
customers must register as an RFED and
become a member of the National Futures
Association, or NFA. The NFA is the
industry's
It handles much of the day-to-day
registration and examination work while
the CFTC retains ultimate enforcement
authority. The headline rule is
leverage. US retail traders receive a
maximum of 50 to 1 leverage on seven
major currency pairs, including Euro US
dollar and USD JPY. In simple terms, $1
of account margin can control up to $50
of exposure. That increases buying
power, but it also means a small price
move can affect a much larger position.
All other currency pairs are capped at
20 to 1. So $1 of margin controls up to
$20 of exposure on those pairs. The
lower limit reduces the position size
available to retail traders, limiting
both potential gains and potential
losses. Those limits are stricter than
offshore norms, where leverage of 500 to
1 or even 1,000 to 1 is common. The US
system is designed to prevent a small
deposit from creating an enormous
position. Another constraint explains
why many international brokers refuse US
clients. The RFED must hold at least $20
million in capital. That is not a $20
million deposit from you. It is the
broker's own minimum financial buffer,
intended to help it absorb losses and
meet customer obligations. For most
international forex firms, maintaining
that capital and complying with related
conduct rules is not commercially
viable. That is why firms such as
Pepperstone, IC Markets, and Tickmill do
not accept US clients. The leverage cap
is only one part of the system. US rules
also require strict segregation of
customer funds, daily reporting, FIFO
execution, and a ban on hedging the same
currency pair in opposite directions.
FIFO means first in, first out. If you
open several positions in the same pair,
the earliest position must be closed
first. Hedging here means holding a long
and short position on the same pair at
the same time. US retail rules prohibit
that structure. These rules can feel
restrictive compared with offshore
brokers, but the mechanism is
straightforward. The regulator limits
the ways a retail account can build
hidden or excessive exposure. Customer
fund segregation works differently. The
broker must hold customer money
separately from its own operating
assets. If the firm fails, those funds
are not supposed to be available for
ordinary company expenses. The collapse
of MF Global in 2011 exposed weaknesses
in the old system. Post-crisis reforms
tightened reporting and response
requirements. Today, customer funds must
be reported daily, and a shortfall
triggers immediate regulatory action.
But CFTC protection has boundaries. It
does not reimburse ordinary trading
losses, and it does not protect you from
an unregistered offshore broker.
Regulation reduces specific counterparty
risks. It cannot make a losing trade
profitable. The CFTC also controls how
trading services advertise their
results. Rule 4.41 applies to commodity
trading advisors and commodity pool
operators. If a service shows
hypothetical or back-tested performance,
it must carry a prominent warning that
those results have inherent limitations
and do not prove that a real account
will achieve similar profits or losses.
That disclaimer matters because
simulated results avoid the emotional
pressure, execution problems, and losses
that appear in live trading. The same
principle applies to enforcement. The
CFTC investigates spoofing, wash
trading, attempts to manipulate closing
prices, retail forex fraud, pool
operator fraud, and certain crypto
derivatives violations. Spoofing means
placing orders with the intention of
canceling them before execution, usually
to create a false impression of demand
or supply. Retail traders can be subject
to these rules too, although enforcement
more often targets institutional and
algorithmic firms. The CFTC's job is
broader than checking broker licenses.
It tries to preserve the conditions
under which prices are formed honestly
and customer money is handled properly.
For a US trader, checking a broker
should begin with the NFA's basic
database. Search the firm name or its
NFA identification number. The record
shows registration status, disciplinary
history, and other regulatory
information. Then check the CFTC's
enforcement database and statutory
disqualification records. For an RFED,
review the NFA's monthly financial
reports, which include information about
capital adequacy, customer fund
segregation, and complaint volumes. A
polished website, a familiar brand, or a
license from another country does not
replace US registration. A broker
serving US customers should be
registered with the CFTC and be an NFA
member. If either registration is
missing, walk away. The $20 million
capital rule, leverage limits, and
reporting requirements are not optional
badges. They are the framework that
makes the broker legally eligible to
serve US retail clients. The final
answer is simple, but the reasoning
behind it matters. The CFTC is the
regulator for US derivatives, not the
general regulator for every investment
product. It created the modern framework
in 1974, expanded into swaps after 2010,
and now affects retail traders through
leverage, segregation, advertising,
execution, and broker registration
rules. For a US trader, open an account
only with a broker registered with the
CFTC and connected to the NFA. Verify
the firm yourself in NFA Basic, check
its disciplinary record, and understand
that 50-to-1 leverage on majors, 20-to-1
on other pairs, and a $20 million broker
capital requirement are deliberate
tradeoffs. The answer to the earlier
question is that the $20 million
requirement removes most international
forex brokers from the US market because
serving American clients demands a much
larger capital base and stricter
operating model. The CFTC cannot protect
you from market losses. It can help
ensure that the broker holding your
money is subject to capital, conduct,
segregation, and enforcement rules. For
a US trader, that is the difference
between a regulated account and a
website making promises.
For US traders, CFTC and NFA
registration brings stronger protection.
Check the description for the complete
breakdown.

metadata.title: CFTC Chair Selig’s First Big Move
metadata.author: Braeden Anderson
metadata.shortDescription:
In a development that underscores the accelerating evolution of financial innovation policy, Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Michael S. Selig has publicly articulated a significant shift in the agency’s posture on prediction markets — just days after industry commentary highlighted expectations for decisive leadership.

In the January 27 Bloomberg Law article “Crypto, Prediction Market Chiefs Gain Sway as CFTC Advisers,” I was quoted observing that “everyone is looking to Selig to provide backbone here.” That characterization was offered in the context of market participants and legal advisors awaiting clarity on the CFTC’s approach to emerging event contracts, especially those offered by platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket. 

Less than 72 hours later, Chairman Selig made clear that the CFTC is moving beyond uncertainty toward an active regulatory role. According to multiple news reports, Selig directed CFTC staff to:

Withdraw a 2024 staff advisory and proposed rule that would have restricted sports and political event contracts under the Commodity Exchange Act, a move that removes prior cautionary guidance and prevents its use as a shield for state action against federally regulated platforms; and

Initiate a formal rulemaking process to provide clear federal standards for prediction markets or “event contracts,” a market structure that has grown rapidly but lacked tailored regulatory guardrails.

Chairman Selig also signaled that the Commission is prepared to defend its exclusive jurisdiction over event contracts in federal litigation, underscoring both the CFTC’s statutory mandate and its willingness to assert that mandate against competing claims by states or other actors. 

These remarks came amid a broader industry debate over the boundaries of federal authority, state gambling regulation, and the proper role of the derivatives regulator in overseeing new market forms. Selig’s comments — emerging immediately after industry calls for leadership — suggest a heightened focus by the CFTC on delivering clarity, consistency, and institutional support for lawful innovation in prediction markets.

For market participants, legal advisors, and policymakers alike, these developments signal a material shift: federal regulators are not only listening to industry concerns, they are acting on them with concrete direction and regulatory intent.

That’s all for now,

Braeden

metadata.title: I Tested OddsJam's NEW Parlay Tool (Here's What Happened)
metadata.author: Billy Collins
metadata.shortDescription:
Download the OddsJam app and try the Parlay Tool for FREE:
App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/oddsjam-sharp-sports-betting/id6448072108
Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.oddsjam.app&hl=en_US

OddsJam built a parlay tool, and I was skeptical. Everything I like about their other
products comes down to control: picking the exact type of positive EV bet I want. A
parlay generator sounded like the opposite of that, and parlays already have a
reputation as a sucker bet.

So I tested it, and this is the honest version of what I found.

First, the part most people get wrong. Every leg of a parlay carries its own edge,
positive or negative, and those edges do not add up, they compound. One leg at a
slightly bad price is survivable. Four or five of them, and the math is buried before
the games start. That is the real reason parlays have the reputation they do: people
build on the pick instead of the price. Flip it, take legs that each have an edge on
their own, and a parlay stops being a lottery ticket.

That is the only question worth asking of any parlay tool. Not whether it looks good,
and not whether it builds long shots that pay huge. Can it find legs that actually have
an edge?

WHAT THE TOOL DOES. It lives in the OddsJam mobile app, under Parlay. You can sort by
recommended, by EV, by liquidity, or by probability. You pick which sportsbooks to
attack, how many legs you want, which markets, a minimum odds threshold, and any profit
boost you have been offered. Then it generates slips, and you can filter by sport.

WHAT I LIKED. The sharp money reads are genuinely useful: on a Colts moneyline I could
see a bettor had put sixteen thousand dollars behind it at plus 270, which is real
conviction, not noise. Price shopping is built in, and it matters. The same two-leg
parlay came back at plus 652 on FanDuel and plus 527 on DraftKings, on identical legs.
One-click bet loads the whole slip into your sportsbook for you, which saves a lot of
time on four and five leg builds. And being mobile only is quietly an advantage, since
books read app traffic as more casual than desktop.

WHERE I WANT MORE. There are no de-vig methods, and no way to choose which sharp books
the tool leans on. That matters, because the tool will happily show you an edge in a
market no sharp book prices at all. I walk through a Cal Raleigh player singles slip
showing a 1.95% edge that I do not believe is a real edge, because no Pinnacle or Circa
is pricing it. If everyone in the group project has a C average, there is no A student
to check your work.

So: impressed, with a list. De-vig methods, sharp book selection, and a custom EV
formula would turn this from a nice starting point into something I would use every day.

Tell me what you would change in the comments.

metadata.shortDescription:
Try OddsJam for FREE for 7-days:
Platinum: https://oddsjam.com/lp/ads/zeke-platinum?ref=otvhmwj
Sharp Money: https://oddsjam.com/lp/ads/zeke-sharp-money?ref=otvhmwj
Prediction Traders: https://oddsjam.com/lp/ads/zeke-prediction-traders?ref=otvhmwj

Learn how Prop Geek Zeke uses the OddsJam Positive EV Tool to evaluate NBA main lines and player props. In Part 2 of this three-part course, he walks through fair odds, devig settings, and the checks behind a potential betting edge.

A high displayed EV percentage is only a starting point. Zeke explains how the books in a comparison, market liquidity, and time until tip-off affect his confidence in a price. Follow examples involving Jalen Brunson, Keegan Murray, and Tyler Herro, plus a main-line demonstration using an NHL market.

You will learn:
• How Zeke uses Pinnacle as a main-line reference
• What devigging does and how Worst Case works
• Why the quality of the comparison books matters
• How to use line movement and exchange liquidity
• How his approach differs between main lines and player props

This is Part 2 of 3. Start with Part 1: The Sharp Money Tool. The next lesson covers the Prediction Traders Tool.

Explore OddsJam: https://oddsjam.com

CHAPTERS
00:00 Introduction and Part 1 recap
00:49 Why NBA injury news matters
01:50 Evaluating NBA main lines
02:01 Pinnacle and devig settings
03:10 Main-line example: price and liquidity
04:35 Zeke's main-line checklist
05:02 Switching to NBA player props
05:15 General filter and book weights
05:36 Worst Case devig explained
06:27 Why a high EV percentage needs context
07:26 Jalen Brunson: comparing prices
09:12 Tyler Herro: checking exchange liquidity
09:53 Sharp reference prices and betting timing
11:06 Main lines vs. props: the key takeaway
11:48 Course recap and Part 3 preview

Examples are for learning how to evaluate prices, not current picks. Positive expected value does not guarantee that an individual bet wins.

OddsJam has four betting tools: Momentum, Sharp Money, Traders and +EV. They all carry some risk, and they don't all fit the same bettor. In this video I walk through each one on my own screen, show you who it's built for, and rank them by your bankroll, your risk tolerance and how much time you actually have to bet.

DON'T WANT ANY RISK? WATCH THESE FIRST
If you want consistent returns without taking on risk, start with these two tools:
Arbitrage tool: https://youtu.be/bKaCBMQuXgk
Promo Converter tool: https://youtu.be/nNcvcG8GYBc

THE 4 TOOLS
01 Momentum: a pre-game tool, about 90% player props. When the sharp books move a line, Momentum alerts you so you can pick off the rec books that haven't adjusted yet. It also covers DFS apps like PrizePicks, Underdog and Betr. Volume is your best friend here, so it fits if you have time to bet a lot of plays.

02 Sharp Money: tracks the massive size going through prediction markets and exchanges like ProphetX and Novig so you can tail the professionals. It shines in markets where sharp books stay small, like college basketball, the WNBA and props. Best if you sit down about an hour before the games.

03 Traders: by far the friendliest tool if you only have 10 to 15 minutes. It follows profitable traders on Kalshi, Polymarket, Novig and ProphetX, and works well for mainline markets at rec books. My #2 pick for live betting.

04 +EV: the tool with the most utility. Build your own formula with the sharp books you trust, then customize filters for pre-game, live, DFS, rec books and offshore books. My #1 pick for live betting.

WHICH ONE IS RIGHT FOR YOU?
Want the fastest signals on player props? Momentum. Want to tail the biggest money? Sharp Money. Short on time? Traders. Want to get deep in the weeds? +EV.

How are the smartest affiliates adapting to new regulations and scaling their traffic in 2026? With new compliance standards and shifting acquisition models, the most successful media buying teams are upgrading from single-GEO strategies to building resilient, agency-level portfolios.

This Revpanda LIVE episode focuses entirely on growth, adaptation, and smart strategy. Oleksandr Hloza, Team Lead Affiliate at PIN-UP Partners, to reveal how top affiliates are diversifying their approach and successfully moving their budgets back to premium markets. If you want to optimize your ROI and build a sustainable business this year, this is your blueprint.

Key takeaways:
🌍 Balancing the right GEO ratio for fast cash-flow markets with long-term stability
💰 Why top media buyers are shifting budgets back to “expensive” T1 markets for ultimate predictability
📜 How to stop fighting strict advertising regulations and turn them into a massive competitive advantage
⚠️ The hidden financial dangers of relying solely on cheap, sensitive niche markets without diversification

Upgrade your 2026 playbook with proven market strategies. Click 'Attend' now and join the conversation!

🎤 Revpanda LIVE is brought to you by Alea, together with our Global Roaming Partner Esimatic.App.

🔗 Useful Links
Revpanda Group: https://revpanda.com
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/revpanda.group/
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/revpanda.agency
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/revpanda/
Telegram: https://t.me/+PjzrZTuKTRU5ODc0


Timestamps:
00:00 – Trailer and Introduction
02:18 – How do you manage risks when a market changes overnight?
03:15 – What are the current top-performing markets for Pin-Up?
04:30 – How to handle high competition in popular markets like Brazil
05:45 – The importance of localized creative content for different regions
07:10 – How to maintain high player retention in regulated markets
08:50 – What should affiliates look for when choosing a partner program?
10:15 – How Pin-Up supports affiliates with data and optimization tools
12:04 – Why transparency between the operator and affiliate is crucial
13:17 – How affiliate managers provide insights beyond just raw data
14:03 – How to get in touch with Pin-Up Partners (Telegram & Instagram)
14:43 – Closing thoughts on the future of the affiliate market

metadata.author: Three Markets – The Prediction Market Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Potential biases in prediction markets, the "just buy no" strategy, and how one trader turned $286 to $1M by ‘Reversing Stupidity’.

Andrew Lunardi's "Just Bet No" strategy: https://x.com/cryptonardez/status/1967338492696109425

DISCLAIMER: Content is provided for entertainment purposes only, does not constitute tax or investment advice, and is not a recommendation for any security or trading strategy. All investments involve risk, including the possible loss of capital. Past performance does not guarantee future results. Any hypothetical examples are provided for illustrative purposes only. Actual results will vary.

This week, Chris and Henry welcome trader Clay Alter to discuss his move from sportsbooks to live trading on Kalshi and Polymarket US. Clay breaks down his hands-on approach to market making, how he managed first-touchdown orders between plays and why late-game situations remain some of his strongest opportunities. metadata.title: How to Build a Kalshi & Polymarket Arbitrage Bot with ChatGPT
metadata.author: Scrape Atlas
metadata.shortDescription:
In this tutorial, I’ll show you how to use ChatGPT together with ScrapeAtlas to build a basic prediction-market arbitrage tracker across Kalshi and Polymarket.

The core idea is to look for the same prediction market on both platforms and compare the prices of opposing outcomes. If the combined cost of buying YES on one platform and NO on the other falls sufficiently below the $1 settlement value, there may be an arbitrage opportunity after accounting for fees and execution costs.

I’ll walk through how to connect ScrapeAtlas to ChatGPT, access the available Kalshi and Polymarket data, and then use ChatGPT to continuously monitor a single matching market for price discrepancies.

For the first version, I intentionally keep the workflow simple:

- Find an identical market on Kalshi and Polymarket
- Compare YES and NO prices across both platforms
- Account for platform fees and other costs
- Monitor the market repeatedly
- Surface potential arbitrage opportunities
- Use ChatGPT Scheduled Tasks for ongoing checks

I also explain why market matching matters. The event, settlement criteria, deadline, and outcome definitions need to line up before comparing prices between the two platforms.

ChatGPT is useful for prototyping the workflow, but if you want to monitor markets at much higher frequency, you may eventually want to move the same logic to your own server while continuing to use ScrapeAtlas for the underlying market data.

Resources mentioned:
ScrapeAtlas: https://scrapeatlas.com/

metadata.title: Master Prediction Market Visuals: Event Charts, Order Books, History & More in Qwidgets
metadata.author: Quantcha
metadata.shortDescription:
Deep tour of Qwidgets' visualization suite built for experienced traders. Event charts optimized for categorical, cumulative, range, and spread markets—horizontal bars for multi-outcome, vertical columns for strikes, color-coded liquidity & probability heat.

Toggle over/under views, switch player groups in multi-group cumulatives, normalize spreads for team perspectives. Dive into market gauges, candle history, depth-of-market order books (levels vs cumulative), and event history filtering. Context menus launch related widgets instantly.

Essential for rapid assessment of liquidity, edge, and mispricing across Kalshi, Polymarket, PredictIt.

Site: https://www.qwidgets.com
Quantcha: https://quantcha.com
Follow for updates: @Quantcha on X

#PredictionMarkets #MarketVisualization #OrderBook #KalshiCharts #Polymarket #PredictIt

a series of markets in which only one

horizontal bars.
