segments.text: IBKR clients can now purchase contracts
based on their own expectations
regarding questions about economic data,
capital markets, central banks,
sovereign debt, and climate.
These contracts include yes or no
answers to questions about published
outcomes, such as will job creation
exceed a specified number.
Investors who purchase a contract with
the correct yes or no answer receive a
payout, while both parties receive
coupon payments, similar to interest,
which serve as income streams.
Clients can purchase the contracts
through Forecast X, an IBKR affiliate
that operates both a designated contract
market and derivative clearing
organization licensed by the CFTC.
Macroeconomic and climate considerations
can significantly impact portfolios.
And until now, there hasn't been a
convenient way to manage these risks.
Forecast X, however, makes it possible
to complete near-term investments on
pending data releases, as well as
pairings on the longer-term evolution of
the economy or climate trends.
Contracts are available with short,
medium, and long-term durations.
They have low fees and provide money
market-like coupon yields for contracts
held overnight.
The coupon yield is distributed
throughout the life of the contract,
providing competitive, and in some
cases, above-market rates to investors.
As the value of the contract increase or
decrease, the corresponding coupon
payments are adjusted proportionally.
The exchange collects only one charge
per pairing that is baked into each
contract order, effectively half a penny
on each yes and no contract.
Available Forecast contracts are based
on data releases from reputable
providers, such as government agencies,
central banks, and other organizations.
The contracts include some of the most
followed indicators, including nonfarm
payrolls, retail sales, the consumer
price index, housing starts, central
bank interest rates, unemployment
claims, sovereign debt measures, global
temperatures, and more.
Each Forecast contract uses official
data releases with contract settlements
available as soon as the next
publication to as far as several years
out for some indicators.
This makes it possible to enter a
near-term pairing on a pending data
release, as well as make a longer-term
investment on the evolution of the
economy.
Forecast X users can enter yes and no
bids on questions, such as will an
economic release be higher than a
specific value.
The positions are executed when Forecast
X receives bids for both yes and no
positions in the market.
The combined yes and no bids include the
1 cent fee, total $1.01.
At settlement, if the yes answer is
correct, the holder of the yes position
receives $1 per contract, and the no
position receives zero, and vice versa.
Both sides do receive coupon payments,
however.
The exchange collects 1 cent per pairing
and pays out the remaining $1.
No additional exchange, clearing, market
data, premiums, or brokerage payments
are charged.
Forecast X's inclusive fee structure of
just 1 cent per contract is advantageous
for investors and helps level the
playing field for forecast contract
buyers.
Additionally, Forecast X's income stream
incentivizes contract buyers to hold the
investments over the long haul.
Here is an example of fees and payouts.
Assume a yes contract buyers cost is 41
cents and the contract is correct when
data is released.
The contract owner makes 59 cents of
profit or the difference in the $1
payout and the investors contract
purchase cost of 41 cents.
At the same time, the buyer of a no
contract would have paid 60 cents and
would have earned coupon payments.
Broadly speaking, the more likely an
outcome is to occur, the more expensive
a yes contract will be and the less
likely it is to occur, the less
expensive it will be.
In another example, we have the
question, will the US non-farm payroll
reading in Sep- tember be higher than
Clients may choose to buy a yes contract
if they estimate that the published
outcome will exceed the chosen threshold
and consider the odds favorable.
Or they might buy a no contract if they
anticipate the published outcome will
fall short of that number while finding
the pricing of the no attractive.
Similar contracts would also be
available with different jobs numbers
and have prices that reflect the
likelihood of different outcomes.
If the published print for non-farm
payrolls turns out to be 149,000,
the yes contract for 150,000
will be incorrect and will settle at
zero.
The investor who paid 75 cents for the
yes contract receives nothing other than
the coupon payments on the contract

Investors who purchase a contract with the correct yes or no answer receive a payout, while both parties receive coupon payments, similar to interest, which serve as income streams. Clients can purchase the contracts through Forecast X, an IBKR affiliate that operates both a designated contract market and derivative clearing organization licensed by the CFTC. metadata.shortDescription:
Interactive Brokers launches new prediction exchange called FORECASTEX.  The exchange will allow for binary outcome events such as economic numbers and weather events on a new exchange exclusively for IB clients.  These binary outcomes can be used as a hedge for portfolios, floods, insurance, and other events.  

The Wall Street Journal article:

https://www.wsj.com/finance/want-to-bet-on-the-cpi-or-jobs-report-a-prediction-market-is-coming-to-this-brokerage-8a174b52?mod=djemMoneyBeat_us

#trading 
#hedging 
#binarytrading 
#newmarket

metadata.title: How to Trade Prediction Markets (Kalshi, ForecastEx, CME Inside Interactive Brokers)
metadata.author: closeuptrading
metadata.shortDescription:
How prediction markets work, and how to trade them from an Interactive Brokers account (Kalshi, ForecastEx and CME Group in one place, no separate account). Price = probability, a worked example, bid/ask and spread, limit orders, how to exit before the result, trading the probability, the costs per contract, what to check before any trade, and the risks. Screens are IBKR's public pages on 28 Oct 2026. My own Kalshi tests start this week.

I chart my strategies on TradingView: https://www.tradingview.com/?aff_id=118942 (affiliate link: if you sign up through it I may earn a commission, at no extra cost to you).

Build it with me, step by step (6-part series): https://youtu.be/KE0R1jGRrQc

CHAPTERS

0:00 The idea
You can trade the odds of real world events, from your Interactive Brokers account, with the money already in it. Here's how prediction markets work, before I test them with real rules.
0:10 What it is
A prediction market is a yes or no question with a deadline. Will the Fed cut rates? Will this candidate win? Each contract pays one dollar if you're right, and zero if you're wrong. So the price, between one cent and ninety nine cents, is the market's probability. Twenty cents means the market thinks it's about a twenty percent chance.
0:30 One example
An example. Yes at thirty cents. You buy ten contracts for three dollars. If you're right, they pay ten dollars: plus seven. If you're wrong, you lose the three dollars. Your max loss is what you paid.
0:43 On Interactive Brokers
At Interactive Brokers, you get Kalshi, ForecastEx and CME Group in one place. No separate prediction market account. You trade from the same account, with the same funds.
0:54 Bid, ask and spread
Here's the markets page. Each contract shows a yes price and a no price. Look at this one: yes, sixty five cents. No, thirty six cents. Together, a dollar and one cent. That extra cent is the spread: what it costs to get in and out. So use limit orders. You name your price, and wait for someone to take it. In a quiet market, the spread can be wide, and a market order would pay it.
1:19 You can get out early
And this is the big difference from a bet. A bet is win or lose. Here you can get out before the result, if someone takes the other side. On Kalshi, you sell. On ForecastEx, you buy the opposite side, and the two cancel out.
1:32 Trade the probability
Which means you can trade the probability, not just the outcome. Buy at thirty cents. News moves the odds to forty five. Sell, for fifteen cents a contract, without waiting for the answer. And it works the other way too.
1:45 Costs
The costs. ForecastEx: zero commission, plus a one cent exchange fee. Kalshi and CME: one cent, plus one cent. And ForecastEx pays an incentive coupon on open positions: three point three eight percent a year right now, and it can change.
2:03 Before any trade
Before any trade, check three things: the exact question, the deadline, and who decides the result. Two questions that sound the same can settle differently.
2:13 The risks
The risks. Thin markets and wide spreads. A contract can go to zero. It's for eligible clients, twenty one and older. And none of this is financial advice.
2:24 What's next
What's next. My Kalshi tests start this week, with rules, tested like my other strategies. Real results in a few weeks, green or red.
2:33 The prompt
Here's a prompt to use before any event contract trade.
► Before I trade this event contract, explain the exact question, the deadline, the settlement source, my max loss, my break-even price, and how I could exit early.
Subscribe for the test results. And comment: what event would you trade? 

Education only. Not financial advice. Made with AI (Claude + AI voice).

metadata.title: Thomas Peterffy on ForecastEx: Building a Buy-Only Market to Transform Event Contracts Trading
metadata.author: John Lothian News (JLN)
metadata.shortDescription:
Event contracts trading has found a novel home on ForecastEx, an innovative platform designed by Thomas Peterffy, founder of Interactive Brokers. In an interview with John Lothian News., Peterffy shares insights into his latest venture. ForecastEx provides traders a unique “buy-only” model where participants take yes or no positions on the probability of future events, challenging traditional speculation while aiming to yield broader societal insights. 

Peterffy addresses ForecastEx’s current progress and explains that while few competitors exist in this space, ForecastEx distinguishes itself through its novel market structure involving interest payments on positions to encourage participation in long-term questions and its educational approach aimed at preparing new traders.

Peterffy elaborates on how ForecastEx plans to address educational gaps, especially given that its contracts focus on the interest payments, differing significantly from conventional binary options. He explains the platform's proactive stance in jurisdictions that ban binary options and the unique process ForecastEx uses to handle disagreements on true-or-false event outcomes. 

The conversation also explores the implications of a buy-only market model, where no selling occurs, and Peterffy shares his vision for future contract listings while acknowledging the potential challenges of listing too many.

Reflecting on the broader impact, Peterffy discusses the potential societal value of ForecastEx, noting how successful contracts could provide valuable, crowd-sourced insights into major events.


QUESTIONS
How is ForecastEx going so far?
Are there any other exchanges in this space?
How will ForecastEx tackle education?
How are these contracts different than binary contracts?
How are you dealing with jurisdictions that have bans on binary contracts?
How do you deal with people who disagree with your true or false decision?
What does it mean to have a market where you can only buy and there is no selling?
What contracts would you like to see listed?
Could there be a problem if you are listing too many contracts?
What would be the value to society if these contracts were successful?

segments.text: Today, we will talk about the
definition, role, registration, and
examples of an introducing broker IB.
An introducing broker is a broker in the
futures markets who has a direct
relationship with a client, but
delegates the work of the floor
operation and trade execution to another
futures merchant, typically a futures
commission merchant FCM.
The IB is usually affiliated with the
FCM either as an independent entity that
is partnered with that merchant firm or
as a direct subsidiary of that FCM.
An introducing broker acts as a
middleman by matching an entity seeking
access to markets with a counterparty
willing to take the other side of the
transaction.
Generally speaking, IBs make
recommendations while delegating the
task of executing trades to someone who
operates on a trading floor.
The introducing broker and whoever
executes a transaction split the fees
and commissions according to some agreed
upon arrangement.
Introducing brokers play the same role
in the futures markets as stock brokers
do in the equities markets.
However, they are regulated by different
authorities.
Stock brokers are registered with the
Securities and Exchange Commission SEC
and are regulated by the Financial
Industry Regulatory Authority FINRA.
Futures introducing brokers are
registered with the Commodity Futures
Trading Commission CFTC and regulated by
the National Futures Association NFA.
Introducing brokers help increase
efficiency and lower the workload for
futures commission merchants.
The arrangement allows for
specialization where the IB focuses on
the client while the FCM focuses on
trading floor operations.
FCMs supply trading platforms on which
clients have the ability to place trades
online and are responsible for account
management.
However, the majority of FCMs would find
it financially impossible to open
offices around the country to serve
their customers.
This is where IBs excel since they
typically operate out of smaller offices
located all over the country.
Many IBs are one-person operations while
others are larger multi-location
businesses.
IBs are better able to service their
clients as they are local and their
primary goal is customer service.
Outsourcing the prospecting and
servicing of clients to the IBs creates
economies of scale for FCMs and the
futures industry.
Most IBs do not have the financial
resources to execute trades for their
clients directly because that requires a
direct relationship with futures
exchanges and the large overhead of
maintaining accounts, trades, and
reporting, as well as developing and
maintaining trading platforms.
IBs allow FCMs to do business on a local
basis while using the FCM's
infrastructure for trading.
Here are three key takeaways.
One, an introducing broker IB advises
clients in the futures market, but
delegates trade execution and back
office operations to others.
Two, the IB is usually affiliated with
the FCM either as an independent entity
that is partnered with that merchant
firm or as a direct subsidiary of that
FCM.
Three, IBs are better able to service
their clients as they are local and
their primary goal is customer service.

videos.full_text: Today, we will talk about the definition, role, registration, and examples of an introducing broker IB. An introducing broker is a broker in the futures markets who has a direct relationship with a client, but delegates the work of the floor operation and trade execution to another futures merchant, typically a futures commission merchant FCM. The IB is usually affiliated with the FCM either as an independent entity that is partnered with that merchant firm or as a direct subsidiary of that FCM. An introducing broker acts as a middleman by matching an entity seeking access to markets with a counterparty willing to take the other side of the transaction. Generally speaking, IBs make recommendations while delegating the task of executing trades to someone who operates on a trading floor. The introducing broker and whoever executes a transaction split the fees and commissions according to some agreed upon arrangement. Introducing brokers play the same role in the futures markets as stock brokers do in the equities markets. However, they are regulated by different authorities. Stock brokers are registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission SEC and are regulated by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority FINRA. Futures introducing brokers are registered with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission CFTC and regulated by the National Futures Association NFA. Introducing brokers help increase efficiency and lower the workload for futures commission merchants. The arrangement allows for specialization where the IB focuses on the client while the FCM focuses on trading floor operations. FCMs supply trading platforms on which clients have the ability to place trades online and are responsible for account management. However, the majority of FCMs would find it financially impossible to open offices around the country to serve their customers. This is where IBs excel since they typically operate out of smaller offices located all over the country. Many IBs are one-person operations while others are larger multi-location businesses. IBs are better able to service their clients as they are local and their primary goal is customer service. Outsourcing the prospecting and servicing of clients to the IBs creates economies of scale for FCMs and the futures industry. Most IBs do not have the financial resources to execute trades for their clients directly because that requires a direct relationship with futures exchanges and the large overhead of maintaining accounts, trades, and reporting, as well as developing and maintaining trading platforms. IBs allow FCMs to do business on a local basis while using the FCM's infrastructure for trading. Here are three key takeaways. One, an introducing broker IB advises clients in the futures market, but delegates trade execution and back office operations to others. Two, the IB is usually affiliated with the FCM either as an independent entity that is partnered with that merchant firm or as a direct subsidiary of that FCM. Three, IBs are better able to service their clients as they are local and their primary goal is customer service. Hope this would help. Thanks for watching.

🚀 Dive into the exciting world of sports betting analysis with our latest tutorial! In this video, we demonstrate how to use Node.js, Axios, and the Odds API to fetch real-time betting odds for various sports, including the NFL and soccer. Perfect for both coding enthusiasts and sports betting aficionados!

🔍 What You'll Learn:
- How to set up a Node.js project to interact with a sports betting API.
- The ins and outs of making HTTP requests with Axios.
- Implementing asynchronous programming in JavaScript to handle real-time data.
- Securely managing API keys using environment variables.

🔑 Key Features of Our Project:
- Fetching live betting odds for multiple sports.
- Insightful error handling and data logging.
- Scalable code structure for adding new sports or features.

🔧 Prerequisites:
- Basic knowledge of JavaScript and Node.js.
- Node.js and npm installed on your machine.
- An API key from The Odds API.

📌 Stay tuned till the end for a step-by-step guide on setting up your environment and running the script. We also discuss potential enhancements and how you can contribute to this open-source project.

📚 Useful Links:
- GitHub Repository: https://github.com/adanzweig/nodejs-oddsapi
- The Odds API Documentation: https://the-odds-api.com/documentation
- Node.js Download: https://nodejs.org/

💬 If you have any questions or suggestions, feel free to drop them in the comments below. Don't forget to like, share, and subscribe for more tech tutorials and coding insights!

📢 Follow us on social media for updates on new videos and projects!

#Nodejs #SportsBetting #ProgrammingTutorial #APIIntegration #RealTimeData #JavaScript #CodingTutorial #OddsAPI

metadata.title: What’s Changing in iGaming Affiliate Marketing? | Affnook Webinar
metadata.author: Affnook
metadata.shortDescription:
What’s changing in the iGaming affiliate landscape? 🎙️

In our latest Affnook webinar, Jeremy Castillo asked the panel about the biggest changes shaping growth in iGaming today. Here’s what they had to say:

🔹 Joe Hatch, VP of Product, StatsDrone
The industry is becoming more data-driven, with companies looking beyond FTDs and conversions to track the full player journey and strengthen attribution across the funnel.

🔹 Brendon Spiteri, Head of Commercial, Routy
New publishers are finding it harder to enter the market, making quality traffic sources more scarce. Established publishers are increasingly focusing on data and maximizing value from every FTD rather than simply chasing volume.

🔹 Danielle Medgett, B2B Partnership Manager, iConvert
With changing regulations, operators are paying closer attention to what happens between the click and the deposit, focusing on player quality, drop-offs, and getting more value from their marketing spend.

🔹 Jeremy Castillo, Head of Sales, Affnook
Launching an iGaming site is only the beginning. The bigger challenge is acquiring players and building sustainable growth once the site goes live.

Different perspectives, one clear message: iGaming growth is becoming smarter, more data-driven, and focused on value over volume.

#Affnook #iGaming #AffiliateMarketing #iGamingMarketing #PlayerAcquisition #AffiliateGrowth #DataDrivenMarketing #PerformanceMarketing

This approach works across NFL, NBA, MLB, and other player-prop heavy sports, and it’s the same process professional bettors use to stay profitable over time. If you’re tired of guessing and want a clear, structured way to bet player props more intelligently, this video breaks it all down step by step.

metadata.title: Complete Cisco FTD VPN Course: Site-to-Site & Remote Access (FMC 7.6 Crash Course)
metadata.author: Hexward Labs | Cybersecurity Tools + AI
metadata.shortDescription:
A complete crash course on VPNs in Cisco Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) managed by Cisco FMC 7.6: how to choose between site-to-site and remote access VPN, policy-based vs route-based (VTI) tunnels, how to verify tunnel status, address pools and connection profiles for remote access users, MFA tokens, split tunneling, SAML authentication, and dynamic access policies.

📘 FMC & FTD Study Pack (notes, labs, quizzes, certificate): https://whop.com/nizar-tuanku/fmc-ftd-study-pack/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=description&utm_campaign=studypack&utm_content=longform

CHAPTERS
0:00 Choosing Your VPN Type
1:15 Policy-Based VPN Topologies
2:28 Route-Based VPN with VTI
3:29 Verifying Tunnel Status
4:36 Remote Access VPN Address Pools
5:33 Connection Profiles
6:35 MFA Tokens for VPN Logins
7:28 Split Tunneling
8:42 SAML VPN Authentication
9:41 Dynamic Access Policies

▶️ NEXT LESSON: Certificates and PKI Before VPN Configuration | Cisco Secure Firewall FTD
https://youtu.be/FJkeLd4PbO4

🛠️ RESOURCES
• Hexward Labs: https://hexwardlabs.com
• Open-source scripts & architectures: https://nizartuanku.github.io
• Full Cisco Secure Firewall series: https://www.youtube.com/@nizartuanku/playlists

💬 Site-to-site or remote access: which VPN takes more of your troubleshooting time on FTD? Tell us in the comments.

🎓 EXAM RELEVANCE: useful prep for Cisco CCNP Security exams 300-710 SNCF (Securing Networks with Cisco Firewalls) and 350-701 SCOR (Implementing and Operating Cisco Security Core Technologies). Independent study material; not affiliated with or endorsed by Cisco Systems.

#CiscoFTD #CiscoVPN #CiscoSecureFirewall #RemoteAccessVPN #NetworkSecurity #Cybersecurity

single devices. Take a 50-person branch
office compared to a single employee

headquarters, the network establishes a
site-to-site VPN. But does each computer

location establish a single permanent
tunnel between themselves. The firewall

wrapper, a process called encapsulation
that encrypts everything in bulk. This
makes the secure connection completely
invisible to the users inside. Now look

laptop lacks a dedicated branch
firewall, a site-to-site link is
impossible. Instead, they must use a
remote access VPN. A software client on
the laptop authenticates directly to the
headquarters firewall, building a
temporary on-demand tunnel just for that
one device. The branch office
communicates transparently through a
permanent bridge, while the coffee shop
laptop securely clicks to connect. How
does a policy-based VPN topology decide
exactly what traffic gets encrypted?
Connecting two entire network sites
blindly can expose highly sensitive
internal systems. Take a corporate
headquarters that needs to share a
specific inventory database with a
remote branch office. The first step is
defining the overall physical
relationship, designating the
headquarters as a central hub and the

encryption.

isolated. How does a virtual tunnel
interface secure your traffic without
traditional complex VPN rules? Imagine
connecting your headquarters to a new
remote branch over the public internet.
Older VPN methods force your firewall to
inspect every single outgoing packet
using complex access rules. It's an
administrative nightmare. Add a new
subnet, and you must manually update all
those matching rules. A virtual tunnel
interface solves this by acting as a
standalone logical interface inside the
firewall. Instead of updating complex
filters, you just point a standard
static route directly at this VTI. The

shield. Any packet sent into this

configuration is completely in sync. So,

IP pool successfully bridged the gap
between the external tunnel and your
internal routing table. If a firewall

remote user would get the exact same
internal access. That is the exact
problem a connection profile solves.

This workaround secures the network edge without forcing administrators to configure custom multi-factor logic on the firewall. And that remote worker? The back-end server validates both pieces of their combined password at once, granting them secure access in one seamless step. Forcing all remote internet traffic through a central firewall wastes massive bandwidth. How does a VPN decide exactly which traffic gets encrypted? The answer is split tunneling. Imagine a remote worker pulling secure database records while streaming a 4K video. By default, both the sensitive database query and the heavy video stream are shoved into the exact same encrypted tunnel, slowing everything down. To prevent this, the VPN client needs to instantly separate business data from public data. And it has to do this before the packets even leave the laptop. The secret? The corporate firewall pushes a predefined list of internal IP addresses to laptop. This list instructs the client to strictly encrypt traffic matching those specific destinations. Now, the laptop evaluates all outgoing traffic against this new split tunnel list. The database query matches the corporate addresses, so it routes securely into the tunnel. But, the 4K video stream traffic completely misses the list, so it automatically bypasses the VPN traveling straight out the user's local internet connection. And that remote worker from the beginning, the corporate database stays strictly secure. The video streams flawlessly, and the firewall bandwidth remains wide open. How does a firewall grant secure VPN access without ever checking a password? That's the SAML flow. By centralizing identities, administrators never have to manage vulnerable local accounts on every single device. Take a remote worker initiating a VPN connection using their existing cloud credentials. Instead of presenting a login prompt, the firewall actively refuses to ask for credentials. Instead, it redirects them to a central cloud system that handles logins, an identity provider. The user proves their identity to the cloud using multi-factor authentication, but the firewall is completely separated from this exchange. How does it know they passed? The cloud system generates a digitally signed tamper-proof ticket verifying the success, a SAML assertion. The user's client automatically passes this signed ticket back to the firewall. The firewall mathematically verifies the signature and opens the secure VPN tunnel. And that remote worker, they get full secure network access without the firewall ever actually seeing their password. How does a dynamic access policy decide to allow or block a VPN session? A password proves who you are, but it doesn't prove your computer is actually safe to join the network. Take a remote worker logging in with perfect credentials, but their laptop's antivirus has been disabled. Instead of opening the tunnel, the firewall hits pause to perform a device posture assessment. It needs to verify the machine's internal state. So, the policy evaluates specific attributes transmitted from the client, checking the operating system, registry keys, or verifying that approved anti-malware software is actively running. Because this incoming connection lacks the required active antivirus, the policy conditions fail. The firewall instantly enforces the action, blocking the connection before the endpoint can ever touch your internal network. And that vulnerable laptop from the beginning, it is completely denied access despite having the correct password, keeping your internal network totally safe.

metadata.title: How to Configure Cisco FTD High Availability in FMC | Active-Standby Firepower Setup | HA Explained
metadata.author: Daily Support
metadata.shortDescription:
#cisco  #ciscofmc  #firepower  #ciscosecurity  #networksecurity  #CiscoFirewall #FTDHA #ciscotraining  #ciscotutorial  #networkengineering  #cybersecurity2024 #cybersecurity2025 #firewall 

“In this video, we’ll configure Cisco FTD High Availability (HA) using Firepower Management Center (FMC). This step-by-step tutorial covers how to add FTD devices, link them to FMC, and configure Active-Standby failover for redundancy.”

Please like and share this video with your friends and family. Also, Don't forget to subscribe to our channel for more videos.

Community: https://www.facebook.com/dailysupport.net
E-Mail: alsafiuladiat@gmail.com

segments.text: How to create a port channel infos for
data interfaces. How to assign dedicated
interfaces for hail lover and state
links. How to configure ha on the
primary FTD using FMC. How to parent
sync the secondary FTD. How to verify
active standby status and ensure
configuration synchronization. First log
into your FO chassis manager. Navigate
to interfaces. Add port channels and
click create port channel. Assign a name
and port channel ID for example 43.
Choose the type data and speed 10G and
set the mode to active. Then go to
interfaces. Select your physical
interfaces and click okay.
Port channel configure compete. This
port channel will later be used for your
data interfaces such as inside or
outside.
The port status is currently down
because the port channel is not
configured on the other side. Now assign
port channel to the logical device. Go
to logical devices. Then select your FTD
logical device. Click edit. Under data
ports, assign port channel 43 for data
traffic.
Click save. FTD add the interface.
The same process applies when
configuring other FOS and FTD instances.
Once complete, both devices will have
identical interface mapping. Then log
into the FMC firepower management
center. Log into the FMC using admin
user. You must first register each FTD
to the FMC before forming the a pair.
Navigate to devices then device
management to view the FTDs within their
groups. All FTDs have already been
added. The video demonstrating this is
available on my channel. Select the FTD
and go to the interfaces tab. Then sync
the device for synchronizing the
interfaces in the FMC.
After sync need to save the current
interfaces.
You can now view the current interfaces
of each FTD. Before starting the high
availability HA configuration, we need
to check for any pending deployments. If
pending deployments exist, they must be
deployed first and only then can we
begin configuring HA between the FTDs.
Navigate to devices, then device
management. Click add and select the
high availability option to configure
HA.
Set a standard name of h a pair.
After setting the name, select the
primary firewall that was added earlier
and then select the secondary firewall.
Click continue to begin the setup
process. During this time, snort
processes of both devices restarts
temporary causing traffic interruption.
You'll be prompted to choose select
failover link interface and state link
interface same as LAN failover link. Set
a logical name like failover link.
Then set the primary IP within the same
IP block such as /30. After setting the
primary IP, configure the secondary IP
and subnet as shown. Click add to begin
the configuration deployment and device
synchronization process. After adding
the high availability pair, configure
the monitor interfaces and apply the
same health policy to both hodes. After
completing the high availability
configuration, check the interfaces and
IP addresses.

metadata.title: I Built a Sports betting Arbitrage Scanner for FREE (AI Tutorial)
metadata.author: Odds Breaker
metadata.shortDescription:
Arbitrage scanners usually cost hundreds of dollars a month. Today, I’m building one in 5 minutes for zero dollars using Python and AI commands.

We use TheOddsAPI to scan over 800 live sporting events across major US sportsbooks (DraftKings, FanDuel, MGM, etc.) to find mathematical guarantees where the implied probability is less than 100%.

But does it actually work in the real world? We test the code live to see the results and discuss the logistical reality of capturing these trades.

🤖 THE AI PROMPTS I USED
Want to build this yourself? Copy and paste these 4 commands into ChatGPT, Claude, or Cursor:

1. Fetch the sport list
"Run `GET /v4/sports/?apiKey={api-key}` and save the response to `data/raw/odds_sports_list.json`."

2. Filter out futures
"Read `data/raw/odds_sports_list.json`, keep only entries with `active` true and `has_outrights` false, and write the result to `data/raw/odds_sports_active.json`."

3. Pull odds for every sport
"For each `sport['key']` in `data/raw/odds_sports_active.json`, request `GET /v4/sports/{sport}/odds/?apiKey={api-key}&regions=us&markets=h2h,spreads,totals&commenceTimeFrom={UTC now}`. Save each response under `data/raw/odds_by_sport/{sport}.json` and append all events to `data/raw/odds_all_sports_us.json`."

4. Scan for arbitrage
"Read `data/raw/odds_all_sports_us.json`, find the best h2h odds per outcome, compute `margin = 1 − Σ(1/price)`, and print each event with `margin greater than 0`, plus a summary by margin band and by sport."

🔗 LINKS MENTIONED
TheOddsAPI: https://the-odds-api.com/

⚠️ RESPONSIBLE GAMBLING DISCLAIMER
The purpose of this channel is to show you the math behind why you lose money—not to help you lose it.

While arbitrage is risk-free in principle (mathematically), execution risk is real. If you do not get your bets down on both sides instantly, the lines can move against you, turning a "guaranteed profit" into a potential loss.

Please gamble for fun and only with money you can afford to lose. Sports betting is entertainment, not a job. In the end, the bookie always has the edge. If you or someone you know has a gambling problem, please seek help.

#betting #sportsbetting  #coding  #arbitrage  #TheOddsAPI #sportspredictions

We talk midterms, election odds and what the market might be missing with trader and political junkie, Gavin. Then, we talk with our Head of Engineering, Michael, about how he got into prediction markets and what it takes to build the tech behind the business.

metadata.title: Novig Climbs to #1 in Sports: What’s Behind the Downloads?
metadata.author: Inside Prediction Markets
metadata.shortDescription:
This week, we discuss the CFTC’s potential collaboration with the SEC, Novig’s climb to #1 in the App Store’s sports category and prediction markets’ growth as the NFL season unfolds. Then, we get into what bettors actually want: what makes someone choose a sportsbook over a prediction market, how app design shapes that choice and why a simpler experience might matter more than better odds.

📅 New Episodes Drop: Wednesdays 
👇 Subscribe now.
@insidepredictionmarkets  

OpticOdds is a global leader in sports betting data solutions, empowering sportsbooks, DFS, prediction markets and platform providers with the fastest, most reliable, and most comprehensive odds data and trading tools in the industry.

"Another federal appeals court has ruled that states can enforce their gambling laws against the prediction market Kalshi, which asserts that it can only be regulated by the US government. On Friday, a three-judge panel in the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ruled unanimously against Kalshi and in favor of Ohio and Tennessee.

While the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission has exclusive jurisdiction over “swaps,” the judges found that sports wagers offered on Kalshi do not meet the legal definition of swaps. Moreover, the court found that even if Kalshi wagers were swaps, the regulatory scheme created by Congress would not prohibit states from enforcing gambling laws on prediction markets."

It has increased the number of people who have gone into bankruptcy because of their gambling addictions. It makes gambling a lot easier. But what could possibly be more insidious than that? Well, it turns out there's something known as prediction markets. And what's even worse about prediction markets is that they're not regulated the same way the gambling apps are. And we already know the gambling apps have some real problems. So imagine even less regulation. So let's talk about the difference between the gambling apps and the prediction markets because prediction markets are considered different from gambling apps even though the actions you take on the prediction market apps, it's gambling. Like that's what you're doing. You're engaging in gambling. In fact, prediction markets are user-to-user financial exchanges. That's how they're how they're described. Where participants buy and sell binary contracts tied to the outcomes of future events. So you can, let's say, bet on whether or not Republicans will maintain control of the House of Representatives after the midterms. Like that's an example. You're making a prediction and you're making a bet based on your prediction. Um whereas with gambling apps, the users place wagers against a centralized house that's that sets fixed odds, okay? Now I want to I want you to see how dystopian this all has gotten, especially when it comes to the advertisements we all have to sit through. Uh let's put up this video and I'll explain what you're looking at if you're viewing um the show. So this is an example of a Cal sheet ad, for instance. And there's like something kind of dystopian about how these ads are. And what's even more dystopian is how many more Americans month after month turn to these prediction markets in order to make a buck. I had a conversation with one of my younger male colleagues, and he was talking about how a lot of young people in this country, especially young males, they don't see a path forward for themselves. They don't see opportunity for themselves. And when you think about the resources it takes just to go to work. Like you have to pay money to go into the office and work for or to your place of work to earn a living. With these apps, whether it's a sports betting app or an app related to the prediction markets, you just place bets and you could make money. But the problem is, well, a lot of people don't make money. Most people actually lose a lot of money. So, look, the distinction is important because gambling apps are subject to state gambling laws. Those laws, in my opinion, don't go far enough in regulating. However, the prediction markets are even worse because they're not even subject to those regulations. They're regulated as marketplaces by the Federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission. More on that in just a minute. But because of this distinction, Kalshi and Polymarket, those are the two major prediction market apps, uh they're the two biggest at least, are able to operate in all 50 states. Sports betting apps are not. So, sports betting apps are limited state by state, and they are also operational in about 50 to 30 states depending on the platform, and the states are free to essentially regulate them as they please. But because of this loophole, apps like FanDuel and DraftKings have decided, "You know what? Maybe we create a prediction market uh on on our platforms in order to operate in all 50 states." Now, let's talk about the explosion of the betting markets. And by the way, not the betting markets, the prediction markets. So, like when Polymarket came came around, I don't gamble. I don't I don't play around on these apps. I just I'm not really interested. So, I didn't really know what it was. I thought it was just another gambling app, but it's not. It's It's part of the prediction market predictive marketplaces. And the thing that people bet on the most, sports. So, they're literally betting on sports with these prediction market apps. So, please tell me how this is different from these sports betting apps. It's really not. In In practice, it's not. And if If you look at this chart, okay, it details monthly trading volume on Polymarket and Kalshi over the last 2 years, broken down by trade type. And you don't need to be an expert on any of this to see that it's increasing. It is rising exponentially. It's the case when it comes to placing sports bets, bets on politics, we'll touch on that in just a minute, cryptocurrency, other issues. About 70% of Kalshi's daily trading volume comes from sports betting, according to the prediction market operator. >> [snorts] >> And so, on prediction markets, 79% to 84% of all accounts um lose. They realize net losses. Which isn't good. Only 0.1% of accounts on Polymarket take home, get a load of this, 67% of the profits. And that's according to the Wall Street Journal. And look, I'm sure you guys have come across some of these stories where suddenly there's a big political decision made by the Trump administration, whether it has to do with the war against Iran or or otherwise, doesn't matter. And then you'll see some headlines about how one one or two people made a killing on the prediction market betting that Trump was going to do this. Gee, I wonder how. So, I'm going to explain how in just a minute. Obviously, it's insider trading. But since Kalshi's launch, ordinary users have actually lost quite a bit of money uh to the tune of half a billion dollars. So, uh this is taking an already devastating economic situation for most Americans and exacerbating them or exacerbating it if they've fallen into the trap of using these predictive market apps. Now, research reveals that retail users lose a higher percentage of their capital on prediction platforms, a median return of -8% than they do on traditional sportsbooks, which is -5% or slot machines, -6.55%. Although I got to say, I love me the penny slots if I ever go to Vegas. Like, I'm not really a gambler, but I will eff around with the penny slots. And I don't know how, but I get really lucky. I win money on the penny slots almost every time. But don't That's not me promoting it, okay? Don't do it. Don't do it. Now, um this is only grown like the predictive markets have only grown. Kalshi has traded over 239 billion dollars this year alone, which is setting an all-time record uh single month high of 59.5 billion this September. And I'm sure NFL season had something to do with that. And these prediction markets also come with um some new risks. So, Kalshi, for instance, was sued following bets on whether the former now assassinated leader of Iran, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, uh would retain power. metadata.title: Explaining Prediction Markets with the CEO of Kalshi
metadata.author: Natalie Fratto
metadata.shortDescription:
Natalie Fratto (Creator of Charts & Crafts) sits down with Tarek Mansour, the CEO of Kalshi to better understand how prediction markets *actually* work, the counter-intuitive impact of prediction markets on elections, and why he believes they can make the world a better place.

We cover:
- How Kalshi works (hint: a lot like the NYSE)
- 60¢ = 60%: how event contracts price probability
- Prediction markets vs. sportsbooks 
- Gambling or market? 
- Why federal regulation beats a state-by-state patchwork
- Polls vs. markets: skin in the game & the pursuit of truth
- Why markets reward the boring take
- What you can't trade on (no wildfire markets)
- Hedging 101 at the ice cream shop
- Goku, growing up in Lebanon & the 120% rule

Highlights:
(00:00) Gambling, markets and their historically flirtatious relationship
(00:34) Opening Kalshi for the first time
(01:19) How a contract works: 60¢ = 60% odds
(02:10) Why not just use the stock market? CFTC & derivatives
(02:58) Prediction markets vs. sportsbooks: who sets the price
(04:35) Where the gambling line is, according to Tarek
(05:30) In favor of federal regulation
(06:17) The vision: free markets in pursuit of truth
(06:39) Why polls miss & markets don't (2016, 2024, Mamdani)
(07:24) Echo chambers, hot takes & rewarding the boring take
(08:15) What you can't trade on & why
(08:54) Hedging 101 at the ice cream shop 
(10:17) Goku, Lebanon & the 120% rule

metadata.title: Unpacking Prediction Markets: Kalshi (CFTC-regulated) and Polymarket (crypto-based)
metadata.author: R. Capital Intelligence
metadata.shortDescription:
Prediction markets are rapidly moving from the fringe into regulated financial infrastructure — and most investors are not paying attention.
In this episode, we break down:
• What prediction markets actually are
• How event contracts work
• The difference between Kalshi (CFTC-regulated) and Polymarket (crypto-based)
• The legal battle over election contracts
• Why institutions are watching this space closely
• The regulatory implications for U.S. investors
• Whether prediction markets could become a new asset class
Platforms like Kalshi are operating under U.S. derivatives law, while Polymarket runs on crypto infrastructure outside traditional U.S. regulatory frameworks. That distinction matters — legally, financially, and structurally.
As courts allow regulated election contracts and capital flows increase, prediction markets may evolve into a mainstream financial tool for pricing uncertainty.
This episode explores the money implications, the risks, and the long-term outlook — without hype.
This is educational analysis only. It is not financial advice.
If you value serious breakdowns of regulation, crypto infrastructure, and capital markets, subscribe to Practical Finance to support the research behind this channel.

segments.text: Look at this carefully. There is a
market right now where people are
trading on who will win elections, what
inflation will be next month, whether
the Federal Reserve will cut rates and
even whether certain laws will pass.
Billions of dollars are flowing through
it and most investors are not paying
attention. That market is called
prediction markets and they are going
mainstream.
Today we're going to talk about what
prediction markets actually are, why
they are growing fast, the difference
between regulated platforms like Khi and
crypto platforms like Poly Market, the
legal battles behind them, and why this
matters for investors because something
important is happening at the
intersection of regulation, finance, and
information. And if you invest in
stocks, crypto or anything else, this
matters.
What are prediction markets? Let's start
very simple. Imagine this. Let's say
your school is voting for class
president. You think Sarah will win.
Your friend thinks, "Uh-uh, Michael will
win." Instead of just arguing, you both
put $10 down. If Sarah wins, you get
$20. If Michael wins, your friend gets
$20. That is a very simple prediction
market. It is a market where people buy
and sell contracts based on the
probability of an event happening. Now
scale that idea up to elections,
inflation data, interest rate decisions,
economic reports or court rulings.
Instead of guessing, people trade
probabilities and the price of the
contract reflects the collective belief
of the market. If a contract trades at
70 cents, that implies a 70%
probability. It's like turning opinions
into tradable assets.
But let's see why this is different from
gambling. Now you might say, isn't this
just betting? And that's a fair
question. The difference is a structure
and purpose. Gambling is designed purely
for entertainment. Prediction markets
can serve as information aggregation
tools, risk hedging tools, economic
forecasting mechanisms. For example, if
you run a business and you are worried
that interest rate may rise, you could
potentially use prediction markets to
hedge that risk. It becomes closer to
financial derivatives than to a casino
betting. That's where the legal and
regulatory complexity begins.
Why are they growing now? Prediction
markets are not new. But what has
changed? Three things. Technology,
crypto infrastructure,
legal shifts. Crypto made it easier to
create global platforms. Smart contracts
made automated settlements possible. And
recent legal decisions in the US have
opened the door for regulated event
contracts which bring us to the key
players.
Kalshi versus Poly Market. There are two
major models. On one side we have
Kalshi. Kalshi is a US-based commodity
futures trading commission regulator
exchange offering event contracts. It
operates within the US regulatory law.
Users trade in US dollars. It went
through legal battles to offer political
event contracts. On the other side, we
have Poly Market. Poly Market operates
using crypto primarily US dollars. It
serves global users. It is not regulated
in the US the same way Kali is. So the
core difference is regulatory status.
Kali is building inside the system. Poly
market is operating outside the
traditional US regulatory framework.
Think of it like this. Galshi is
building a bank. Poly market is building
a decentralized financial platform. Both
offer prediction markets but the legal
environment around them is very
different.
Let's simplify it even more. Imagine two
lemonade stands. One gets a permit from
the city. They follow all the rules.
They pay taxes. That's kalshi. The other
sets up outside the city limits. They
don't need city approval. That's closer
to poly market. Both sell lemonade, but
one operates inside regulation. one
operates outside traditional regulation.
That difference matters for investors.
But the real turning point wasn't the
platform structure. It was the legal
battle.
Let's see the legal shift. In 2020, Khi
was officially approved by the Commodity
Futures Trading Commission as a
regulated exchange. That means it became
legally allowed to offer event contracts
in the United States. This was the first
step towards legitimacy.
In 2022, the Commodity Futures Trading
Commission charged Poly Market for
operating an unregistered derivatives
platform accessible to US.
Poly Market settled the case and paid a
civil penalty. This confirms something
important. Prediction markets fall under
the US derivatives law when offered to
Americans.
the Commodity Futures Trading
Commissions blocked Kali from offering
congressional election contracts. The
regulator argued that these contracts
involve political activity and could be
against the public interest. This was a
major restriction. It signal that
election markets might not be allowed
even on regulated platforms.
Then in 2024, a federal court ruled in
favor of Kalshi. The court allowed the
listing of certain election contracts.
This was a turning point. It limited the
commodity futures trading commission's
ability to block political events
contracts and it reopened the door to
regulated election markets. Let's
explain this in a very simple way.
Imagine you want to open a school club
where students trade predictions. First
the principal says yes. Then the school
board says no. Then a judge says yes
again. That is essentially what happened
here. The regulator said no. The court
said yes. And that changed the direction
of the entire market.
This timeline shows the shift from
restriction to expansion. And when
regulation shifts toward expansion,
capital usually follows. This is not
just about betting on elections. is
about whether uncertainty itself can
become a regulated financial product.
Recently, US courts allow regulated
platforms to offer election contracts.
There was a major moment because it
blurred the line between political
forecasting, financial derivatives, and
betting law. This isn't just a tech
story. It's a regulatory evolution
story. again and whenever regulation
shifts capital flows. This timeline
shows the shift from restriction to
expansion.
But why investors are not ready? Here's
the uncomfortable truth. Most retail
investor don't understand derivatives,
don't follow the US commodity futures
trading commission's ruling, don't
monitor event contracts approval. So
when this market scales they will
encounter it after institutions do that
is usually how financial innovation
works. First infrastructure
then institutions
then retail awareness. We are somewhere
between stage one and two.
Important disclaimer before we go
further. This is not financial advice.
This is educational analysis. Prediction
markets carry legal risk, liquidity
risk, and volatility risk. Always do
your own research and understand your
jurisdiction. Now, let's continue.
Let's see the money implications and why
does this matter financially? Because
prediction markets could become a new
asset class, a hedging tool, political
risk pricing mechanism, and a
macroeconomic forecasting tool. So
imagine this scenario. If prediction
markets show a 90% chance of a major tax
change, markets may adjust before the
law passes. Information becomes tradable
and tradable informations moves capital
that changes how investors interpret
signals.
Now let's stay grounded. Risk include
manipulation, low liquidity, regulatory
reversals, platform risk, political
pressure. If governments decide these
markets distort democracy, regulation
could tighten. If liquidity dries up,
prices become unreliable. So this is not
risk-free innovation. It is financial
experimentation in real time.
Let's see the future outlook. Here is a
key question. Could prediction markets
become as common as a stock exchanges?
Possibly, but only if regulation
stabilizes, institutional participation
increases, public trust grows. If that
happens, we may see banks offering event
contracts, hedge funds hedging political
risk, corporation pricing, regulatory
outcomes.
This is still early, but it is no longer
fringe. It is moving towards mainstream.
Remember that prediction markets
represent something deeper. They
represent the financialization of
uncertainty. Instead of debating
outcomes, we price them instead of
arguing. We trade probabilities. That
changes how society processes
information. And most investors are not
thinking about that yet, but they will.
Thank you for watching until the end.
And if you found this episode valuable,
please like and subscribe. These videos
require research and preparation, and
your support truly helps this channel
grow and continue delivering thoughtful
financial analysis.
Until next time.

segments.text: Welcome to Market Matters. I'm Marley
Kaden. Throughout financial history,
capital markets have relentlessly
expanded what we can price, hedge, and
trade. From the first grain futures on
the Chicago Board of Trade to modern
interest rate swaps, markets are built
to strip away uncertainty and turn the
unknown into a tradable asset. Today,
our guest is at the center of a capital
allocation boom that attempts to turn
real-world events from inflation prints
and election outcomes to sports and Fed
rate cuts into a legitimate standalone
asset class. Her story is one of the
most remarkable in modern finance. A
Brazilian ballerina trained at the
Bolshoi Theater School who became an MIT
mathematician, quant trader, and
ultimately co-founder and COO of Kalshi.
Alongside her co-founder Tariq Mansoor,
she spent years in the regulatory
trenches convincing federal agencies
that future events could become
federally regulated financial
infrastructure. Today, with Kalshi
commanding an intense public debate
across Wall Street, sports books, and
state capitals, we look beyond the price
tickers to ask a fundamental question

She also said she views this as a part of the reasoning that sports has become such a significant growth engine for Kalshi and the prediction markets overall. And last but certainly not least is when we were looking ahead to the future this dream that the co-founders have of connecting all of the nodes of financial infrastructure and she says they're just getting started. We are going to have to leave it there but thank you so much for being with us today. This has been Market Matters. You can find us wherever you get your podcasts. Please make sure to rate, review, and subscribe. I'm Marley Kaden. We hope you'll join us again next week.

The legal battle for prediction markets just shifted from federal to state courts, and the implications for Kalshi and Polymarket are massive. In this video, I break down the recent lawsuits filed by Nevada and Massachusetts and explain the strategic "lesson learned" by state gaming regulators.

We dive into the core legal arguments:

The "State Court" Strategy: Why regulators stopped sending cease and desist letters and went straight to filing suit [00:39].

Preemption & The CFTC: Does the CFTC have exclusive jurisdiction over event contracts, or is sports wagering a "state issue" traditionally reserved to the states? [02:31]

"Elephants in Mouse Holes": Explaining this famous canon of statutory construction and how it applies to federal vs. state authority over gambling [04:17].

The Commodity Question: Is the outcome of a sports event actually a "commodity"? I discuss the 2010 motion picture receipts precedent and what it means for the future of these exchanges [06:55].

Are these exchanges trading futures or just facilitating gambling? Let's look at the law behind the headlines.

Contact me for professional consultation: [Insert your contact link/email from bio]

The information provided in this video is for educational and entertainment purposes only and does not constitute legal or financial advice. Accessing this content does not create an attorney-client relationship. Laws vary by jurisdiction; please consult with a qualified legal professional regarding your specific situation.

metadata.title: CFTC Chair Faces Tough Questions on Fast-Growing Prediction Markets
metadata.author: Congress Clips
metadata.shortDescription:
At a House Agriculture Committee hearing, Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chair Michael Selig faced intense questioning from lawmakers over the rapid rise of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket. Lawmakers raised concerns about insider trading risks, fraud prevention, and whether current regulations are strong enough to keep up with the fast-moving industry. Watch the full exchange right here.

#CFTC #Congress #PredictionMarkets #Kalshi #Polymarket #HouseAgriculture #InsiderTrading #CryptoMarkets #Regulation #FinanceNews #BreakingNews #Hearing #USCongress #MarketOversight #MichaelSelig

segments.text: At a House Agriculture Committee
hearing, Commodities Future Trading
Commission Chair Michael D. Selig was
grilled by lawmakers over prediction
markets like Kalshi and Polymarket with
sharp questions on insider trading,
fraud, and whether regulators can keep
up with the fast-growing industry. Watch
the exchanges right here.
>> identify which betting line is from a
regulated major sports book and which
one is from an event contract from a
prediction market?
Congressman, I I'm not an expert on
identifying betting lines, so I'm not
certain. Why don't you um please
enlighten me.
Well, it's clear to me that you can't
tell, and that's the problem because the
average consumer also can't tell. Um
here you see that the
results from the prediction market and
the state-regulated gaming entity and
the lines that are put on these sports
bets aren't much of a difference, yet
they're regulated completely
differently. And although the odds are
functionally the same, the outcome for
the end user is the same. Consumers
couldn't care less if they're using an
official sports book or engaging with a
prediction market. The purpose of
engaging in the activity for monetary
gain is the same. So here's the problem,
Mr. Chairman. Tribes in my district and
across the nation have gone through
decades-long negotiations, agreements,
and settlements with states and the
federal government to have the ability
to engage in sports betting. States
themselves have as well. They've built
out legal gaming systems with compacts,
licensing, integrity rules, age
verification, and consumer protections.
So when a federal agency like the CFTC
allows prediction markets to bypass
these established long-standing legal
requirements but under a different label
and uses loopholes to evade regulation
and consumer protection standards, it it
undermines tribal sovereignty and state
protection. What this means in practical
terms is that tribal communities like
the Pueblo of Laguna in my district,
which I just visited, are losing out on
vital revenue to pay for their child
care, education, infrastructure, and the
overall well-being of their community.
Not fair, right? Now I understand the
CFTC's role is to oversee derivatives
markets. Traditionally, that has meant
helping businesses hedge real economic
risk. Airlines hedge fuel costs, farmers
hedge crop prices. That is very
different from putting money on the
outcome of a baseball game. On a
prediction market, consumers can trade
on whether, as an example, Astro second
baseman Jose Altuve hits a home run in
tonight's game against the Rockies. Does
a contract on a single player's
performance on a single statistic hedge
any real economic risk?
Congressman, there are many risks that
could be hedged through various
contracts in our markets. The bottom
line is that these markets need to be
well-functioning and and comprehensively
regulated by the CFTC. Our statute
mandates it and we'll continue to do it.
Well, Commissioner, with all due
respect, I don't think this is hedging.
I think this is a bet as is clearly
outlined
in in the way that these transactions
are taking place. And so let me make
this clear. Uh the CFTC was not created
or intended to regulate sports gambling.
States and tribes have systems for
licensing, integrity monitoring, and
responsible gaming such as age
verification and addiction support and
enforcement. If this product looks like
sports betting, the public should expect
sports betting type of protections and
regulations. So at the end of the day,
this comes down to a simple question.
Are we regulating real economic risk or
are we allowing prediction markets to
steal billions of dollars in an
unregulated free-for-all with no
consumer protection as Congress and the
CFTC turns a blind eye? The CFTC should
focus on ensuring that the integrity of
the derivatives and commodities markets,
ensuring that farmers and businesses
receive fair prices and protections, and
preventing our country from facing
another financial crisis. That should be
the focus. I believe the CFTC does not
have the know-how and it doesn't need to
be focused on sports betting because our
tribes and our states can't do that. Now
in your earlier comments in your
introduction, you mentioned what you
were focused on was modernization, rapid
speed, and response to innovation, and
that is your focus. Now what I did see
with rapid speed was the withdrawal of
the 2000 2024 proposed rule on political
and sports contracts. What I would also
similarly like to see in terms of that
rapid speed and response to innovation
and modernization is actual regulation
so that we can allow our tribal
communities, our tribal nations with
their own negotiated contracts not to
lose out on vital revenue for their
communities as these event contract
managers enter states like New Mexico
where online gambling is already legal.
This is crucial for our tribes, and I
suggest that you talk to the Indian
Gaming Association about how they feel
about this because they do represent
gaming casinos on tribal nations all
across the country. So let's be clear. I
support innovation. However, I am deeply
concerned about current and growing gaps
in the existing regulatory regime and
the lack of investigation from the CFTC
into unethical behavior. Public
reporting has described highly
suspicious, well-timed trading ahead of
the US-Iran ceasefire announcement.
Ruder Reuters also reported the White
House warned staff not to use their
positions to place market bets amid
concerns about insider trading and
suspicious trading around Iran-related
events.
This raises serious questions around
public trust and corruption risk when
markets are tied to government actions,
political outcomes, diplomacy, and
official decisions. So my concern is
simple. As the CFTC takes on more
responsibility, Congress needs
confidence that the agency has the
resources, the staffing, the legal
clarity, and the enforcement posture to
adequately regulate these markets, allow
innovation to advance, and protect
consumers. So, [snorts] Chairman, giving
the Commission's vacancies, expired
reauthorizations, current staffing
constraints, and growing workload, do
you believe the CFTC today has the
staff, technology, and enforcement
capacity to effectively oversee not only
the traditional derivatives markets but
also digital assets and rapidly
expanding prediction markets?
Congressman, we're running more
efficiently and effectively than ever
before thanks to right-sizing things
within the building, and this is all
thanks to the President's leadership. We
are a cop on the beat. We're policing
fraud, manipulation, and insider
trading, and I think your allegations to
to the contrary are completely
unfounded.
Well,
that's interesting. What more do you all
need from Congress in order to ensure
that you have an agency that is
well-resourced enough to respond to the
market innovation that we have seen
explode in the last few years?
Congresswoman, we are adequately staffed
right now. We're continuing to bring on
new staff, and the resumes speak for
themselves. As I've said, we've brought
on real experts from the outside of uh
you know, private sector expertise, and
we're functioning better than ever. It's
really critical that we continue to
bring on new software systems like AI
tools and surveillance uh tools to make
sure that we're better suited to police
the markets, but we are running very
effectively and efficiently, and I think
a lot of this um fake news out there
about uh us being under-resourced is
incorrect. We have a very well-resourced
building, and we'll continue to fulfill
our mission. Just a point of
clarification. So you said you're
adequate adequately staffed, and you're
bringing on more staff. So which one is
it? Congresswoman, we are bringing on
additional talent where it can be
helpful to fulfill our mission, but we
have the staff and resources to make
sure that we're carrying out our mandate
as an agency.
Will you commit to
robust enforcement ensuring anyone
trading on government or military
information is held accountable
regardless of their political party?
Congressman, as I've said countless
times today, we have a zero-tolerance
policy. That's zero tolerance. That
means that we will hold whoever is
engaging in fraudulent, manipulative, or
insider trading activity accountable to
the American people.
Well,
I think what
this boils down to, and I'm going to
give you credit for agreeing with the
fact that these are dangerous issues
related to national security. So
I'm going to I appreciate your
commitment to holding bad actors
accountable and hope to work together to
crack down on anyone endangering our
national security and our troops with
these types of bets. That's why I sent a
letter to Polymarket last week
instructing the company to preserve and
share with Congress all information
related to suspicious bets on national
security matters that may link to
government officials.
I ask unanimous consent to enter my
letter into the record.
Without objection.
Thank you, Chair.
So we need to find out who's placing
these bets, no matter how high-level or
well-connected they are, and hold them
accountable. For more content like this,
stay tuned to Congress Clips, and thanks
for watching.

This is crucial for our tribes, and I suggest that you talk to the Indian Gaming Association about how they feel about this because they do represent gaming casinos on tribal nations all across the country. So let's be clear. I support innovation. However, I am deeply concerned about current and growing gaps in the existing regulatory regime and the lack of investigation from the CFTC into unethical behavior. Public reporting has described highly suspicious, well-timed trading ahead of the US-Iran ceasefire announcement. Ruder Reuters also reported the White House warned staff not to use their positions to place market bets amid concerns about insider trading and suspicious trading around Iran-related events. This raises serious questions around public trust and corruption risk when markets are tied to government actions, political outcomes, diplomacy, and official decisions. So my concern is simple. As the CFTC takes on more responsibility, Congress needs confidence that the agency has the resources, the staffing, the legal clarity, and the enforcement posture to adequately regulate these markets, allow innovation to advance, and protect consumers. So, [snorts] Chairman, giving the Commission's vacancies, expired reauthorizations, current staffing constraints, and growing workload, do you believe the CFTC today has the staff, technology, and enforcement capacity to effectively oversee not only the traditional derivatives markets but also digital assets and rapidly expanding prediction markets? Congressman, we're running more efficiently and effectively than ever before thanks to right-sizing things within the building, and this is all thanks to the President's leadership. We are a cop on the beat. We're policing fraud, manipulation, and insider trading, and I think your allegations to to the contrary are completely unfounded. Well, that's interesting. What more do you all need from Congress in order to ensure that you have an agency that is well-resourced enough to respond to the market innovation that we have seen explode in the last few years? Congresswoman, we are adequately staffed right now. We're continuing to bring on new staff, and the resumes speak for themselves. As I've said, we've brought on real experts from the outside of uh you know, private sector expertise, and we're functioning better than ever. It's really critical that we continue to bring on new software systems like AI tools and surveillance uh tools to make sure that we're better suited to police the markets, but we are running very effectively and efficiently, and I think a lot of this um fake news out there about uh us being under-resourced is incorrect. So which one is it? Will you commit to robust enforcement ensuring anyone trading on government or military information is held accountable regardless of their political party? Congressman, as I've said countless times today, we have a zero-tolerance policy. That's zero tolerance. That means that we will hold whoever is engaging in fraudulent, manipulative, or insider trading activity accountable to the American people. Well, I think what this boils down to, and I'm going to give you credit for agreeing with the fact that these are dangerous issues related to national security. So I'm going to I appreciate your commitment to holding bad actors accountable and hope to work together to crack down on anyone endangering our national security and our troops with these types of bets. That's why I sent a letter to Polymarket last week instructing the company to preserve and share with Congress all information related to suspicious bets on national security matters that may link to government officials. I ask unanimous consent to enter my letter into the record. Without objection. Thank you, Chair. So we need to find out who's placing these bets, no matter how high-level or well-connected they are, and hold them accountable. metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of Prediction Market Movers, host Chris Gerlacher sits down with Andrew Kim, Partner at Goodwin Law and one of the leading attorneys advising fintech, trading, and derivatives platforms. Together they unpack the real stakes behind the Kalshi case and what it means for the future of prediction markets in the U.S.

Andrew breaks down how federal regulators — especially the CFTC — are approaching event contracts, why states are suddenly redefining what counts as a “swap,” and how recent court decisions could reshape the entire industry. From Nevada’s interpretation battles to the broader question of whether political and event markets should fall under gambling law or derivatives law, this episode gives you the clearest legal roadmap you’ll hear anywhere.

The conversation also explores:

- The newest developments in the Kalshi–CFTC legal fight
- How state definitions of swaps may conflict with federal jurisdiction
- The collision between crypto, prediction markets, and traditional financial regulation
-What responsible trading should look like as markets grow

#PredictionMarkets #Kalshi #CFTC #EventContracts #Swaps #GoodwinLaw #FintechLaw #Regulation #SportsBettingLaw #CryptoMarkets #ResponsibleTrading #ChrisGerlacher #AndrewKim

35:00 - The future of a decision

For more information on the prediction markets visit www.prediction news.com

metadata.shortDescription:
In Europe, operators chase affiliates. In the US, affiliates chase the operators - and if you don't land a deal with a licensed brand, your traffic is just wasted. Levon Nikoghosyan, Founder and CEO of AffPapa, the largest affiliate-operator directory in iGaming, sees the deal flow the rest of the market never sees. We break down where US and Latin American affiliates actually make money in 2026.

Recorded one week before AffPapa Conference landed in Cancun, on the Where Is My Money Podcast.

📢 PARTNER

🅰️ AffPapa Conference - Cancun, November 23-25. Operators, affiliates and B2B brands, real Latin American deals, dedicated recording stand on the floor. Peaky Ads is the official podcast partner. Want a broadcast like this one? DM Vasilii on LinkedIn or write hello@peakyads.com.
🔗 {AffPapa Conference URL}

👤 ABOUT THE GUEST
Levon Nikoghosyan - Founder and CEO of AffPapa. Started as a physicist and programmer, spent 7 years building affiliate software at Partner Matrix, then grew AffPapa into an ecosystem: the directory, iGaming Club events, Venture Papa, The Gamblist and the AffPapa Conference series.
🔗 Levon on LinkedIn: {URL}
🔗 AffPapa: {URL}

✅ Why US affiliates chase operators while in Europe it's the other way around
✅ What Brazil's ban actually did to affiliate traffic - and where the money went
✅ Why Mexico is set up to become the LatAm iGaming hub (50% tax, no standalone online license)
✅ The #1 reason affiliate-operator deals fall apart - and it's not the money
✅ How deal structures are shifting from RevShare and CPA to spend campaigns

01:46 - Who is Levon Nikoghosyan and what is AffPapa
03:09 - From physics student to iGaming (expelled, no regrets)
04:57 - The #1 data pattern: AI eating SEO traffic
08:01 - Why affiliate-operator deals die: lack of trust
13:35 - Red flags of a new operator before you sign a deal
16:36 - US market: why your traffic is wasted without a licensed brand
19:20 - US vs Europe: who chases whom
20:53 - Sweepstakes, prediction markets and Polymarket on AffPapa
25:44 - Brazil's ban: no gambling ban in 20 years ever worked
34:33 - Mexico: the next LatAm iGaming hub
41:22 - Which LatAm country to start with in 2027
46:58 - Deal structures: RevShare, CPA and spend campaigns
50:36 - Building the AffPapa ecosystem (no middleman fees)

In this episode of The iGaming SEO Show by Big Pond Digital, Ari is joined by experienced affiliate manager Tero Päivärinta to talk about the changing relationship between iGaming affiliates, operators and iGaming SEO, and what AI search could mean for the traditional affiliate model.

We get into whether operators are becoming too reliant on affiliates, rising acquisition costs, CPA vs revenue share, player quality and whether some operators are paying affiliates for players they could be acquiring directly.

We also look at why affiliates have historically been so strong at SEO, whether operators should be investing more aggressively in their own organic acquisition, and what happens when affiliates start competing with operators across branded and non-branded search.

Then we move into GEO and AI search.

What happens when players start asking ChatGPT for recommendations instead of searching Google? Could affiliate sites become important sources for AI recommendations? And could visibility across Google and AI platforms eventually influence how much an affiliate placement is worth?

We cover:

• The state of iGaming affiliate marketing in 2026
• CPA, revenue share and the real value of an FTD
• Why affiliates have traditionally dominated iGaming SEO
• Operators vs affiliates in Google
• Brand SERP protection
• SEO strategies for affiliates in 2026/27
• ChatGPT, GEO and AI search
• How AI could change comparison sites
• Affiliates as part of an operator's GEO strategy
• The future of iGaming player acquisition

Plus, Ari puts Tero on the spot with a few uncomfortable questions, including whether affiliates are overpaid, whether revenue share is still sustainable, and where he'd put £1 million of acquisition budget today.

Subscribe to The iGaming SEO Show for more conversations around iGaming SEO, GEO, AI search, link building and organic acquisition.

Big Pond Digital
Precision SEO for iGaming Brands

metadata.title: Are CPA and RevShare Models Starting to Change? | Paul Puolakka
metadata.author: iGaming Real Talk Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
In Episode 80 of iGaming Real Talk, recorded at AffPapa, our host Surya Palli was with iGaming Marketing Executive Paul Puolakka to discuss how CPA, RevShare and hybrid affiliate models are changing as traffic becomes harder and more expensive to acquire.

Paul explains why affiliates and operators may need to work more closely after acquisition, why long-term player value matters more than simply counting FTDs, and how affiliation could expand beyond traditional SEO into a broader media model supported by AI, testing and better data.

What the industry is facing:

- Traffic is becoming harder and more expensive to acquire
- Affiliates have limited control once they send players to an operator
- Poor retention can reduce the value of traffic for both affiliates and operators
- Data and transparency between affiliates and operators remain a challenge
- Focusing too heavily on FTDs can overlook long-term player value
- Changes in Google, ChatGPT and search behaviour are pushing affiliates beyond traditional SEO

What this conversation explores:

- How CPA, RevShare and hybrid affiliate models could evolve
- Why affiliates may become more like media businesses across multiple channels
- How affiliates and operators could work together on CRM and player reactivation
- Why long-term player value should matter more than FTD volume
- How AI could support retargeting, A/B testing and tracking
- What new affiliates should focus on when entering the market
- How affiliates test new markets and decide where to invest
