metadata.author: 3SNET

Affiliates in iGaming are increasingly coming under direct regulation, with rules for CPA, RevShare, SEO and influencer traffic changing across multiple countries.
In this video, we break down what is happening in Bulgaria, Brazil, Japan and the Philippines, and how the new requirements are affecting affiliates, operators, advertising channels and payment infrastructure.

📌 Detailed analysis with figures, requirements and the potential impact on affiliates:

metadata.title: iGaming Affiliate Marketing in 2027: What Operators Need to Get Right | SiGMA Rome
metadata.author: Ace Alliance
metadata.shortDescription:
📊 Is quality becoming more important than quantity in iGaming affiliate marketing?

As customer acquisition becomes more competitive, operators are paying closer attention to where their traffic comes from, how well it converts, and the actual value each partnership delivers. Simply generating high volumes of clicks is no longer enough. The focus is shifting towards quality traffic, meaningful KPIs and stronger relationships between operators and affiliates.

At SiGMA Rome, Ace Alliance spoke with Erica Anderson, VP of Marketing and Product at Income Access, A Paysafe Experience, about the evolution of affiliate marketing, changing acquisition strategies, and what operators should prioritise heading into 2027.

📊 What we discuss

• Why traffic quality is becoming more important than traffic volume
• How operators can evaluate affiliate and media partnerships
• The growing importance of high-value KPIs and conversion data
• How Income Access is evolving beyond traditional affiliate tracking technology
• Connecting operators with traffic sources and acquisition opportunities
• Why regulated markets and compliant partnerships matter
• How affiliates can use data to deliver more value to operators
• Why communication and collaboration are essential for successful affiliate programmes
• How operators can get more from their existing affiliate partnerships
• The role of AI and technology in customer acquisition
• Why the human element will remain essential in iGaming marketing in 2027

🎯 Quality traffic and meaningful partnerships

One of the biggest changes Erica identifies is the industry's growing focus on the value of traffic rather than simply its volume. Operators want to understand where their visitors come from, what converts and whether their acquisition partnerships are delivering the right results.

This also means looking more carefully at media and affiliate partners, particularly when entering new markets. Understanding local audiences, working with suitable partners and focusing on relevant KPIs can help operators build more sustainable acquisition strategies.

🤝 Beyond tracking: The evolution of Income Access

Income Access has traditionally been known for its affiliate tracking technology, but its offering is evolving.

Erica explains how the business is working to connect operators with additional traffic opportunities, while continuing to provide the data and insights needed to understand campaign performance and optimise acquisition across multiple channels.

The goal is to combine technology with a deeper understanding of affiliates and their business models, helping operators make better decisions about where and how they acquire customers.

🚀 What should iGaming operators focus on in 2027?

Erica's advice is to get back to the fundamentals of marketing: know your KPIs, understand your traffic sources, and communicate regularly with your partners.

Rather than simply setting up affiliate relationships and waiting for results, operators should ask affiliates what they need to perform better, understand what is working, and identify where improvements can be made.

Technology and AI will continue to influence customer acquisition, but relationships remain just as important. Behind every click and conversion is a person, and successful marketing still depends on understanding people.

For affiliate marketers, operators and iGaming professionals, this conversation explores why the next stage of acquisition is about better partnerships, better data and better-quality traffic.

👤 About Erica Anderson

Erica Anderson is VP of Marketing and Product at Income Access, A Paysafe Experience.

https://www.linkedin.com/in/ericaanderson81/

metadata.title: World Cup 2026 iGaming Affiliate Battle: SEO, AI, & End of Cheap Traffic
metadata.author: Revpanda Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Skyrocketing CPCs. The "Google Ads Hunger Games." And a $3.1 Billion betting pool. ⚽

World Cup 2026 is the most high-stakes traffic surge in iGaming history, but the old affiliate rules no longer apply. The market is facing a brutal margin squeeze, driven by AI-generated content and hyper-expensive traffic. The affiliates and operators who rely on traditional, "click-and-forget" SEO are going to look back and realize they were running a completely outdated playbook.

In the fourth episode of our World Cup 2026 Series, Faruk Aydin sits down with a panel of absolute industry powerhouses to break down the technical and commercial clash of the 2026 tournament. Discover why utility apps and Reddit are outperforming legacy SEO, how to prevent massive revenue leaks during tracking stress tests, and how to scale your business to capture the $3.1 Billion global betting pool.

🎤 Meet the Playmakers:
John Wright – Co-Founder at StatsDrone
Fraser Bricknell – Founder at Tipman Group
Marcin Kumiega, MBA – Business Development Director at Voluum

🚀 What You’ll Learn:
🔥 The Paid Traffic Reality Check: How to optimize your ad spend and survive the intense CPC bidding wars during matchdays.

📱 Audience Ownership over Clicks: Why capturing registrations, email, and SMS via dedicated apps or active community channels beats legacy search keywords.

🛡️ Revenue Leak Prevention: How to protect your affiliate margins and ensure your tracking stack handles the ultimate tournament traffic spikes without dropping data.

🤖 Smart AI Integration: Why long-term winners aren't using pure AI automation, but rather pairing AI statistical processing with professional human context.

📍 The Micro-Keyword Strategy: Why chasing broad terms like "World Cup betting" is a losing game compared to localized, granular player props and micro-markets.

🌎 The Transatlantic Opportunity: Tactical insight into capturing the newly shifted North American sports betting power center.

🤝 This Episode is Brought to You By:
✅ TrafficStars ✅ Boomerang Partners ✅ Traffy

Most payment apps prohibit online casinos and sportsbooks. Here's how iGaming payment processing works for licensed operators: where online gambling is legal, merchant category codes and card network registration, what underwriters check, deposits, declines, payouts, chargebacks, the gray zone of sweepstakes, skill games and fantasy sports, costs and how long approval takes. Gambling merchant accounts: https://adaptivpayments.com/industry/gambling-merchant-account

What's covered
1. Why gambling is high-risk: legal state by state, a target for fraud and money laundering, more disputes. Visa treats online gambling as high-integrity risk.
2. Where it's legal: sports betting in nearly 40 states plus DC (about 30 with mobile); online casino gaming in a handful of states, including New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Michigan. Sweepstakes casinos are banned in several states, including California and New York.
3. Codes and registration: MCC 7995 with the online gambling indicator; 7801 for US-licensed online casinos and sportsbooks. Visa and Mastercard both require registration before you process.
4. What banks check: state licenses, identity and age checks, geolocation, responsible gaming tools, AML program, owners with 25% or more, and Visa's site disclosure.
5. Deposits: debit cards, ACH and bank transfer, digital wallets. Massachusetts and Iowa ban credit cards for sports betting, and issuers often treat gambling as a cash advance.
6. Declines: some issuers block gambling transactions. Offer another way to pay at the decline.
7. Payouts: winnings go out as payouts, not refunds (a Visa Original Credit Transaction to the card, or ACH), and only to the verified player.
8. Chargebacks: no 3-D Secure liability shift on US gambling codes, and no special chargeback allowance for gambling.
9. The gray zone, costs, backup processors, and how long approval takes.

What to bring: your gaming license for each state, company documents and owner IDs, a legal opinion, your identity, age and geolocation providers, your responsible gaming policy and your processing history.

How gambling affiliate commission models actually work.

You’ve probably heard the terms Rev Share, CPA, and Hybrid Deals — but what do they mean in practice? And more importantly, which one is right for your business model, traffic sources, and long-term goals?

This video will give you everything you need to know to make an informed, profitable choice — so you don’t leave money on the table or sign up for deals that don’t suit your strategy.

What Rev Share, CPA, and Hybrid affiliate models actually mean

The pros and cons of each deal type — based on real-world affiliate experience

How each model fits different business styles: blogs, YouTube, paid ads, influencers, and more

What negative carryover is (and why it matters)

How to avoid signing deals with shady fine print or unrealistic player requirements

The exact questions to ask before choosing a gambling affiliate program

Tips on how to balance short-term income with long-term passive growth

Whether you're brand new or looking to optimize your existing deals, this video is your no-fluff, straight-talking guide to commission structures in the iGaming industry.

Commission Models Explained:

🔹 Rev Share (Revenue Share)
Earn a percentage (typically 20%–40%) of your players’ net losses over time.
✅ Great for SEO-driven content and long-term passive income.
⚠️ Be cautious of programs with negative carryover — they can wipe out your month.

🔹 CPA (Cost Per Acquisition)
Get a fixed fee (like $100–$250) every time a player signs up and deposits.
✅ Ideal for paid traffic, influencer marketing, or quick cash flow.
⚠️ Often comes with strict qualification rules and referral caps.

🔹 Hybrid Deals
The best of both worlds? Maybe. You get a smaller CPA + reduced rev share.
✅ A balanced approach when testing new traffic sources.
⚠️ Can result in lower total earnings if you’re not careful.

📌 Which One Should You Choose?

Running a content site or YouTube channel? → Go with Rev Share

Running paid ads or high-volume social media? → CPA might be better

Testing mixed traffic or just starting out? → Try Hybrid or CPA

Already got conversion data and stable traffic? → Scale with Rev Share

Every affiliate business is different — the goal is to align your monetization with your traffic intent, consistency, and audience behavior.

Before joining any affiliate program, ask these questions:

✅ Does the rev share model include negative carryover?
✅ Are CPA payouts locked behind strict terms or thresholds?

metadata.title: The Future of Affiliate Marketing in iGaming: SlotCatalog’s New Marketplace | SBC Summit Lisbon 26
metadata.author: Ace Alliance
metadata.shortDescription:
🎮 Is the traditional affiliate model still enough to build a major iGaming business?

Affiliate marketing remains a major part of the iGaming industry, but established affiliates are finding new ways to create value beyond player acquisition. With access to valuable audience data, strong operator relationships and extensive game databases, companies can develop new products and become more influential across the industry.

At SBC Summit Lisbon 2026, Magda Klimko-Aydin spoke with Mickey Winitsky, Investor and Managing Partner at SlotCatalog, to discuss the company's evolution from a B2C affiliate business into a broader B2B player, including its new marketplace connecting affiliates and operators.

🎮 What we discuss

• Why SlotCatalog is expanding beyond its traditional affiliate business
• How its new marketplace connects operators and affiliate partners
• What SlotCatalog's position between operators and affiliates makes possible
• How affiliate companies are becoming more influential in the iGaming ecosystem
• How audience data can help shape industry decisions
• What SlotCatalog's database of more than 55,000 reviewed games offers partners
• How operators can use data to make better decisions about target markets
• How game providers can use insights to inform game features and development
• Why B2B products are becoming an important part of SlotCatalog's strategy
• Whether the traditional affiliate model will be enough to support long-term growth

📊 From B2C affiliate to B2B marketplace

SlotCatalog has spent more than a decade building relationships with operators and attracting players through its affiliate business. Mickey explains how the company is now using its position in the ecosystem to create new opportunities for both sides.

Its new marketplace is designed to bring operators and affiliates together, allowing affiliates to connect with operators through SlotCatalog's existing relationships and network. This represents a significant step in the company's evolution from a primarily B2C model towards a combined B2C and B2B business.

🧠 Turning iGaming data into business value

SlotCatalog's game database has grown to more than 55,000 reviewed games, while the company attracts around 1.5 million unique people daily, according to Mickey.

That scale creates opportunities to turn audience and game data into practical insights for industry partners. Operators can use the information to make more informed decisions about geographic markets, while game providers can gain insights to help guide decisions about game features and future development.

Rather than simply directing traffic to casino brands, SlotCatalog aims to use its data and industry relationships to contribute to decisions across the iGaming ecosystem.

🚀 Is affiliate marketing enough for the future?

Mickey expects affiliate revenue to remain a significant part of SlotCatalog's business for years to come. However, he believes that relying solely on sending traffic to operators is no longer enough to unlock the company's full potential.

Expanding into B2B creates another way to deliver value, using the company's audience insights, game database and relationships to support operators and providers. SlotCatalog's familiar guiding question, “what to play and where to play,” remains central to its approach as the business evolves.

For affiliate marketers, operators, game providers and iGaming entrepreneurs, this conversation explores how established businesses can build on their existing strengths while finding new ways to grow.

metadata.shortDescription:
Podcast by Pierre Lindh #69 - Michael Daly, CEO, Catena Media.

Together with Michael Daly, we talk about 'Catena Media Q2 results and what comes next'.

✌️Pierre’s iGaming NEXT Podcast is sponsored by Pragmatic Solutions – Leading iGaming platform technology. For more info, click here: https://bit.ly/3lSy1B5

🧐Michael Daly is the CEO for Catena Media, one of the largest lead generation companies for iGaming, Sports Betting, eSports and financial services worldwide. As such he oversees the company’s 400+ team and its global expansion across Europe, LATAM, APAC, and North America, where it is the dominant affiliate by value delivered to operators.

Prior to taking the reigns as CEO in March of 2021, Michael was the VP of North America for Catena Media, growing that business to over 50 affiliate sites, generating in the range of $40,000,000+ annually with a team of approximately 60, all working remotely.

Prior to Catena Media, Michael setup and ran divisions of online gambling technology companies, has rolled out numerous new products for banking and gaming, as well as served 8 years as a Naval Officer. He is a graduate of MIT and holds an MBA from the University of Utah.

metadata.title: How iGaming Affiliates Can Create Value for Operators and Studios
metadata.author: Ace Alliance
metadata.shortDescription:
📊 Can iGaming affiliates turn years of player data and industry experience into new B2B revenue streams?

For years, the primary goal of iGaming affiliates was to attract players and drive traffic to operators. But established affiliates have built more than audiences. They have accumulated valuable data, market knowledge, and insights that can create new opportunities across the industry.

In this episode of the Ace Alliance Podcast, Mykhailo Kachanov, Chief Business Officer at SlotCatalog, joins us to discuss how affiliate businesses can expand beyond traditional player acquisition, build relationships directly with game studios and suppliers, and turn years of experience into valuable B2B products and services.

We also explore The Mechanic Wars, our joint report examining slot game mechanics, what it takes to produce meaningful industry research, and how companies can make better decisions with the data available to them.

🎙️ What we discuss

• How established iGaming affiliates can develop new business models beyond traffic acquisition
• Why player insights and audience data can create value for operators and game studios
• How affiliates can turn years of data into B2B products and services
• What The Mechanic Wars reveals about popular slot game mechanics
• Why data needs context and interpretation to be useful
• How operators can learn from insights that their own analytics might not reveal
• How affiliates can build direct relationships with game studios and suppliers
• The opportunities that emerge when affiliate expertise becomes a business asset

📈 Beyond traffic: Building new B2B opportunities

Affiliate businesses spend years learning about player behaviour, content preferences and market trends. Mykhailo explains how this accumulated knowledge can become an additional source of value beyond traditional affiliate revenue.

By developing B2B services and working more closely with operators, game studios and suppliers, affiliates can use their experience to contribute to decisions across the iGaming ecosystem.

🎰 Inside The Mechanic Wars

Our joint report, The Mechanic Wars, explores popular slot mechanics and what industry data can reveal about the games attracting player interest.

But collecting numbers is only part of the process. Meaningful research requires careful interpretation, an understanding of the context behind the data and the ability to turn findings into useful insights.

The conversation looks at how research can help industry professionals understand trends more clearly and make more informed decisions about content and product development.

💡 What operators can learn from affiliate data

Operators have access to their own analytics, but affiliate businesses may see different patterns through their broader audience reach and experience across multiple brands and games.

Combining these perspectives can help operators and game studios identify opportunities, question assumptions and better understand player preferences.

For iGaming professionals, this episode explores how data, research and industry expertise can become valuable business assets, and why the affiliate model may offer opportunities well beyond sending traffic.

👤 Meet the guest

Mykhailo Kachanov is Chief Business Officer at SlotCatalog,

🎙️ About Ace Alliance

Ace Alliance connects and supports iGaming professionals through dynamic events, expert-led content, and strategic networking that drive growth and visibility. 


Follow Ace Alliance for more conversations with the people shaping the global iGaming industry.

#AceAlliance #iGaming #SlotCatalog #AffiliateMarketing #B2BiGaming #TheMechanicWars #GameData #SlotGames #iGamingPodcast

metadata.title: How iGaming Affiliates Can Create Value for Operators and Studios
metadata.author: Ace Alliance
metadata.shortDescription:
For years, the main goal of iGaming affiliates was to attract players and generate traffic. But what happens when years of experience, player data and industry knowledge become valuable products in their own right?

In this episode of the Ace Alliance Podcast, Mykhailo Kachanov, Chief Business Officer at SlotCatalog, joins us to discuss how affiliate businesses can develop new revenue streams, work directly with game studios and suppliers, and turn data into B2B services. We also talk about our joint The Mechanic Wars report, what goes into producing industry research, and how companies can make better use of the information available to them.

Key takeaways:
📈 How established iGaming affiliates can develop new business models
💡 Why player insights can be valuable to operators and game studios
📊 How affiliates can turn years of data into B2B products and services
🎰 What The Mechanic Wars reveals about popular slot mechanics
🔎 How to interpret data when the numbers don't tell the whole story
🎯 What operators can learn from affiliate data that their own analytics might miss

📅 Join us live on October 27 at 14:00 CET on LinkedIn and YouTube.

This episode is brought to you by Darpha Studios.

#AceAlliance #AceAlliancePodcast #iGaming #AffiliateMarketing #SlotCatalog

metadata.title: Sports Betting Taxes in 2025 + 2026: CPA Explains Why the 90% Rule Isn’t the End for Pros

metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode, we sit down with Gary Kondler (CPA) from Kondler & Associates to break down one of the hottest topics in the betting world right now — the “Big Beautiful Bill” and the change from 100% → 90% gambling loss deductions.

Gary gives a very different perspective than what many bettors have been hearing online:
👉 Professional sports betting is NOT ending in 2025.
👉 You should NOT panic about the new deduction rules.
👉 There are smart ways to structure your betting activity so you stay protected.

We cover everything sports bettors need to know heading into 2025:

📌 When you should consider filing as a professional
📌 Whether the “phantom income” fear is actually real
📌 How prediction markets fit into your tax picture
📌 What recreational bettors should expect
📌 How to keep clean, organized, defensible betting records
📌 What the IRS actually looks for
📌 And how the new rules might impact long-term bettors

If you bet seriously — or plan to — this is a must-watch conversation with one of the most respected CPAs in the gambling space.

Contact Gary directly for a free consultation 👇

https://kondlercpa.com

metadata.title: The CFTC’s Vision for Prediction Markets with Dorothy DeWitt | Prediction Market Movers
metadata.author: PredictionNews
metadata.shortDescription:
Former CFTC official Dorothy DeWitt joins Chris Gerlacher on Prediction Market Movers for an in-depth look at the evolution of prediction markets, Kalshi’s early years, and the regulatory challenges shaping the industry today.

DeWitt led the CFTC team that worked on Kalshi’s designation as a Designated Contract Market, giving her a unique perspective on how Kalshi navigated the regulatory process and what the CFTC was thinking about prediction markets in the early days. She explains the original pitch behind Kalshi, the challenges surrounding event contracts and self-certification, and how regulators approached an entirely new type of exchange.

The conversation then turns to the biggest issues facing prediction markets in 2026, including CFTC regulation, prediction market guardrails, SEC-CFTC harmonization, and the classification of prediction market products. DeWitt explains why perpetuals are so important for institutionalizing prediction markets, why swaps versus futures classification matters, and the potential regulatory consequences of exchanges listing contracts with securities-related characteristics.

DeWitt also dives into arbitration and customer disputes, conflicts of interest, exchange rulebooks, market surveillance, and the importance of developing a taxonomy for prediction market contracts. She explains why a well-designed taxonomy could help bring institutional liquidity into the industry while also giving regulators and exchanges better tools to monitor manipulation, insider trading, and other forms of market abuse.

👉 Subscribe to Prediction Market Movers for weekly conversations with traders, legal experts, entertainers and industry insiders shaping the future of prediction markets.

For more information on the Prediction Edge and the upcoming midterms visit www.predictionedge.com

And you know, there were some uh ups and downs on our end and there were a few on their end that well, we all got it all worked out and you know, here they are. >> Once you get past that first year in operation, once we're past 2020, it's the second year. There's more of a relationship there. There's also a new administration. What is the approach to prediction market in the early Biden years um aside from the election contract case that is going to be well known by this audience? >> Yes, so what we discovered in 2020, and this is under the early Biden administration >> [clears throat] >> is that the Commodities Exchange Act in relation to event contracts did not match the rule promulgated by the CFTC implementing that statute. They were just different and I can explain why if you want. And that was a real challenge like how do we address this? We don't think that the rule was intended at all to be inconsistent but you know, mistakes happen in rule making all the time. This rule had been implemented in about uh 2011 or 12 and the act says that if there are certain types of contracts gaming or terrorism things that are against state or federal law and and things like that the CFTC may conduct a public interest review and if it decides that uh after conducting that review that it's against the public interest then it can stay that contract. Don't know what the criteria are for public interest review. The rule itself says we were the the the the act I'm sorry the act suggests that it's contract by contract review but the rule itself that was promulgated in 2011 or 2012 says categorically but on a categorical basis those enumerated contracts war terrorism gaming etc. etc. are are banned and it's not clear that a public interest review is performed and it's on a category not a contract by contract basis etc. And so they didn't match like when the public interest review happens and how and whether it's categorical or um or or or by contract uh so they didn't match. So what are we going to do? And we didn't fix or change that rule and it hasn't been fixed or changed since. There was a proposal under later Biden administration to make some changes but that that didn't take effect and the CFTC later uh lost in district court in kind of early early action in the in the appeals court before the CFTC withdrew it under the new administration. So there there's some new rule-making that's trying to reconcile the rule and the act, which is good. Good, you know, good on the CFTC. >> We'll get into guardrails in a few minutes. I want to hover a little bit on 2025 and 2026, where you have acting director Carolyn Pham and now we've got Mike Stealing in his chairmanship. What are the main differences between these two people who a lot of people may see as a like one continuous mass tenure? >> It's great It's a great question. I don't see them as different in direction. I see them more as sequential and consistent. So Carolyn Pham was the acting chairperson at the CFTC. She had She was a chair who was Republican and she had two During a change of administration, the the minority party folks can tend to resign and so can the majority if they don't get the chairmanship. And so she had, you know, at one point two Democrats and herself, so you it's hard to get an affirmative vote on, for example, an enforcement action, etc., that, you know, is maybe consistent with the sprint that Carolyn Pham wanted to do. But eventually she everyone left and she became the only chairperson at the CFTC, which was the first. And you can get a lot more done if you're the single chairperson. You could also be, you know, you're everything you do is also subject to litigation risk because you're doing it as a single chairperson. So she did a lot of work of avoiding or remediating what she saw as regulation by enforcement. She appended the enforcement department and got got rid of a lot of senior enforcement folks. She also pursued, you know, crypto and prediction market friendly policies. And it's hard to know how much direction she had from the administration. The administration had Giancarlo and Atkins and Tarbert, former Republican chair pre people to make sure that they understood kind of the key issues. And I think the administration and the CFTC are working fairly seem it appears my sense is they're working fairly seamlessly together to implement the administration's priorities. And as you can see from chats and, you know, um gatherings in the White House of of uh of those who own companies that offer prediction markets, the administration is very favorable to the industry. >> What about Mike Ceeleg? What is his apparent priorities been as we've uh seen him in the chair for almost a year now? >> Yeah, so his priorities have been fairly consistent in that he said early on, we want to onshore perpetuals and we want to allow for real perpetuals to trade. And he's done that. Um he has also said, you know, we want clarity as to who has who has uh jurisdiction over what SEC and CFTC. We want to have harmonization between the SEC and CFTC and they have done that. That's always been a challenge. I I knew myself I I worked very well with the my counterparts at the SEC and there were times that, you know, we didn't see eye to eye and the commission didn't see eye to eye, but I think they have been working very hard to have uh harmonization and coming up with some creative ideas like if you need to be registered with the CFTC and the SEC, historically you'd be it just be two different processes. You'd be examined by both. You're kind of facing off to do two different regulators. The SEC The SEC is much more prescriptive. CFTC has is principles-based, so it's a little it's more flexible in some ways that you can comply with all the requirements. And that can be very hard. And so, I think the CFTC and the SEC have come up with some are working on coming up with some very creative solutions of like a primary regulator to secondary regulator. You know, there may be some litigation challenges around that to make sure that those, you know, those um structures are consistent with the with the act with the act. Um but anytime you have a unitary commissioner, just one commissioner instead of five, which is very very typical having five, um you you you're a little bit more subject to litigation challenge. And you can see that. The CME sued the CFTC on perpetuals. >> How might the legal landscape change if the next administration, regardless of party, Republican or Democrat, takes a look at the single chair model and says, "Well, let's do a chair of my party plus two more of my party, no more uh minority party." How one, how possible is it, and two, how might the uh the legal threat um or legal risk change in that scenario? >> Yeah, so two things have changed since the norm in the last administration of five commissioners and prior to that. The first is that the Supreme Court said that the president can fire commissioners at will as opposed to for cause. And so, as a result, it's harder to get minority commissioners to agree to the job. They're paid crazy low amounts uh the the commissioners, and they could move to DC and get fired anytime, right? So, you know, part of why you don't have Democratic commissioners may be because uh maybe in part because it's it's hard to find folks with experience. I think that's a real it's too bad, but um the second thing is that norms have been So, the Supreme Court has ruled. The second thing is that norms have changed. And so, those norms reflect that there's a unitary commissioner and etc. I think at a minimum the next administration would have let's say if it's uh the same administration or same party, it's probably going to stay consistent. If it's a different one like a Democrat administration, um I think at a minimum they would have a chairman and two Democrat commissioners, so you have three instead of one. And uh that sort of mitigates a little bit the some of the litigation vulnerability, but you know, I don't know whether they'll appoint five and I don't you know, it's hard to know. Like we're living in uncharted territory. >> Sure. Let me Well, I'll take us back into uncharted territory then and ask you about some of the guardrails that are beginning to go on the prediction market industry. So, I know Seelig has implemented some rule making and we're beginning to see restrictions and concerns become a little more uh obvious from the CFTC. What kinds of guardrails are beginning to be put on this young industry? >> Absolutely. Um so, first uh there's been a pause in some mention markets. Uh for example, Kalshi agreed to a pause in mention markets in sports based on some real concerns in the industry and the and the commission. Um Polymarket US doesn't currently have mention markets and the um FCM uh uh uh >> [clears throat] >> the some some of the FCMs are not allowing their customers. Robinhood, for example, doesn't allow its customers to trade mention markets. I think mention markets, in my my own view, as a former regulator that ran the group that reviewed application and self-certifications and whether things are readily susceptible manipulation. I have always thought mentioned markets are maybe inconsistent with core principle three. Which is you can't no exchange whether it's prediction or traditional contracts like oil or gas, no exchange can list a contract that's readily susceptible to manipulation and they have to do a big analysis on that among other analysis that gets submitted with a self-certification and the CFTC just came out with a kind of advisory guidance saying, you got to put more information into your self-certification. You don't see you and I don't see all that information because um it's it's redacted for FOIA protection, but the CFTC does and um it's clearly signaling it's not getting enough information to for for them to evaluate whether the self-certified contracts are consistent with regulations and core principles and such. So, I think that I I really laud the CFTC for that. Um they've also done some uh some guidance by staff on um on incentive programs and that that will be helpful as well. They basically have said you know, you have to if you're going to change your rulebook um DCMs have rulebooks they're usually like 100 pages and they include all kinds of things like how you're going to be you know, how discipline works and how trading works and how incentive programs work and affiliated market maker, you know, the market makers and how they address the incentive programs and and things like that and um and so DCMs have been filing rules in that rulebook or rulebook changes around incentive programs that the CFTC has recently communicated are insufficient or non-compliant with their obligations. And they've given some guidance on how to do that better. >> There are some other current industry issues that have become a little more, if not contentious, at least that have gotten more attention. And I want to turn to those. Why is vertical integration one of these increasingly hot topics in the industry right now? >> Yeah, it's funny. It's like with anything, um you know, when we designated Calchas in 2020, they were doing a lot of new types of contracts, but it really took to 2025 for it to be headline news. And all the issues that we were addressing in uh at first impression are issues that are at at issue in litigation and and other things. And the same thing with vertical integration. Vertical integration has been an issue for 10 years or more. So, vertical integration means an exchange, which is a DCM, an intermediary like a broker-dealer, which is an FCM, and a clearinghouse, which is a DCO. And vertical integration is where you have kind of all three in affiliated in one as subs in one entity. They're all three affiliated. And you might even introduce a fourth affiliate, which is an affiliated market maker. And vertical integration really poses some significant conflicts of interest that have to be addressed. So, for example, if the FCM is a member of the exchange, so it's an intermediated or hybrid model, and it's affiliated, there will likely also be other FCMs on the exchange. And so, does that FCM have access to additional information, which is conflicts of interest, information barriers? If the exchange goes down or there's some problem with the FCM or some problem with the the affiliated FCM, and or the affiliated FCM's customers, are they going to be treated the same or differently than all the other FCMs that are on the platform? There are lots of incentives, conflict of interest incentives in vertical integration that have been addressed and been the subject of concern by the commission for over a decade. But I think what's happening now is that there's a more of a willingness to designate all three plus an affiliated market maker. And so you're it's not just a theoretical concern. It's a it's a reality. And so that's why I think it's getting more recent attention. >> What are some of the proposed solutions to the conflicts of interest that accompany vertical integration? >> Yes, we we help um our clients on this all the time. Um So you want to make sure your rulebook, that that long document, is very clear on how your members are going to be treated and conflicts of interest are going to be addressed. There's a core principle that's specific to conflicts of interest. You need to basically identify all the conflicts of interest in your model, and then you need to go through them one by one and figure out how to uh mitigate or solve those conflicts of interest. You basically make a kind of matrix of conflicts. And then you, you know, you integrate policies and procedures and information barriers and and other type and other types of things like like um other types of thing in operating the exchange to make sure that everyone is being treated equally. And then when there is a problem, you need to make sure that everyone is treated equally, and that needs to be really well documented. And and because otherwise you'll get complaints from the other FCMs or from customers and things like that. And those complaints will go to the CFTC, and the CFTC will take them very seriously. And I I laud the commission for taking these conflicts of interest issues very seriously, and and as they should be. And I laud our clients for also doing that. There are not perfect, but very good kind of solutions or mitigants to most all of them and really the proof's in the pudding. It's one thing to have a policy to treat everyone equally and how, you know, the procedures as to what that means and how you operationalize that. It's another thing to actually do it in the middle of an issue. And so that's, you know, those are things you need to think through and we we work with clients on that all the time. >> [laughter] >> One of the other big issues is not only 24/7 trading, but now perps as well. Why is this structure of a contract so disruptive for the CFTC? >> It's it's a change in a few different ways. The CFTC has considered perpetuals to be over the years to be swaps or futures or futures or swaps. And different admit different chair people can and different commissions can change their interpretation consistent with kind of their remit. As long as those interpretations are reasonable, it's a little more challenging when they're kind of diametrically opposed. And you know, we're kind of skirting the border there. Um, up until very recently, these perps were considered swaps and the current chair has been very clear that he believes that they are futures. Futures usually expire. Like you have a futures in oil that expires in a month and another one that expires a month later and another one that expires a month later and you have to roll. So if you have a hedging position that expires this month, you have to roll to the one that expires the next month or further out in the future, etc. Um, and futures are kind of by definition, they expire and either cash is exchanged or there's physical physical delivery on a future date. Perpetuals don't have expiration. They uh go on forever in perpetuity and the way that they are you need to have alignment between the spot market and the futures market at expiration traditionally. And if when you don't have that it's it's a mess. The way that alignment is created in the real perpetuals market under the CFTC and and elsewhere is you know an exchange of payments that incentivizes the futures price to be consistent with the spot price. There are some benefits to futures. Um for example, if you have a a prediction market or something like that you have a bunch of people piled into a market and then the event happens and then all the liquidity goes away. And so there's a desire to institutionalize prediction markets and perpetuals can help doing that because you have continuous funding and you have continuous liquidity. You don't have you know cliff expirations where liquidity goes away and you hope liquidity will come back for the next event or next month and thing like things like that. So perpetuals are important for institutionalizing and bringing in liquidity. Uh but you know it's a little bit touchy as to how they're categorized and and and their you know their their use case and that's why CME sued the CFTC saying uh >> [clears throat] >> perpetuals are not futures. The other part about perpetuals is if they're on things that are traded on spot >> [snorts] >> the exchanges that do spot are probably going to lose some of their volume because it would be just as easy to get the equivalent of a spot position in a perpetual future without putting up as much money because you you know you've got some leverage and things like that. So it's a it's a real uh business model challenge. >> Walk me through why from the CFTC's perspective the regulatory difference between swaps and futures is so important for confronting some of these questions. >> Well, I'll just give you two examples. Um first of all the rate as a as a they're just treated differently under the law and the regulations, the Commodity Exchange Act and the regulations, and they have different swap being uh uh For something to be designated as a swap, there's a lot more regulatory requirements for trading. There's a very onerous swap data reporting uh mechanism and and and some other things like that. So, swaps can be a little bit onerous. But, swaps are the only avenue for prediction markets to have potentially um uh you know, the ability to trade nationwide and to to trump um state law in sports and a couple of other areas. So, the you you know, you're kind of pushing the swap definition for certain for prediction markets and you're pushing the futures definition for perpetuals. And you know, sometimes those can be often those can be consistent, there can be some inconsistencies there. Futures are more easily traded in the sort of operational and reporting and other mechanisms around futures are uh a little bit simpler. Uh so, I you know, one one wouldn't be wrong to wonder if those you know, pushing into each of those definitions, each of those products is related to a desired outcome. Uh and the key is whether there's consistency in the law and the rules and the application. >> One of the other interesting issues that I haven't seen discussed very much in this space is arbitration and customer disputes. How might the handling of those issues change in a mature prediction market industry? >> Yes, I've been thinking about that a lot. Uh So, most prediction market bets are pretty small. And you know, if you think back 20 years ago, exchanges if there were issues on exchanges, it was like some huge contract by Delta on fuel oil. Like, those were big denominations, right? And arbitrating something with a big denomination versus something with a 10, 20, 100, $200 denomination or or um uh notional, I mean, is a they're very different. And so, anything related to a broker-dealer uh the SRO for the industry um NFA does the arbitration on that, but for prediction markets, if I disagree with the outcome, say there's an ambiguous outcome and there's a decision, I'm just using an example by Kalshi, um Kalshi Let me just back up a little bit before I go there. Um under the law and statute, the exchanges can require arbitration uh for disputes. And those are in all the member agreements. And so, generally, everything is arbitrated. But let's go through the process. There's some event that happened this morning. I didn't agree with the resolution. I had, you know, money that was meaningful to me at stake, or maybe $10, you know, it doesn't even matter. And so, I Kalshi gives a fairly narrow window to file a kind of complaint, and they have a uh they have a um outcome resolution committee that looks at that. And they generally will have the outcome resolution committee review it, and then, you know, they may settle to make me whole, or they may half, or whatever it tends to be. If they don't, and I'm still unhappy, um I can ask for arbitration. And it's one thing if it's a huge number, it's another thing if it's smaller number. And so, there's some real creative solutions out there for arbitration. Like, I know the American Arbitration Association has an AI product that supports very small stakes as well as supports more cost-efficient large stake um arbitrations, and I think those types of um models can be really useful. Like AI with a very limited could, you know, decide very small disputes very cost-effectively. And I can see there there being some development in that area. >> Probably some new regulations as well, even for the smaller resolution sizes, I imagine. >> I don't know about new regulations. I think that I think the market will bear what the market will bear. If they are really unhappy, they can file a whistleblower complaint, um and you know, that can be part of a investigation because maybe they violated their rulebook or something like that. But I think there's going to be there's a future in small stakes arbitration in this industry, and probably big stakes, too. >> Well, it's going to be a fascinating area of the industry to watch grow. The other one, and this one I've seen a lot of headlines about, but I always feel short on detail, is uh the SEC-CFTC harmonization efforts. What is important and interesting there, and how how many of the announcements and press releases can I ignore until um Well, I'll let you go ahead and take that. I'm I'm rambling now. >> My guess is you'll see product listing approval that has securities and commodity uh attributes. Like maybe some of them are securities-based swaps, and some are commodities, um and that will be a approval or some relief or something like that from the CFTC and the SEC that will simplify the ability to list these things with either simplified registration with the SEC and the CFTC being the main um the main uh regulator or the other way around. I will say this. So, there was a, uh, Innovation Advisory Committee meeting last week, and that's like, um, the CFTC has like five committees, and they're, you know, they're kind of they're important, but they don't really get a lot of visibility outside the industry. It's like an Agriculture Committee and, um, Market Risk and things like that. They've been around forever, and usually one commissioner, there are five commissioners, one commissioner oversees each one of each. There's a new commis- committee that's called the Innovation Advisory Committee, and there's only one commissioner, so he's overseeing all the committees. And there are 35 members, and they're, you know, like Brian Armstrong and, um, you know, Glad and, uh, the the Winklevoss twins and other other, you know, really big big stakes, Kraken and other other big stakes, um, members. [clears throat] And they all convene last week. Never, I believe, in the history of these committees has it not been open to the public. Like, you just walk in and listen to the committee, you know. But bec- I imagine because the security risk of bringing together all those CEOs was so significant, it was only available online. Anyway, long story short, there were some fireworks a little bit, and the CBOE, um, the CEO really raised a very critical issue. CBOE has is listing under its SEC registration KPIs for companies. I don't know, like, will Tesla, you know, beat its manufacturing numbers or some specific stuff. And they call them KPIs. Cal-She has been listing KPIs, the kind of similar stuff, um, for a few years now. Now, regardless of what CBOE thinks or Cal-She thinks, there is a very colorable argument under securities law that if an exchange lists an unregistered security that hasn't had a um you know that hasn't been registered, there's a recession right by anyone who loses money against the exchange. And I've been thinking about that for several years now. They're you know some of the prediction markets are listing KPIs and um in the past when I was uh DMO director this I worked with my counterpart the SEC and they took took the position without uh compunction that a KPI like that is a security base swapped and they have to and the exchange has to be registered with the SEC. The key issue is not what the SEC is going to do about it, although that's important. The key issue is that a in civil court, I losing money on a KPI trade, can sue an exchange on KPI and the judge may determine that that is an unregistered security regardless of the SEC's input and then I have a recession right. And that could be like class action kind of stuff. So I think that's a real key issue that we're going to have to watch very carefully. Uh Atkin said a few months ago that he's very focused on prediction markets, but I think they'll come out with something publicly that may address that. And that may be the harmonization. >> Where does taxonomy fit into this conversation? >> Oh, taxonomy is my favorite topic. We have on our team two people who developed taxonomies for the CFTC and the SEC for swaps and that's a very big project. And um we are developing a taxonomy that the industry can use. In last week's meeting the industry said we don't want a taxonomy because it'll be a snapshot in time and we won't be able to innovate with flexibility. I actually disagree with that. A taxonomy is absolutely critical for market growth and for regulation and for um and for uh surveillance. Every asset class like securities and swaps and even crypto recently has a taxonomy. And the taxonomy is sort of breaking these contracts down into, you know, different categories and subcategories, etc. It's important for industry growth because a hedge fund will say, "Gee, I really want to put on a a hedge in for this type of risk, right?" But there's not a lot of exposure I mean, there's not a lot of liquidity there. And so, with a taxonomy, they can look at correlation. And they can say, "Well, this other contract which seems unrelated is really highly correlated, so there's a lot of liquidity there. I can put on a hedge." So, it's really important to be able to uh attract um institutional um trading and and other things to have a taxonomy. It's also important for uh you know, regulation and surveillance, and etc. If you can see if you have kind of identifiers in a taxonomy for each type of contract, you can do a lot more in preventing, detecting, and mitigating insider trading and other market abuse or manipulation, etc. etc. So, I think a taxonomy is a gift to the exchanges who are under pressure to, you know, identify these issues, a gift to the exchanges because more liquidity comes in with a taxonomy, and a gift to the CFTC because they're able to um also surveil and enforce um with a taxonomy much better. And it it just is a sign of a mature market. So, we have been working kind of offline to use our expertise to develop, you know, an open-source taxonomy that may be of use to um the industry. >> I know a lot of reporters will be looking forward to seeing it as well. And Dorothy, it's been so good to have you on and get all this explained to us. Where can we follow you, keep up with your work? >> Oh, thanks for asking. Um so, I'm on LinkedIn, I'm on X, and so is Toll Strategies. So, that And then, of course, we have our website, which is tollstrategies.com. >> Very easy to find. Well, you know where to find her and Toll Strategies. Here's where you find us. Follow us on X over at Prediction Edge, and subscribe to our YouTube channel right here at Prediction News. And while you're here, give this video a like. It's a great way to support the channel. We always appreciate the support. Dorothy, thanks again for coming on. >> Thank you.

metadata.shortDescription:
This video breaks down the key details of **CFTC Letter No. 25-26**, a crucial no-action letter that impacts binary options and event markets. We'll explore what this letter means for market participants and the future of trading in these unique financial products.


In this video, we'll dive into the intricacies of binary options, event markets, and the recent **Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) no-action letter, number 25-26**. The letter, issued to **Railbird Exchange, LLC** and **QC Clearing LLC**, provides temporary relief from certain swap data reporting and recordkeeping requirements for specific binary options and variable payout contracts.

We'll explain what a **no-action letter** is and why this one is significant for the designated contract market (DCM) and derivatives clearing organization (DCO). By understanding this regulatory move, you'll gain insight into how the CFTC is navigating the evolving landscape of event-based trading and the conditions under which these contracts can be offered.

metadata.title: 🔮What are @mention contracts? 🇺🇸CFTC staff's guidance to this new type of event contract 📈
metadata.author: 🎓Profeissor.com🚀Digital Assets, AI & FinTech
metadata.shortDescription:
🎬Video explainer | CFTC advisory on prediction markets listing "mention contracts".  
 
🎯 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 “𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝘀” 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗙𝗧𝗖 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱? 📢📊
Will a public figure use a particular word during a speech? 🎤
Will a CEO mention a specific term during an earnings call? 📈
Will two individuals appear together at an event? 📸
 
These questions can form the basis of event contracts known as “mention market” contracts.
 
The CFTC’s Division of Market Oversight has issued a staff advisory explaining why these contracts may present heightened manipulation risks and what regulated prediction markets should consider before listing them. ⚠️
 
🔍 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘀?
Event contracts allow market participants to take positions on whether future events will occur.
They are often structured around binary outcomes:
✅ Event occurs: payment is made
❌ Event does not occur: no payment is made
These contracts trade on prediction markets, where participants take positions on the likelihood of future events. 📊🔮
 
🗣️ 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁?
Many conventional event contracts settle on independently generated and externally verifiable outcomes, including:
📉 Economic data releases
🗳️ Election results
🏟️ Regulated sporting event outcomes
 
Mention market contracts are different because settlement depends on the discrete conduct of a named individual.
That individual, or someone with access to or influence over them, may be able to affect the outcome.
This creates distinct concerns about manipulation, nonpublic information and external pressure. 🚨
 
🏛️ 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗙𝗧𝗖 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲𝗱?
The CFTC regulates US derivatives markets, including futures, swaps and certain listed options.
Prediction markets offering event contracts to the public generally operate as CFTC-registered designated contract markets, or DCMs, subject to applicable exemptions or exclusions.
DCMs must comply with 23 statutory Core Principles under the US Commodity Exchange Act.
DCM Core Principle 3 requires DCMs to list only derivative contracts that are not readily susceptible to manipulation. 🛡️
 
⚠️ 𝗔 𝗿𝗲𝗯𝘂𝘁𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
CFTC staff may view mention market contracts as presumptively readily susceptible to manipulation.
A DCM seeking to list one should therefore expect to make a heightened showing in support of its submission. 📋🔍
But this is not an absolute ban. 🚫
In certain circumstances, a well-designed contract supported by appropriate trading rules, surveillance and controls may rebut the presumption.
 
CFTC staff identifies four particularly relevant factors:
 
1️⃣ 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀: Is the controlling individual subject to legal, professional, contractual, fiduciary, confidentiality or organizational obligations that deter conduct designed to affect settlement?
 
2️⃣ 𝗘𝘅𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲: Could someone influence the outcome through social engineering, inducements or public pressure campaigns directed at the controlling individual? 🎯
 
3️⃣ 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝘀𝗰𝗿𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘆: Can the outcome be transparently and independently verified?
Is the relevant conduct subject to contemporaneous and meaningful public scrutiny? 🔎
Words or actions occurring in informal or private settings, or involving nonpublic persons, may be especially difficult to verify.
Conduct lacking materiality or substantive impact may also escape meaningful scrutiny.
 
4️⃣ 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗿𝘂𝗹𝗲𝘀, 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹𝘀: Can the DCM identify potential controllers and known insiders, detect suspicious trading and prevent misuse of nonpublic information? 🕵️
 
Relevant measures may include:
✅ Position limits and position accountability
✅ Reporting and recordkeeping
✅ Identification of controllers and known insiders
✅ Enhanced market surveillance
✅ Contract-specific compliance controls
 
🔮 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴 𝗽𝗶𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲
Prediction markets continue to innovate, but contracts controlled or influenced by identifiable individuals raise distinctive market integrity risks.
 
The message for DCMs is clear:
📌 Engage with CFTC staff early
📌 Conduct a contract-specific risk assessment
📌 Identify potential controllers and known insiders
📌 Build safeguards around the actual manipulation risks
📌 Explain those safeguards clearly in regulatory submissions
 
💬 What do you think?
Can mention markets be designed and regulated safely?
Or does individual control over settlement create an unavoidable market integrity problem? 👇
 
#cftc #predictionmarkets #mentionmarkets #eventcontracts #derivatives #marketintegrity #financialregulation #finreg #compliance #marketsurveillance #innovation #digitalmarkets 🚀📊

metadata.title: CFTC Chairman on Backpack: "The First On-Chain DCO/DCM"
metadata.author: Backpack Exchange Official
metadata.shortDescription:
U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commissioner Chair Michael Selig gives his full answer on bringing on-chain derivatives into the U.S. regulatory framework, and names Backpack as the first on-chain exchange and clearinghouse (DCM/DCO) to be approved.

Key points from the Chairman:
- Backpack was “the first on-chain DCM/DCO, so exchange and clearinghouse, approved this past week,” which he calls “a significant step in this direction.”
- Backpack built both its exchange and clearinghouse, “got a full stack registration,” and registered an FCM broker with the NFA.
- Derivatives offered to U.S. retail must be on a registered exchange; on-chain platforms get the same requirements, not more lenient ones.

Glossary:
DCM = Designated Contract Market (a CFTC-regulated derivatives exchange)
DCO = Derivatives Clearing Organization (a CFTC-regulated clearinghouse)
FCM = Futures Commission Merchant (a registered futures broker)

Recorded at a The Hill event, November 2026. Clip courtesy of The Hill.

metadata.title: Part I: CFTC Staff Roundtable on Position Limits for Physical Commodity Derivatives, 06/19/14
metadata.author: CFTC
metadata.shortDescription: The roundtable focused on hedges of a physical commodity by a commercial enterprise, including gross hedging, cross-commodity hedging, anticipatory hedging, and the process for obtaining a non-enumerated exemption. The discussion included the setting of spot month limits in physical-delivery and cash-settled contracts and a conditional spot-month limit exemption. Also the discussion included aggregation of positions based on ownership interests of greater than 50 percent of an owned entity and aggregation based on substantially identical trading strategies.
keywords: United States Commodity Futures Trading Commission (Government Agency)

metadata.title: Open Commission Meeting to Consider a Supplemental Proposal to Automated Trading Regulation
metadata.author: CFTC
metadata.shortDescription: CFTC held an open meeting on Friday, November 4th at 10 a.m. to consider a supplemental proposal to Regulation Automated Trading (Regulation AT).

metadata.title: Day 1: Roundtable to Discuss Additional Customer Collateral Protections
metadata.author: CFTC
metadata.shortDescription:
Staff of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) held a two-day public roundtable to discuss additional customer collateral protection. The roundtable was to gather public input on a variety of ideas to further protect customers.

Day one discussions focused on issues related to the advisability and practicality of implementing the legal segregation with operational commingling (LSOC) model as the segregation model for collateral posted by futures customers (the Commission has already approved this model for swaps); alternative models for the custody of customer collateral; enhancing futures commission merchant (FCM) controls over the disbursement of customer funds deposited for trading on U.S. futures markets; increasing transparency surrounding an FCM's holding and investment of customer funds; and lessons learned from commodity brokerage bankruptcy proceedings.
