The client has the segregation of initial margin. the client can also can always um claw back excess right can choose not to leave excess margin with its FCM so it's exposure uh remains the initial margin which is now segregated and in terms of the lean issue and I can't speak for others at the table but I think the concern there is not so much giving of the lean it's ensuring that if the FCM were to become insolvent that those positions can now be ported right so as long as that ability to move uh positions to another FCM uh is preserved and is not tainted by there being an FCM lean over this account. However, it's structured. I think that's the the paramount concern certainly for us. Um there was a discussion of the custodian bank risk here. Um you know, cash we recognize is a deposit with the bank and is at risk. Um however, you know, the segregated assets of customers today we imagine are sitting in these exact same custodial banks where these segregated accounts would be held. So, you know, we've done a fair amount of research with our settlement banks or our custodial banks in terms of, you know, the FDIC implications of a bank failure, the protection of uh fully paid customer assets sitting in the custody range at these accounts at these banks and we're confident that um those would be those would be preserved for customers or beneficial owners. Cash is a different matter. Um one I'll just shift back a moment. Uh I don't think this room would be nearly as crowded if um the MF Global events hadn't occurred. Um and you know the the um malfeasants risk you know we think is real. Those customers who choose to opt out you know means that there's a lot of customers who remain in these pools you know who may not have the uh um budget to to pay for the additional services. And so you know uh as I mentioned in our prior in the prior panel you know we think uh significant attention needs to be paid to how does that uh customer seg pool um what are the maximum optimal protections around that pool of assets that prohibits the FCM from whether inadvertently or uh by design you know notwithstanding rules to the contrary uh from dipping into that pool um at the moment when it's you know customers are most at risk. Jeff Jeff Hanline representing advanced trading and the national grain and feed and like Ken uh we represent the buy side but the exh probably from the uh most of the other participants farmers ranchers and agra businessmen. uh the risks that uh ELSOC covers and the risks that are still exposed seem uh there still seems to be many risks in the ELSOC regimen and moving forward with that regimen with those risks still exposed in this environment doesn't seem appropriate to our customers. Um while it is better than where we may be today, it still has many holes in it, not the least of which is the malfeasants, the investment risks. And so as you look at these other regimens, whether it's the URX or the CME SIBA, particularly the voluntary nature of the CME SIBA would be uh very attractive as as an investment. it it transfers the opportunity to have a higher degree of certainty at an expense at the buyer's uh choice. And so those are the kind of things that as we go forward, I hope the commission weighs heavily. Take taking me back a few minutes here, but uh just on on the question of uh custodial risk, it seems there are a couple of levels of custodial risk. Um and and we we've talked about uh perhaps part of it, but there's also the risk there there's there are the risks in custody that were observed when Finsseg 10 was amended in 2005. And in fact, the CFTC saw some custodial accounts that had come up short uh with questions raised as to exactly how the accounts had been managed. But there's also a problem for custodians who successfully manage their account. And in the CME SIBA proposal, that would be somewhat more complicated than the typical case because uh CME SIBA raises the prospect of a quadparty custody account. And so you have a custodian with three parties around it with rights and obligations to be served. And there there's the risk of the custodian simply a and and and perhaps for good cause throwing up its hands and throwing the whole thing into an interpleer which of course doesn't particularly serve anybody's um uh long-term interests. It's it's for these reasons that uh we thinking about this at ISDA thus far really prefer the model Bob that you were perhaps broaching where that that seemed custodian free and and that essentially kept the money for the most part kept the collateral for the most part at the DCO subject to rule and perhaps security interest. We would say that that both is is is the way to go. But that seems to take one level of risk out of the picture. At the risk of interrupting the flow, I do need to raise one other thing. Ken, earlier you had asked what might be the impact of one of these models on guaranteeing FCM's other customers. And I gave you what I should hasten to add is one man's view. But I probably maybe shouldn't have done that, but having regardless I should I want to reopen that question because in looking at costs I think we need to look at costs and benefits. But we also need to be attentive. What costs does this kind of an optional model impose on those who do not opt in? And I think that's something to be concerned about. And so if folks have views on that, I I definitely don't want whatever I might have said to squaltch that, but rather perhaps inform it. And so Ken, you you looked like you had Thank you. That's a very good segue to the question I was about to ask. Um quick quick comment and and then then a question. Um first the the comment. This has been a very helpful um conversation in looking at these different options, the strengths and weaknesses of of each. Um but clearly at the end of the day I think it'll be incumbent on the the industry and the commission as been said several times today to come up with a solution so that the outcome of this exercise is a system that still allows another MF global type event to occur five years from now as we as was the outcome with the volume investors um exercise a couple of decades ago. Um the the the question I had is this and this is this is for for Mark and again this is just trying to understand the the pro the process. Um you've made the point that the um that the GCP program would be voluntary um that people could opt in or opt out as as you envision it. Are there classes of people who you would expect to opt in and you would expect to opt out? Um, specifically, is this a system more designed to benefit the larger players in the market? Is this designed to benefit uh Kalpers or or the GM pension plan? Would this be as suitable for an individual farmer or an individual member of the grain trade, someone from the agriculture world, the people who are in a fix right now in in the wake of MF Global? Mark Sure from SA. Um, with respect to benefits, I I again I'll maybe answer your question more directly in a moment, but I I just want to be clear or at least try to be clear that that our view is that that this model or this this option if you will um benefits all participants to the extent that first um it is available to all recognizing of course that with respect to whether it's a DCO settlement bank, whether it's a sponsoring FCM No one's forced to do business with anyone they otherwise would not do business with. Um now we did say at the outset that that we urged the commission to make it mandatory that DCOS offer this because obviously that if that part of the chain uh you know is isn't available no one else can no one else can effectuate these arrangements. But that said we would view this as a as since it's an option to all we would also view this as it's a detriment to none. Even if it turned out that certain types of clients by and large might opt for this and certain might not. Um we also think that to the extent that perhaps a larger number of clients opt into this uh there may be some fixed costs that can be spread um somewhat more broadly and thus the cost of this come down to other clients. But perhaps to more directly answer your question, I I think we would somewhat have the expectation um that some of the larger clients that are uh fiduciaries to uh pension plans and other clients and furthermore have by the nature of their positions. um demands for a very very significant amount of collateral or margin and therefore have a lot to be risked um a lot at risk whether it's operational risk, fraud risk or other risks would perhaps be the more likely at least initially uh more likely clients to opt in but again that that does not preclude other clients from opting in and I think just a last comment is that um there are many many pension funds, institutional investors, insurance companies, and others who have similar arrangements um in OTC land as it is. And they're not we we think to some extent the the cost issue um is a bit of a red herring. Um, not that there aren't some additional costs, but frankly, the the cost of a couple of thousand dollars for a custody account and some of the other processing accounts, uh, processing costs, um, we don't believe are necessarily well beyond, um, the reach of a large percentage of the clients. Now, of course, they may feel that even, you know, an extra dollar of cost doesn't buy them enough to make it worthwhile, but we think that that's a that's a commercial decision and it's not based on on class or size of clients, per se. Okay. And so, we're building up a bit of a line, Oliver, Ron, Seth, Dan, and then Joe. Well, I'll try and be quick. So um one of the one of the obligations of uh the GCP model um I think to make it works for guaranteeing FCMs is that the GCP um funds its own margin calls and doesn't rely on the um the guaranteeing FCM which is a is not so much a cost but it's an ownus um you know with the potential for default if it's not done properly. Yeah. Um the another issue is um not so much for that but the you know I'm not sure how we get to solve the security interest requirement. I I still haven't seen a solution. And on the basis of those two things, I I would also recommend that we think about the ELSOT model uh the 2213 uh C U paragraphs that um allow for a DCO to uh provide greater protection to protect excess collateral in the account so that malfeasants and so on it so to protect it against an FCM's malfeasance and so on. So given that we have in swaps clearing anyway um multiple CCPs clearing the same product, I I would think perhaps the forces of competition would get them to uh uh create rules and procedures that would uh also protect for clients that wish it at the extra cost of so doing their own excess collateral at the FCM. Thank you Bob. Uh first let me try to answer your question. Ron Fer, New York Law School. Sorry. Uh let me try to first answer your question and I have a question for the group if you don't mind. um in in the clearing world, a zero sum game. If I lose a dollar, somebody else makes a dollar. And if I'm one of the GCPs and I lose a dollar through the trading through that DCO and the FCM acting as guarantor doesn't have enough capital to meet my dollar loss, then you have to look to the DCO rules because somebody's entitled to get a dollar. They made a dollar that day. And you have to look to the respective DCOS as far as which priority who they go after to collect and under the futures world they would go after the other customers of the the futures of that FCM they had some of the DCOS have that type of right. So I think there is a potential fellow customer risk even under the the GCP model. um only other than if you can somehow t you strongly believe it takes it completely out of the bankruptcy code and but then who pays that dollar to the customer who made a who made the profits that they and because if the FCM doesn't have the capital to pay so that would be my answer to it and I have a question um I've been hearing this uh concept called concern about portability and I've heard it today a couple times in the first panel and again today and I'm just trying to understand exactly what the concerns are on the right or ability of a client to transfer their positions from uh FCMA to FCMBB. I mean in in in the aftermath of Refco in the aftermat of Lehman, I'm not aware of any large institutional customer who doesn't have multiple clearing arrangements today. I mean they have clearing arrangements at many different FCMs and they have the ability to transfer futures and in the world in the future clear swaps from a FCM to B. Now I think the concern is that what if FCMA is about to file for bankruptcy or has filed for bankruptcy. Is is the issue on portability that you want to have the right to transfer it to another firm without the other clearing firm accepting these positions or is it more that if the FCM files that you have clearing those products file for bankruptcy, you want to take whatever measures possible to make sure the trustee doesn't liquidate the open positions and give you a certain number of times to either open an account or transfer it or whatever. I mean the bankruptcy rules already provide you some gives the trustee some discretion. They have the right to liquidate the same day but that I mean Leman and MF Global uh both trustees in place gave basically a five days to transfer your position whether five days is adequate or not. I would like to hear from the group who's concerned about portability what really they're seeking. I'm not sure. I've heard different explanations and I'm just trying to understand that issue from a um their concerns. Thank you. Seth Seth Cro Sandler uh representing FIA. Uh a number of points. First of all, Bob, on prejudice to the other customers who don't opt in, it's an obvious thing, but I'm not sure it's been stated to the extent that there is an investment loss or a fraud loss, uh it's going to be shared by those folks and not the people who opted into this. So you're just shifting those losses to that pool of people who for whatever reason lack of sophistication or sophisticated didn't want to do it or lack of money whatever didn't opt into this proposal. You're shifting those kinds of losses uh to those folks. Um the going back probably an hour now there was some some talk about why would the uh why would a DCO require more margin from a customer in the SIBA model. uh and you know if we are able to solve all of this and get the FCM in the same position it's in under current models with respect to its rights visa v the customer I think that's right that you don't you don't change things but we have all of these issues even if there is a lean is the is the FCM in control of the situation right if it's not then maybe it's more at risk uh the more that you put risk onto the FCM the more the DCO is logically going to think that FCM is not as good a credit, right? So, I need more margin from somebody else. Uh the the question of whether the lean makes a customer property or not. I actually do think that um the SIBA model does a very good even if there were a lean that it wouldn't be and so it goes to the the porting issue uh more uh but if we make the FCM more in control of liquidation proceeds right in a double default situation right those proceeds may in fact be at the FCM level and then the defaulting customer now has defaulting FCM risk. Now, maybe that's something you're not so worried about, but it it doesn't entirely solve the uh customer property risk. And again, as I said at the outset, there are still issues in my mind about is this consistent with what Congress was thinking when it mandated clearing of swaps, made commodity contract a broader definition, and it knew that there was um a sharing regime. The last thing I wanted to mention was in all of this we just need to bear in mind uh underlying state commercial law the uniform commercial code 50 different states um for perfection of security interests it was drafted with the futures model in mind accounts at the FCM for the customer and it's not necessarily an issue with all of these things but just need to you know not miss that going forward. Dan, thanks. Just to be very brief. Um, so it seems under the GCP model, which definitely has some merit, we're taking customers and turning them into some form of members. So, first question is what do customers or clients lose by being reclassified? Is there any downside to this? Second thing is we're saying that somebody has to guarantee the participant in this to my knowledge and this is relatively new at the moment in in this space is is that limited to FCMs or is that it just needs to be a direct clearing member because that doesn't necessarily mean FCMs and thirdly just on some of the points that were touched upon in terms of leakage when we talked about ELOC there was a there was a concern about um bringing in any form of optionality because you could have leakage between an LSO group and a gross omni group and I've not heard so far is there any danger of any leakage between the GCP and let's say ELSOC or gross omnid that in terms of how the the rules and the code would work. Joe then Tim Joe KC board of trade. Uh Bob I just want to address the DCO cost issue real quick. Uh last week I was on a conference call with other market participants as well as other DCOS with SIBA and the DCOS had expressed some concern about the costs to implement this this structure and the response from SIBA was well this will be a financial windfall for DCOS once mandatory clearing comes into place. I just I I guess I want to point out that um currently each DCO has a limited number of of CLA members they deal with on a daily basis and with this new structure that could increase substantially and as an example uh let's just say in January a customer puts on a December week calendar swap the week calendar swaps are marked to the market on a daily basis. Therefore, you'd have 250 days of variation margin with the DCO. At $4 a wire, that comes up to around $1,000 of expense to the DCO, whereas the fees we're going to charge for that swap are $4. So, I don't think there's any guarantee that this is going to be a financial windfall uh for DCOS. Um on some of the lighter traded swaps, it may not make any sense to to have this type of a structure in place. Tim Tim Dor CME um you know I I guess to to answer one question you know we it's our expectation that those who guarantee these GCP type accounts would be clearing firm FCMS just to be to be clear about that um Ryan you had mentioned earlier uh questions around portability it's our expectation we consider to be a best practice that particularly with respect to cleared swaps that clients have relationships with more than one FCM uh that would go for a GCP. Um, in the eventuality of an FCM default under ELSACH, you know, our expectation would be that we'd be in a position to better ascertain the status of any GCP that goes through the guaranteeing FCM than any client that remains in ELSAC. Now, that's not to say that we don't have the ability to assess individual client exposures to value them to to generally risk manage them. We will know who the likely suspects are who are causing an FCM default, but we are governed by the portfolio of rights and obligations in terms of how we administer that default. We I expect that we would have to undergo some pains to asssure that we know which client or clients were actually at the source of the default so that we could then go ahead and and do our stuff and administer the default event. Uh the point being that there might be different timings associated with when porting could occur for non-defaulting clients within the the ELSC pool, if you will. So I offer that up only as some degree of color over the types of distinctions that we would foresee with the utilization of a of a GCP type construct. Um, if anything, I think that the immediacy of knowing whether a GCP client is the source of the default or not is actually a benefit to the overall construct. Mark from SIBA. Um, Ron, with respect to a couple more quick points on portability, um, no, we absolutely do not have any intention of foisting ourselves upon a clearing member who, um, chooses a commercial matter not to do business with us. Um uh but as far as what do we hope to achieve or at least ensure uh regarding portability is I think three things. Um the first of which is uh the certainty that our positions are maintained. That is that they're not liquidated. We as a large pension fund and many of our peers use swaps to hedge uh very significant uh inherent risks in our pension plans, interest rate, foreign exchange and other risks. and we need to be very very certain that those positions are maintained through any sort of market or other other stress. Um second of all a logical followup to that is that that there is a mechanism by which we can expeditiously move those positions to an FCM that is in fact good in good standing so we can make sure our merchant payments and other obligations continue to uh be maintained as they would otherwise be again through no fault of our own something gone arry at the FCM. Um and and last but not least is to ensure that any margin that we've posted initial margin uh with the FCM that's having an issue uh is in fact available to us to move to the new FCM in so far as then we don't have a double up situation. That is we've got a substantial sum that's posted with FCMA that has a problem. Now FCMBB says great you know we're happy to accept the positions but now we've got to repost in essence that sum again with FCMBB because FCMA's um our margin is tied up with them. Mark can I just ask how that differs under GCP versus LSO because our understanding is that under ELSOC we'd move the positions and the associated collateral that will be in the DCO as well. So I'm just trying to understand where's the difference there. Um I I think I think in Danny I think in principle you're you're absolutely right and and I think on paper it should work that way. we just have I think we would just derive a great deal more comfort if in essence we were holding or at least the FCM wasn't holding any collateral um and we were in a better position to I guess have fewer entanglements and and have fewer steps that we would need to go through um in order to extricate ourselves from an FCM situation. Um, and as described with the GCP model, we believe if we've structured it correctly legally and operationally, in essence, we're doing nothing more than replacing the guarantor um with another guarantor, a solvent guarantor, which should in principle be easier than again the the extrication from a from a a more stringent. I guess the only point I'd say is that the FCM under LSOT doesn't hold the collateral, the DCO does. I mean again different models but Christine was that yes um so I just wanted to add a couple of things I mean I think the question on portability Mark tried you know answered um but I just want to say from Fidelity's point of view we are worried about portability but at the end of the day what we are worried about the most is segregation and really protecting the customer collateral excuse me there was a point made I think earlier in the earlier panel that we wouldn't be here but for MF Global and what we're really focused on as futures because we didn't really worry about the segregation in the swaps market. Not true. Uh you know, we're required by the 40 act obviously to segregate our collateral. We've been doing it, you know, since 1940. Um so it's something that we're focused on. It's something that we think our customers deserve. We agree with Tim that there is a difference between the swaps and futures, you know, uh markets. And we've we've argued that from the beginning, which is why we think we do need increased protections in the swaps market. And at the end of the day, when we think about it, we see, you know, we we hear if you want to increase protections, it's going to cost you more. And we can't give up a lean. And, you know, it when we look at it, we see the customer is the one who's bearing most of the burdens here. the increased costs, the reduced segregation protections, and I'm not sure that's the way this was intended to go. When I sit and think about how to solve this because I've heard all of the concerns and all of the proposals, I don't know what the right answer is, but it seems to me that we keep going round and round because we need a lean, but that makes it customer property and we have severe bankruptcy issues. I realize that we're going to talk about 190 later on today and that tomorrow there's going to be some more bankruptcy uh discussion, but I really think that in order to solve almost all of the issues that we've all brought up here, we really have to focus on a bankruptcy fix. Uh getting back to portability, we think the key to portability is ensuring that guarantee funds uh size is not too large. uh because if you think of the perspective of the FCM to whom the positions are ported um if they have to post a guarantee fund for that port not only do they have to fund it during a period of market stress it's also subject to mutualization so getting back to my earlier point on the defaulter pays model we believe that it's very important to ensure seamless portability and and thus understand segregation is incredibly important but if portability is successful you don't even have to get to segregation so we believe it's equally important um I'd like to piggyback on what Christine was saying um as well. Again, Christine Cochran with the Commodity Markets Council I really appreciate SIBA. They have been very kind to us as an organization in spending a lot of time walking through their proposal because as I said earlier today, you know, we represent a wide variety of market participants. Um and what I would just like to what we are taking from this right now is that this is a this is a very thoughtful proposal. It addresses a lot of concerns that a number of market participants share. However, um we are hesitant to pass judgment on it in a vacuum. We are still waiting for the MF Global bankruptcy or MF Global investigation to be complete. You know, there are a matrix of solutions to be considered and this is what I think Christine did a very nice job articulating whether they are back office solutions like reporting and disclosure requirements whether they are bankruptcy changes or these more structural changes. I don't think we can consider any single one in a vacuum. We have to look at them together, how they inter interact within each other and the costs and benefits across all market participants because we need to be very careful that we're not choosing solutions that benefit um one class of market participants any more or less than any other class of market participants. [Music] uh Tim Doris, CME uh you know um I think underlying the tone of many of the comments here is the idea that when we talk about swaps perhaps you're talking about interest rate swaps or credit default swaps but there is the 8515 rule for instance which uh promises to recast many products that are currently cleared as futures particularly in the energy space but honestly I don't know what the bounds of this 8515 process will be so okay apparently nobody does but um uh many products my colleagues who who focus on that do but I'm just that's not my all right sorry I didn't mean to make a metaphor here but uh I think uh um we do take a different view to the types of recordkeeping requirements that are associated with Elsac due to um uh our station in the world we do offer clearing services for interest rate swaps obviously and for credit default swaps as well but with the workings of the 8515 rule Many products that are currently classed as being futures, as many as 600, our last estimation will be reclassed as swaps. So that means that if you are an FCM and you have any kind of activity on Clearport, for instance, you are going to have to get very used to ELSC standards, your requirements under ELSC's methodology and the reporting requirements there, which is perfectly fine. But it's, you know, it strikes us that it's a it's a it's a place to exercise some degree of caution for the reasons that I tried to articulate earlier. Many of the accounts that were put in place to service business under Clearport were developed within a futures context. At least in swaps, when we're talking about rates and credit, we are at the beginning of things and we can set the accounts up in a way that they can be optimized with respect to whatever the end end regulatory requirements become. within the the context of a of a futures uh the traditional futures FCM uh and it's its back office business infrastructure accounts have been set up for a variety of purposes uh for a variety of reasons uh related accounts do exist in this world um you know knowing which account or set of accounts to report under in an ELSAC methodology may not be a problem but it might be you know so that the disposition of the portfolio of rights and obligations report going up against the broad class of products will be classed as swaps is not a trivial issue in my mind. I may be alone on this but I wouldn't trivialize the issue. There are issues that we are going to have to delve into as this regulation finds its face and uh it will have an impact on our FCMS as well. Well, um obviously in terms of portability, in terms of the URX individual segregation, uh portability clauses can be introduced into the agreement, but also URX uh will have an interim participant facility. So the in the event of an FCM default, a byside firm can make margin direct to URX clearing for a 5-day period, which gives that byside time to switch to another clearer. So that that's part of URX's cleared swaps offering. Okay, I'm going to have to let that be the last comment. I apologize. I think this is the sort of topic one could spend all day talking about and I would very much enjoy that. But we only have 45 minutes for lunch. We are going to be starting very promptly at 1:30. There are a number of places to get sandwiches or salads both in this building and within a oneb block radius. And so I look forward to seeing you all in 45 [Music]

metadata.title: CFTC Roundtable on Enhancing Protections Afforded Customers and Funds Deposited by Customers: Part 1
metadata.author: CFTC
metadata.shortDescription: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission held a public roundtable to discuss the Commission's proposed rulemaking, "Enhancing Protections Afforded Customers and Customer Funds Held by Futures Commission Merchants and Derivatives Clearing Organizations".

metadata.title: CFTC to Hold an Open Commission Meeting on March 25
metadata.author: CFTC
metadata.shortDescription:
Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chairman J. Christopher Giancarlo held an open meeting on Monday, March 25, 2019, at 10:00 a.m. to consider the following:

• Interim Final Rule Regarding Margin Requirements for Uncleared Swaps for Swap Dealers and Major Swap Participants in Light of Brexit; and

• Final Rule Regarding the De Minimis Exception to the Swap Dealer Definition – Swaps Entered into by Insured Depository Institutions in Connection with Loans to Customers
keywords: Major Swap Participants in Light of Brexit
Insured Depository Institutions in Connection with Loans to Customers

metadata.title: Compare Live Sports Odds Across Sportsbooks in 3 Minutes (Next.js + SportsGameOdds API)
metadata.author: SportsGameOdds API
metadata.shortDescription:
Build a live odds comparison dashboard that puts every sportsbook side by side and highlights the best price for each team, using Next.js and the SportsGameOdds API. From getting your API key to a working dashboard in about three minutes.

We follow the Odds Comparison Dashboard example from the SportsGameOdds docs, with real NBA and NFL odds.

Get your free API key: https://sportsgameodds.com
Guide to odds comparison dashboard: https://sportsgameodds.com/docs/examples/odds-comparison-dashboard

WHAT YOU'LL BUILD
Odds from multiple sportsbooks for each game, side by side
Best price for each team highlighted in green
League switcher (NBA, NFL, NHL, NCAAF)
Auto-refresh every 30 seconds

USEFUL LINKS

Pricing (free plan + 7-day free trials on paid plans): https://sportsgameodds.com/pricing

Quickstart: https://sportsgameodds.com/docs/basics/quickstart

GET /events endpoint: https://sportsgameodds.com/docs/endpoints/getEvents

Bookmaker IDs: https://sportsgameodds.com/docs/data-types/bookmakers

Building with AI (Claude, Cursor, Copilot, MCP): https://sportsgameodds.com/docs/info/ai-vibe-coding

Next tutorial – Live Odds Tracker: https://sportsgameodds.com/docs/examples/live-odds-tracker

metadata.title: Get Sports Odds and Data with an Odds API
metadata.author: SportsGameOdds API
metadata.shortDescription:
If you’re looking to pull your first NFL odds or player props from the SportsGameOdds API, you’re in the perfect spot. This guide is a fast, beginner-friendly walkthrough that takes you from zero to making real API calls in just a few minutes.

Your First NFL Odds API Call 
If you want to quickly pull NFL events along with all available odds and player props, the simplest query is: (remember to input your API key) 

https://api.sportsgameodds.com/v2/events?apiKey=API_KEY_HERE&oddsAvailable=true&leagueID=NFL&limit=10

This gives you every market—game lines, totals, player props, and more—in a single response.

If you’d prefer to target specific NFL player props, you can narrow your request like this:

https://api.sportsgameodds.com/v2/events?apiKey=API_KEY_HERE&oddsAvailable=true&leagueID=NFL&oddIDs=rushing_yards-PLAYER_ID-game-ou-over,rushing_yards-PLAYER_ID-game-ou-under

This returns the rushing-yards over/under props for all players. The “PLAYER_ID” placeholder is special—it tells the API to return odds for any player. If instead you replace it with an actual player’s ID, you’ll get props for that player only, for example:

https://api.sportsgameodds.com/v2/events?apiKey=API_KEY_HERE&oddsAvailable=true&leagueID=NFL&oddIDs=rushing_yards-JAMES_COOK_1_NFL-game-ou-over,rushing_yards-JAMES_COOK_1_NFL-game-ou-under

SportGameOdds Odds API Pricing: https://sportsgameodds.com/pricing/

segments.text: This is the crypto trading bot I built
for Polymarket's 5-minute markets.
Predictiv 5 supplies the live data, Jeff
estimates the odd, and the bot checks
whether to buy up, buy down, or skip. It
works within a $10 trading cap, tracks
actual fills, and manages the position.
Today, I'll show you how to build it. If
you saw my Cal Shy bot, this follows the
same idea. This version uses selected
5-minute crypto rounds on Polymarket.
First, it finds the current round and
its up and down tokens. Then it gets the
order books, prices, and the exact
reference used to settle that market.
From there, it builds a snapshot,
movement from the opening price,
volatility,
liquidity, and time remaining. Jeff
evaluates that snapshot, the bot checks
its answers before any money is
committed. So,
what is Jeff?
Jeff comes from a company called
Typecase AI, and it works differently
from the chatbots you know.
They call it a system one model. You
don't ask it to write anything. You tell
it the possible answers up front, and it
picks one with its own odds and a
confidence score. There's no essay and
no reasoning to wait for. And because of
that, it makes it cheap and fast. It
costs 4.2 cents per million of token it
reads, and nothing for what it answers.
So, to get your Jeff API key,
first you sign in and create an account
with them,
and go to this
page. You get a key from Typecase's
console and add credit under billing.
Once you've done that,
you can go to API keys
and create a key.
Name it anything and grab this and put
it in a safe place.
Next, head over to Predict It Fi. Go to
products.
API and SDK. You register for an account
and you get your free API key. And make
sure you have a valid account so you can
have access the free Predict It Fi's API
key on the free plan. Then go to API
key. Create new. Name anything.
And here's Predict It Fi's API key.
You copy the key and keep it aside
first. First, your Polymarket private
key. And to get that, first you go to
the settings. Under account, click start
export. And once you accept all the
terms and condition, you reviews the
private key.
You copy it. Next, you need the re-layer
API key, which is under here. You have
to click on create new and copy these
two values. The ENV file will have the
corresponding name. So, you just copy
and paste to the correct spot. Next, you
need your public address, which you can
just find it here under profile. Copy
and put it in the ENV file. To build it,
copy the full prompt from the
description below and paste it into
Codex or any of the AI coding tool you
use. Let it create a project, then
follow the setup instructions for your
keys and configurations. Select the
crypto markets you want and check the
$10 cap and run the dry run. Look at the
logs before enabling live trades. You
should be able to see the snapshot,
Jeff's estimate, and why the bot trades
or skips. Here's how one round works.
The bot compares Jeff's estimate with
the price it can actually buy at. It
checks that the data is fresh, the
estimated edge remains after fees, and
there's enough liquidity,
and the trade fits within the $10 cap.
If any
fails, it skips. When a trade passes, it
reserves the cash and submits an order
through Polymarket's SDK
with a maximum price it's willing to
pay. Then it checks what actually
filled. The requested size and the
filled size can be different. So, the
position is based on confirmed fills.
While the position is open, it
reassesses selling versus holding. After
the market resolves, it claims and
redeems any redeemable position and
updates the balance. Then it follows the
next round and repeats the cycle. That's
the workflow.
Find a round, read the data, ask Jeff,
check the trade, and manage whatever
actually fills. The built prompt and
links for Jeff, PredictIt, and
Polymarket are in the description below.
Start with a dry run and keep your stake
small. AI can make mistakes and this is
not a financial advice. If you have any
questions, leave a comment or join
PredictIt's Discord. Thanks for
watching.
See you in the next one.
Peace.

(audience clapping) The reality is when economists look at the overall numbers, although insider trading grabs the headlines, it doesn't explain most of the winners. - So the largest known insider case that we have in our sample is Alpha Raccoon. That user falls outside of our top 100 user. It is the largest known insider case, and it's still not among the top 100. - 90% of the markets were classified as not prone to insider trading. Right, okay, and so if 90% of the markets are not prone to insider trading, then insider trading is not going to be the dominant reason why these prediction markets are accurate. - That's Theis Jensen. Together with colleagues from London Business School, he's been investigating the behaviour of winners on Polymarket. So if the biggest winners aren't insiders, who are they? To this day, the biggest Polymarket winner of all time is the anonymous French man, Theo, making $85 million on the 2024 US election. In interviews with the Wall Street Journal and the free press, he reveals that his winning strategy was to simply gather more information. Theo commissioned his own polls in battleground states from the polling firm YouGov. In fact, we could commission a similar poll for around $10,000. But Theo did something cunning. Instead of asking people who they'd vote for, he asked who they think their neighbours will vote for. Research shows that this tiny tweak can improve poll accuracy, and Theo though some people might be planning to vote for Trump, but be too shy to admit it. It gets to the heart of the difference between polls and prediction markets. Polls ask who you'll vote for, what you want to happen. Prediction markets ask who you think will win, which is what you predict will happen, but it illustrates an important point that knowing more than others gives you an edge. We reached out to many members of the 0.1% to ask their secret to success. Most ignored us entirely, but one who didn't is Jester the Goose, who started with only $2 on Polymarket, and as of September 2026, grew that to over $211,000 by betting on everything from world chess championships to the number of times Elon Musk will tweet. It's something like, you know, I think I have some reason to be smarter than the market here, and that's why I'm willing to put up an order or make a buy or a sell. - So what do you need to know to be smarter than the market? He calls these skilled winners. He meticulously analysed their strategies and found they tend to do three things. First, they react faster. When news like a US Federal Reserve rate is announced, they are the first to make a move. - If you are a smart trader, as soon as the announcement hits, you trade the underlying contractor. So we see that skilled traders do this, but no other group does that. - Second, they avoid low probability long shots and focus on the favourites to win. This works because they're betting against other people's biases. - Most people who are betting like to bet on contracts where the payoff in case of them being right is high. Now what happens is that they all sort of bet on that long shot and push the price up to the point where the long shot becomes overpriced. - Third, they look for arbitrage opportunities. Arbitrage is when you take advantage of inefficiencies in the market to guarantee a small profit. Take the temperature tomorrow. We know one of these is going to be right. Now, since each temperature has both a yes and a no side, there are six outcomes you can buy. Only one of the yes sides will win, which means that two of the no sides will also win. segments.text: Your sportsbook just went live in a new state.
The product team is thrilled and the promo calendar is full.
Then someone searches your brand plus the state name,
and finds three affiliate review sites,
a news article, and an old page of yours that still says coming soon.
The traffic you worked so hard to earn is going to everyone except you.
That's an iGaming SEO problem.
This is EVERNET Explains.
EVERNET Consulting has worked in technology since 2007,
and today we run a full marketing,
design and advertising agency alongside our IT and cybersecurity work.
In this video we'll answer one question.
How do sportsbooks and fantasy sites grow in search without breaking the rules?
You'll see how to build accurate state pages,
why responsible gaming content can help you rank,
how to show Google real expertise,
and how to fit compliance review
into publishing without slowing everything down.
This is general information, not legal advice.
Gaming rules vary by state and change often,
so check with your compliance team and counsel.
Chapter one.
What iGaming SEO actually means.
It's search engine optimization for sportsbooks,
fantasy platforms, online casinos and the media sites around them.
The basics are the same as any SEO program.
You need a site Google can crawl,
pages that answer real questions,
and a reputation other sites want to link to.
What changes is the rulebook.
Most industries only answer to Google.
Operators also answer to state regulators and their own compliance teams.
A page that makes an offer in a state where you're not licensed is a regulatory
problem, not a marketing experiment.
So think of it as two jobs at once.
One is growing organic traffic.
The other is making sure every page that grows is a page you're comfortable
defending.
Search for almost any sportsbook or fantasy term,
and the top of the page is full of comparison sites,
best apps lists and review hubs.
Many are affiliates, which earn a commission when a reader signs up with an
operator.
They publish constantly, and they've been building links for years.
Some of that crowding came from shortcuts.
In March 2024, Google announced new spam policies,
including site reputation abuse,
scaled content abuse and expired domain abuse.
Google's own example of expired domain abuse is buying an old medical site's
domain to host low quality casino content.
Tricks that borrow authority tend to get caught.
Authority you earn on your own domain lasts.
Chapter two.
State-by-state landing pages.
These are the backbone of most iGaming SEO programs,
because so many searches include a location.
They're also easy to mass produce and easy to get wrong.
So every state page should include a plain statement of what's available in that
state, and only what you're licensed to offer there.
List the minimum age for each product,
taken from the state regulator.
In Connecticut, for example, the
Department of Consumer Protection lists twenty-one
as the minimum age for online casino gaming and sports wagering,
and eighteen for fantasy contests.
Name the regulator and link to its official site.
Show the responsible gaming help the state requires.
And add a visible last reviewed date,
with the team that reviewed it.
Now, what to avoid.
Don't build pages for states where you're not licensed that read like you're open
for business there.
If you want to rank for a state before launch,
a short, honest page that says you're not available yet,
and explains what's legal there today,
is safer than a page that hints at future offers.
Avoid thin pages that only swap the state name.
Google tends to treat near-duplicate pages as low value,
and regulators won't be impressed either.
Give each page something specific to that state,
like the regulator's rules or eligibility details.
Here's a rule of thumb.
If a state page would make your compliance lead nervous,
it isn't ready to rank.
Chapter three.
Responsible gaming, and why it helps your SEO.
Many teams treat responsible gaming copy as a footer requirement,
small and gray at the bottom of the page.
That's a missed opportunity.
Think about what people actually search.
How do I set a deposit limit?
How do I take a break from my account?
How do I self-exclude?
A clear, step-by-step help page for each of those can rank,
cut support tickets, and show Google your site serves real user needs.
It's good for players, and regulators will notice it too.
This next part isn't optional.
Your content, keywords, images and links should never target or appeal to people
under the legal age.
In practice, that means skipping keywords tied to school sports,
video game terms popular with kids,
or cartoon-style themes.
Use imagery of adults only.
Keep age requirements visible on landing pages and sign-up flows.
And follow each state's advertising rules,
which often cover where and how gaming ads can appear.
Never write copy that pressures people to play more,
or suggests gaming is a way to solve money problems.
Good iGaming marketing informs adults who've already chosen to play.
Chapter four.
Let's talk about E-E-A-T.
It stands for experience, expertise,
authoritativeness and trustworthiness.
It comes from Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines,
which hold Your Money or Your Life topics,
the ones that can affect someone's finances or well-being,
to a higher standard.
Real-money gaming fits that description.
Name your authors, with a short bio.
Add reviewed by notes on pages that touch rules,
eligibility or responsible gaming.
Cite primary sources, like state regulators and official governing bodies,
instead of repeating another site.
Keep rules pages current and dated.
And earn mentions with useful data and commentary.
Paid link schemes put your rankings and your reputation at risk.
Chapter five.
Content that wins.
The operators who do well in organic
search usually stop trying to beat affiliates
at their own game.
They focus on content only an operator can create.
Explain how your contests work,
how scoring is calculated, how a parlay settles,
or what happens when a game is postponed.
Share original data, carefully aggregated and anonymized,
like which positions get drafted earliest or how scoring trends shift across a
season.
That's the kind of insight journalists and podcasters link to.
And open up your help center.
Questions about withdrawals, verification and account limits are high intent.
If your help center is buried behind a login,
those searches go to forums and affiliates.
Chapter six.
Technical SEO.
On app-first gaming sites, content may only load through JavaScript,
or key pages may sit behind age or location gates that block crawlers.
A few checks help.
Make sure public pages, like rules,
promotion terms, state pages and help articles,
are reachable without logging in.
Handle geolocation and age gates so they protect the product without hiding
informational content from search engines.
Give each state its own folder,
linked from a clear hub page.
Redirect expired promotion pages instead of leaving dead offers indexed.
And watch mobile page speed, since that's where most players browse.
Chapter seven.
Can you just run ads instead?
You can, but Google requires gambling advertisers to apply for certification and
follow local laws.
In the US, Google's policy says sports
betting and online casino advertisers must be
licensed by the state where it's legal,
and must not target users under twenty-one or outside the states where they're
licensed.
Ads also need a warning about compulsive gambling,
with help information, on the landing page or in the ad.
Daily fantasy advertisers have their own rules,
including no targeting under eighteen.
Those rules change, so check the current policy before every launch.
And paid ads stop the moment you stop paying,
which is why most operators pair them with SEO.
Chapter eight.
Put compliance into your workflow.
The fastest way to stall SEO in gaming is to treat compliance as the last step.
So build review in from the start.
Agree on approved language with compliance,
a short library of phrases for offers,
age requirements, responsible gaming and eligibility.
Tier your content.
Evergreen education may need a light review,
while promotions, bonus terms and state pages need a full one.
Review the brief as well as the draft,
so a risky keyword gets caught at the outline stage.
Log who approved what and when.
And put state pages and rules content on a regular review calendar,
so nothing goes stale.
iGaming SEO rewards patience and honesty.
Most operators should expect months,
not weeks, before organic traffic grows in a meaningful way.
EVERNET attends Fantasy Sports and Gaming Association events,
and we work alongside your compliance,
product and growth teams.
If you want a partner who understands the search side and the rules side,
schedule a discovery call at evernetco.com.
And if gambling has stopped being fun for you or someone you know,
the National Problem Gambling Helpline is free,
confidential and open around the clock.
Call or text 1-800-MY-RESET.
Thanks for watching EVERNET Explains.

metadata.title: The Dos & Don'ts of Advertising and iGaming
metadata.author: iDEA Growth
metadata.shortDescription: In this webinar, our expert panel explores one of the central challenges of successful online gaming and sports betting in the U.S. - the imperative of advertising for customer acquisition while abiding by differing state laws and prioritizing responsible gaming practices. How can companies position advertising to both meet consumers where they are and remain compliant with varying state rules and regulations? Learn from a leading advertising lawyer, iGaming Media CEO, two state regulators and tech leader in responsible gaming as they discuss the best ways to navigate the complex, but essential business of advertising.

metadata.title: iGaming and responsible compliance | CG New York
metadata.author: CoinGeek
metadata.shortDescription:
Panel discussion: iGaming and responsible compliance | CG New York
Recently at #CGNewYork conference, CoinGeek’s Lead Gaming Industry Reporter Becky Liggero moderated a panel discussion on iGaming and how the #BSV blockchain can improve compliance within the gambling industry. Panelists included Peter Bainbridge-Clayton, Founder & CTO of kompany; Paul Foster, CEO of Crucial Compliance; and Nick Hill, Sales Director at nChain. They discussed about the current status of regulation around the gambling industry and the issues around global legislation that affects gaming operations.

“Data integrity is what drives safer gambling, and if you don’t have data integrity then you can’t drive safer gambling within this industry,” Foster said. Hill also pointed out the importance of the BSV blockchain in assuring compliance and explained how nChain’s Kensei enterprise data integrity platform can solve issues. Bainbridge-Clayton also explained his company’s use case for Kensei and its integration to their operations.

“The work that nChain has done on the Kensei platform, it removed the worry of talking to a specific blockchain. Anything which takes away that level of hassle that is unnecessary is quick to implement for us,” Bainbridge-Clayton said.

metadata.title: The Hidden Compliance Risk for iGaming Affiliates | SiGMA Rome 2026
metadata.author: Ace Alliance
metadata.shortDescription:
🌍 Who should be responsible when iGaming affiliate campaigns cross regulatory borders?

Affiliate marketing campaigns often reach audiences across multiple countries, but not every advertisement is permitted in every jurisdiction. When promotional content appears in a territory where it is not authorised, both operators and their affiliate partners can face serious compliance challenges.

At SiGMA Rome 2026, Magda Klimko-Aydin, CMO at Ace Alliance, spoke with Oleg Samoilenko, Head of Compliance at Tonybet, about campaign leakage, advertising restrictions in regulated markets and why compliance should become a shared responsibility across the iGaming industry.

⚖️ What we discuss

• What campaign leakage and campaign spill mean in affiliate marketing
• Why promotional materials must remain within the territories where they are authorised
• The challenges of geofencing campaigns across different jurisdictions
• Why markets such as Ontario, Alberta and Kahnawake require particular attention
• The risks of advertising through global platforms like YouTube and Instagram
• How campaign leakage can lead to regulatory inquiries and player complaints
• Why compliance teams should review campaigns before they go live
• How regulatory responsibility between operators and affiliates is evolving
• Why affiliates should take greater responsibility for compliant advertising
• How regulators can contribute to responsible gaming beyond issuing rules and fines

🌍 Understanding campaign leakage

Campaign leakage happens when marketing materials intended for one specific territory become visible somewhere they should not be.

Oleg explains why this is particularly important in regulated markets, where advertising permissions can differ between jurisdictions, even within the same country.

He highlights Canada as an example, discussing Ontario, Alberta and Kahnawake, where operators need to pay close attention to territorial restrictions.

Global platforms such as YouTube, Instagram and other media channels make this more challenging. Geofencing settings, location targeting and even the content included in videos and images all need to be considered when preparing campaigns.

🛡️ Why compliance should be involved from the beginning

One of Oleg's key recommendations is to involve the compliance team before creating advertising campaigns, rather than asking them to review everything only after the materials are ready.

Understanding which messages, videos and promotional materials are permitted in each market can help teams avoid problems before campaigns are launched.

Campaign leakage can lead to regulatory inquiries, complaints and additional scrutiny for operators, even when the advertising was created or distributed by an external affiliate partner.

🤝 Making compliance a shared responsibility

Oleg explains that operators have traditionally carried most of the regulatory responsibility for advertising conducted on their behalf. However, he is seeing a gradual shift towards greater accountability for affiliates, including regulatory developments specifically targeting affiliate marketing in some jurisdictions, such as the Netherlands.

He also argues that regulators should contribute to responsible gaming beyond issuing rules and penalties. Preventative education and public awareness campaigns, particularly among vulnerable groups, could help address gambling-related harm before it becomes an issue for operators.

For iGaming operators, affiliates and compliance professionals, this conversation highlights why transparency, collaboration and early compliance involvement are essential when working across regulated markets.

👤 About Oleg Samoilenko

Oleg Samoilenko is Head of Compliance at Tonybet.

segments.text: Hello everybody and welcome to the
weekly Econ podcast Sense of Security.
I'm joined here today with our senior
economist of Interactive Brokers, Jose
Torres. Hi Jose, how are you doing?
>> Marie McNamara, how are you doing today?
>> I'm doing great, great. So tell us about
yesterday's Fed cut. It seems that the
markets were expecting this cut. But
everybody was kind of in the doldrums
about a possible no cut in December. Is
that true? And
>> Absolutely, it was a hawkish cut, folks.
You know, the Fed came out gave the 25
basis point reduction, but quelled the
enthusiasm that market participants had
about additional cuts in future
meetings, namely December, Marie.
December was trading as high as 90% in
terms of odds that it would be a
reduction at that meeting as well.
Now that's paired back quite a bit down
to around 70% or so. Market participants
still expecting a cut in December, but
not as sure as they were prior to the
Powell presser. Forecast contract
enthusiasm related to the Fed day has
been through the roof.
On Tuesday, October 28th, we marked a
new year-to-date high, 3.36
million contracts.
You know, we have a lot of different
kinds of market participants engaging in
our prediction market. We have
investors, speculators, hedgers,
arbitragers, and market makers. I like
to group the participants in those five
buckets. And really we're seeing a lot
of enthusiasm on rate decisions around
the world, mainly the Fed. But what's
really been driving this week's volume,
we're already above 2 million today. Of
course, October 28th, we exceeded 3
million, 3.36 million. So, we're looking
to build on these numbers. If you listen
to our earnings call
for the third quarter, you know, we
mentioned forecast contracts and the
significant amount of new instruments
that we've added, as well as the a
number of transactions that have been
growing and really in broad-based
fashion. When we first got started last
year in August, a big, huge boost came
from President Trump and Vice President
Harris. Now, we're very excited to
notice that we're seeing broad-based
participation across a lot of the other
economic indicators that we have. So,
it's not just elections, economic
indicators, government shutdown,
fiscal things, national debt. Elections
has been really our bread and butter.
When you when you consider the the
record days, you know, it's been
elections. Now, we're starting to
broaden out and we're starting to see a
lot of interest in other areas, as well.
>> So,
also in the news is this Trump Asia
trip.
So, what are the wins and losses? I know
it
rare earth tariff news, soybeans. What
can you tell us?
>> Yeah, so it was a pretty satisfactory
meeting. There was expectations that it
would be a positive
negotiation because prior to the meeting
in South Korea, you had top diplomats
from Beijing and from Washington
essentially set the framework so that
the two heads of states can go and
essentially shake hands and agree on
some things. China agreed to help more
on the fentanyl situation. President
Trump decided to reduce the tariff
there.
That was because he opposed a tariff
that was
directly linked to fentanyl. So, there
were some
positive
conciliatory
matters happening there.
You also had TikTok was under
discussion.
Allowing China to access more
semiconductors under discussion. Soybean
purchases are going to be made. Beijing
committed to that. But, that's one of
one thing we got to wait and see because
remember in Trump 1.0, Beijing committed
to huge purchases of soybeans that
didn't necessarily come to fruition at
the magnitude that was promised. So,
generally speaking, that's, you know,
those are some of the main takeaways
from the meeting. That was part of the
reason why today on October 30th, you
saw investors buy the dip
in the cyclically oriented areas of the
market.
So, the two more cyclically oriented
indices out of the four majors
are the Dow Jones Industrial and the
Russell 2000. So, all those
the the four major benchmarks, the other
two being the Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500,
all four were down sharply in the
morning. But, then investors start
bought the dips in the Russell 2000 and
the Dow. And, that's because of really
strong growth expectations. And, those
companies in those baskets are more
levered to the US economy. And, when you
see that US-China are starting to get
along
and inflation is running at 3% mainly
due to consumer demand being so strong
pushing up services costs, that really
widens the path for those kinds of firms
to do well. Now, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq
100, they're not recovering today
recovering into the green, I should say.
There has been some dip buying in those
two baskets, but it's not as much as the
former two. And, artificial intelligence
enthusiasm waned today after Meta and
Microsoft
delivered some results that weren't well
received by investors. Wall Street
started to question whether these
significant artificial intelligence
investments are going to be worth it in
the long run. Are these hundreds of
billions of dollars
going to generate returns later? You
know, that's top of mind. So, folks
decided to trim some technology stuff,
but add to the more cyclical sectors
like small caps, industrial, materials,
etc.
>> Okay, so that was good about Trump with
G, but what about South Korea and Japan?
Did he also go there as well?
>> So, this week they there was a big
meeting
in South Korea.
President Trump closed a deal
with South Korea a few days ago.
And the new Prime Minister of Japan,
her framework on politics and on
governance and on managing relations
between Tokyo and Washington are similar
to the late Shinzo Abe
>> Mhm.
>> who served as Prime Minister while
President Trump was serving his first
term. Unfortunately, he was
assassinated.
But, Shinzo and Trump were very good
friends. They got along really well.
Part of the reason why
folks
say that their friendship was so strong
is because Shinzo really courted Trump
and was really considerate and gave him
gifts and always made sure that the the
optics were very positive.
And now this new Prime Minister in
Japan, she's sort of abiding by those
same practices. Golden golf ball, Trump
hats, warm ovations upon his arrival.
You know, Trump essentially told her,
"Listen." I mean, of course,
exaggerating in
Trump fashion, but he pretty much told
her, "Listen, whatever you want, you can
have." When the President Trump says
that, you can kind of that's a signal
that relations between the two nations,
you know, they aren't terrible. They're
they're doing all right. So, you know,
Japanese automobiles are very popular.
And President Trump sometimes doesn't
like that a lot of the nations where we
import cars from.
They don't necessarily
take our imports, right? You don't see a
lot of Chevrolets or a lot of Dodges or
Fords in Europe or in Japan, for
example. You know, so President Trump is
critical of that cuz he'd like to see
more balanced cross-border commerce.
>> So, here's something I thought was
interesting yesterday is that Cheryl
Powell
stated that he does not believe the AI
boom is an asset bubble akin to the
dot-com bubble as big tech companies
have huge cash reserves. But, what about
the startups?
And what what was he getting at? What
was he trying to tell the markets?
>> He's trying to calm the markets. You
know, this is a someone that's
traditionally a financier. He worked at
Carlyle for a long time. He's right that
a lot of those dot-com bubble firms,
they weren't very profitable and they
didn't have terrific balance sheets. So,
they couldn't weather the turbulence
like these firms can.
And that's really the general
belief on Wall Street is that any kind
of correction is going to be
short-lived,
you know, or won't be that significant
because these companies actually make a
lot of money. And AI is not really the
only thing they're doing. These
companies have been around for a long
time and they have a lot of other goods
and services. Now, the question is,
however, if artificial intelligence
doesn't deliver the returns, you know,
how much needs to be
given back, you know, in terms of price
advancements.
>> There has to be some patience, right? I
think that's the thing he's trying to
suggest a little bit is going to have
patience. There's R&D involved here.
And it's not going to be just like a
next quarter thing. I mean, that just
makes common sense, right?
>> Yeah, it's a really, really expensive.
That's really the worry is what if this
doesn't do anything
in the end, you know, what if it's
really not that significant?
Did we really just spend
a hundred billion dollars, two hundred
billion dollars? The numbers really
they're really up there. So, that's
ultimately the question.
>> What's going on with the shutdown? What
are you seeing in the predictive markets
about it? And and what are you hearing?
>> It's looking like I'm just opening up my
forecast trader now. It's looking like
it's going to continue
to extend because
both sides are necessarily
looking to concede to the other.
So, yeah, looking like before
Thanksgiving cuz if you look at our
November 21st contract, the yes is 72%.
So,
72% of participants, generally speaking,
believe that
the shutdown will end by November 21st.
>> Are people getting a little nervous
about the shutdown? From an economic
perspective, I would I would seem so
because they're not getting some numbers
or is it just
more muted?
>> It's more muted. The Republicans for a
long time have wanted to trim
government. So, in their mind,
in the Republicans' minds, it's like,
well, they're closed. The government's
closed and everything seems to be
working. So, why should we have to
negotiate with Democrats? The markets
are doing great. Generally speaking,
have a little bit of volatility today
post Fed October 30th. Bond yields are
behaving. The government's closed. In
their mind, it's great.
And then when you consider that food
stamp funding is set to run out in the
next few days, that's another vulnerable
part of the population.
>> There is a huge concentration of that in
the red states. So, I would think they'd
be getting a little bit of pressure on
that.
>> They they just don't seem like they're
going to budge at all at this point.
But, you know, we don't really know
what's happening behind the scenes.
>> True.
>> Of course, they all could always, you
know, the Republican could be under
pressure to make a deal and they're just
not reflecting that pressure. But,
they're just not even talking about it.
>> So, Jose, great. Anything you want to
leave us with? What's going on next
week? Give us a little heads-up on what
we want to talk about.
>> Yeah, so one thing that's new is that
ADP is now releasing weekly jobs numbers
every Tuesday. So, that's going to be
fun. So, they're looking to really
fill that gap of the government not
being able to publish data. So, the ADP
is coming out their weekly numbers. Of
course, we have the weekly economic
index from the Dallas Fed. You know,
that still comes out every Thursday.
Hopefully, the government shutdown ends.
We have corporate earnings coming up.
Big corporate earnings today after the
bell. We have Amazon reporting as well
as Apple. So, that will be big. Yeah,
we're going to be watching corporate
earnings, real-time economic indicators.
We'll be watching interest rates to see
what December's looking like. Let's see
So, 71% chance that the Fed is going to
reduce rates in December. You know, so
we'll be watching that closely. And
yeah, we're watching on geopolitical
things and a few other things that I
don't that I'll remember later.

economist at Interactive Brokers, thank

metadata.title: What Is the CFTC? The US Regulator Behind Futures, Swaps and Retail Forex (2026)
metadata.author: Brokerchampion
metadata.shortDescription:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is an independent federal agency of the United States government — and if you trade futures, options on commodities, swaps or retail forex as a US person, it writes the rules your broker lives under. "Independent" is meaningful here: the CFTC doesn't sit inside the Treasury Department or the Federal Reserve. It reports to Congress and is funded through annual appropriations. It was created by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission Act of 1974, which took regulatory authority for futures markets out of the Department of Agriculture and consolidated it in one dedicated agency, and it began operations on April 21, 1975. Its mandate under the Commodity Exchange Act is to foster open, transparent, competitive and financially sound markets and to avoid systemic risk in derivatives.

What it regulates: US futures and options exchanges such as CME Group, ICE Futures US and MGEX; the derivatives clearing organisations that stand between buyers and sellers; futures commission merchants, introducing brokers, commodity pool operators and commodity trading advisors; swap dealers; retail foreign exchange dealers; and Bitcoin and commodity cryptocurrencies, in both cash and derivatives markets. The dividing line with the SEC is roughly this — securities like stocks, bonds and ETFs belong to the SEC; derivatives on commodities, including currencies, agricultural products, metals, energy and most cryptocurrencies, belong to the CFTC. Where tokens fall is one of the most actively litigated questions in US financial regulation in 2026. Internally the agency runs five main divisions: Market Oversight for surveillance and new contracts, Clearing and Risk for clearinghouses, Enforcement, Market Participants for intermediaries like RFEDs and FCMs, and the Office of the Chief Economist. Day-to-day registration and examination is delegated to the NFA, an industry self-regulatory organisation working under CFTC oversight.

Two shifts made the modern CFTC. First, Dodd-Frank, signed in July 2010: Title VII handed the agency the swap market, which had been largely unregulated bilateral dealing. It brought mandatory clearing for standardised swaps, real-time reporting to swap data repositories, swap execution facilities, registration of swap dealers, explicit position-limit authority and stronger anti-manipulation powers — roughly tripling the notional value of markets the CFTC oversees. Second, crypto: the agency has held since 2015 that Bitcoin is a commodity, the Second Circuit confirmed virtual currencies are commodities in 2018 in CFTC v. McDonnell, and 2023 actions against several DeFi protocols established, subject to ongoing appeals, that developers and operators can be liable as unregistered exchanges and FCMs. On enforcement, FY 2024 saw 58 actions and orders for over $17 billion in monetary relief, dominated by a few large cases — typically spoofing settlements with major banks and crypto-related fraud. The Whistleblower Program pays 10 to 30 percent of monetary sanctions on successful actions of $1 million or more.

US forex brokers must follow strict regulations, including leverage limits of 50:1 on major pairs and 20:1 on others, CFTC and NFA registration, FIFO trade execution, and segregated client funds to protect traders.

Check a broker’s legitimacy by verifying its NFA registration, reviewing CFTC enforcement records, and checking its financial health and complaint history. US clients should only use brokers registered with both the CFTC and NFA.

regulates derivatives linked to

firms. Remember the $20 million

metadata.title: What is the CFTC and What Does it Do?
metadata.author: Earn2Trade
metadata.shortDescription:
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) is an independent body responsible for regulating the futures and options market in the United States. Any firm or person looking to participate in the commodity futures market needs to register with them. The agency looks to promote futures trading in the US and improve competitiveness and efficiency. They do so by ensuring a level playing field for all investors. The CFTC also monitors the commodities trading market for unfair practices like fraud, market manipulation, and other illegal activities. With the evolution of technology, the supervisory activity of the CFTC has become more complicated. Today trades happen at a much faster pace, opening up opportunities for potential exploits.

The scope of the CFTC has also expanded over the years. Now it covers different aspects of the commodities derivatives market. The CFTC also oversees other participants in the futures market like brokers, commodity trading advisors, and commodity pool operators. This makes their task all the more challenging. The agency also needs to monitor the activities of stakeholders outside the marketplace. For example, a commodity trading advisor who oversees a managed futures account may adopt a strategy that may not be in their client’s best interests. The CFTC also has the authority to look into the activities of asset managers and intervene if their practices are not in line with the best interests of their clients.
