videos.full_text: I think we'll begin. Good afternoon everyone and welcome to the inaugural frontier forum on super intelligence. When chairman Celig established the innovation task force, he gave us a clear mission. Ensure that the new frontier finance is built here in America. Key to that mission is bringing together the innovators building the future of finance along with the policy makers who are responsible for overseeing the US markets. I hope that today's forum is a reflection of that commitment. Before we begin, I need to make a few disclaimers. First, the purpose of this forum is for the CFTC to receive information and opinions from leaders at the intersection of technology, policy, and finance. To ensure compliance with advisory committee laws, the agency is not seeking group advice from attendees. Additionally, none of the statements made during this forum should be construed to constitute or imply any endorsement, recommendation, or favoring of any organization, products, or services by the US government, the CFTC, or any CFTC employees. With that, I would like to thank our outstanding panelists and moderators, as well as my many CFTC colleagues who worked tirelessly to make today's event possible. And now it is my pleasure to introduce the chairman of the CFTC, Michael Celig. [applause] Thank you, Michael. Good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to the inaugural Frontier Forum. I want to thank our distinguished panelists and moderators for joining us today as well as the innovation task force for organizing the forum. Before I provide my opening remarks, I must note that the views I share today are my own as chairman and not necessarily those of the commission. We're gathered here today to discuss a technology that's rapidly transforming our financial markets. President Trump calls it super intelligence or SI because there's nothing artificial about it. It's as real as the printing press, the steam engine, and the internet. Like the generational technologies that preceded it, super intelligence promises to reshape our financial markets by continuing a decadesl long evolution towards increasingly autonomous trading systems. Fortunately, automated trading is nothing new to the commission. Some of the earliest algorithmic strategies deployed in our markets date back to the launch of the S&P 500 index futures on designated contract markets in the 80s. Of course, the rise of automated trading was not without controversy. About a decade ago, following the May 2010 flash crash, Knight Capital's runaway algorithm in August 2012, and a sharp disruption in Treasury futures in October 2014, the commission considered special risk control rules for algorithmic trading firms. and a proposal known as regulation automated trading. The commission expressed concern that quote malfunctioning or incorrectly deployed algorithms deploying erroneous messages to trading venues can significantly impact markets and market participants. We hear many of these same concerns today. Yet, a lot has changed since the commission proposed the rule, which it never finalized and which would be ills suited for today's landscape. SI is no longer a tool available only to sophisticated firms and individuals. It's become nearly as commonplace on our computers and personal devices as a web browser or word processor. Many of the most popular SI applications such as Claude, ChatGBT, and Gemini can interoperate with thirdparty applications to analyze market data, identify trends, and help users become more informed. Brokerages are also beginning to incorporate SI tools into their customer offerings, putting capabilities once reserved for Wall Street's largest institutions into the hands of everyday Americans. Meanwhile, individuals are increasingly giving their credentials to their brokerage and bank account to their SI agent and trusting the agent to manage their finances. and blockchains are providing rails for autonomous agents to custody and trade crypto assets without relying on banks, brokerages, or other traditional intermediaries. It's no longer science fiction to imagine your refrigerator autonomously purchasing your groceries with funds that it earns from launching a memecoin or staking ether. We have to think long and hard about how to regulate intelligently in this age of super intelligence. like the printing press, the steam engine, and the internet before it, SI will transform the global economy. But America cannot afford to sit idly by as this transformation takes place all around us. It must lead with rational rules that promote technological innovation while also ensuring that our markets remain the deepest and most liquid in the world. We cannot accept the false choice of winning the SI race or maintaining global financial market supremacy. We must do both. And under President Trump's leadership, we're doing exactly that. At their core, derivatives markets serve an essential economic purpose. They help businesses manage risk, discover prices, and make investment decisions with greater confidence. A farmer can hedge the future price of a crop before harvest. An airline can manage its exposure to variable fuel expenses. A manufacturer can protect itself against fluctuations in the cost of raw materials. SI has the potential to make risk management more efficient. Consider what it takes to assess risk in modern financial markets. A market participant may need to evaluate thousands of instruments, monitor changing market conditions, and understand how a shock in one market could affect positions across several others. That's an enormous amount of information to process. and the consequences of missing something could be detrimental. SI can help process the vast amount of information significantly faster than human brain power with greater accuracy. For large institutional firms, that could mean better informed decisions and more effective risk management. For smaller market participants, it could mean access to capabilities that previously required the resources of a much larger institution. That last point is particularly important. Innovation should create opportunities for more Americans and American businesses to participate in our markets. By lowering the cost of sophisticated analysis and making powerful tools more widely accessible, SI could help level the playing field and expand access to risk management capabilities. It could also improve price discovery by helping market participants better understand the information driving prices and the relationships between different markets. These are meaningful opportunities. More effective risk management, better information, and broader access to financial tools will help our derivatives markets serve businesses across the economy more efficiently. And as these technologies advance, we should be thinking not just about how SI can improve the markets we have today, but also about the new financial activity it could create. The CFTC's regulatory framework was developed around identifiable market participants, intermediaries, and institutions performing specific financial functions. But what happens when those functions are increasingly performed or facilitated by autonomous software? Consider an SI agent that identifies trading opportunities and executes transactions on behalf of a user. Does the developer of that agent become subject to registration? Who's liable if the agent goes rogue? How can regulators know who the agent or suite of agents is acting on behalf of? Do we need a new flavor of know your customer identification or know your agent or KYA? These are precisely the types of questions that we face as Agentic Finance continues to develop in our markets. While they are challenging, the CFTC benefits from already having confronted similar issues in crypto asset markets. For years, software developers and entrepreneurs faced uncertainty about whether publishing code or developing user interfaces could trigger regulatory requirements designed for traditional financial intermediaries. Under my leadership, we've strived to provide greater clarity around these questions. But as agents become more capable, these distinctions will become increasingly important. Our approach must remain grounded in the functions performed, the control exercised, and the economic realities of the transaction. SI agents may respond to market conditions in unexpected ways. Systems relying on similar models may generate correlated trading behavior, and the speed of autonomous transactions may create new challenges for market surveillance and risk management. But these technologies also offer opportunities to strengthen market integrity. SI systems can help exchange identif uh exchanges identify suspicious activity, enable clearing houses to monitor exposures more effectively, and improve regulators ability to detect misconduct. The industrial revolution depended on coal, iron, and steam power. The 20th century saw the rise of oil, electricity, and modern industrial infrastructure. The SI revolution depends on computational power or compute. Advanced SI systems require enormous amounts of compute, specialized processors, electricity, and data center infrastructure. As demand for these resources grows, businesses will increasingly need tools to manage exposure to changing prices and availability. This is the role of America's derivatives markets. And it's a role that the derivatives markets have played for generations. Farmers hedge agricultural production. Airlines hedge fuel costs. Manufacturers manage exposure to industrial commodities. In the SI economy, developers, infrastructure providers, cyber security firms, and frontier investors may need similar tools to manage SI related risks. Earlier this year, the CFTC sought public comment on the development of compute derivatives markets. We want to understand how these markets are evolving and how our regulatory framework can support their responsible development. The responses have been substantial with more than a 100 commenters weighing in on the risks and opportunities these markets present. The CFTC has an opportunity to help establish the financial infrastructure of the SI economy, and we intend to take that opportunity very seriously. Nearly 70 years ago, an IBM computer scientist named Arthur L. Samuels taught a computer to play checkers, helping establish the principle that machines could do more than just follow instructions. I suspect he could have scarcely imagined a world in which intelligent systems might one day manage financial portfolios, hedge commodity exposures, and transact directly with one another. The convergence of super intelligence, crypto, and modern financial infrastructure could transform our markets. It could expand access to sophisticated financial tools, enable businesses to manage risk with greater precision, and create entirely new forms of economic activity. But realizing that potential will require thoughtful engagement between the innovators building these technologies and the policy makers responsible for overseeing our markets. And that's precisely what we hope to accomplish today. Our first panel will explore the implications of SI in the derivatives markets, including how increasingly capable systems may transform trading, price discovery, and risk management. Our second panel will examine the emergence of agentic trading, and the questions raised by autonomous systems capable of conducting financial transactions. At the CFTC, we're committed to ensuring that America's derivatives markets remain the most innovative, competitive, and resilient in the world. metadata.title: AI Trading Agents: The CFTC's Know Your Agent Question
metadata.author: AI in Regulated Industries
metadata.shortDescription:
AI trading agents are coming, and the CFTC wants to know who they work for. At the agency's first Frontier Forum on 28 October 2026, Chairman Mike Selig asked whether AI agent developers should register, who is liable when an agent goes rogue, and whether markets need a 'know your agent' check alongside KYC.

My take: it's the right question, but most of the answer already exists. Under MiFID II, European firms must identify the algorithm behind every trade decision and tell regulators about their strategies, limits and kill switches. So register the principal, not the developer, and tag every order with an agent ID. The catch is crypto and self-run agents, where no regulated firm sits in the middle.

In this video:
• What CFTC Chairman Mike Selig asked about AI agents at the Frontier Forum (28 Oct 2026)
• Why 'know your agent' is less new than it sounds: MiFID II algorithm IDs and notification rules
• Why regulators should register the principal, not the AI developer
• Where KYA breaks: crypto, self-run agents and herding
• A four-step checklist for banks, brokers and builders running trading agents

Chapters
0:00 Your fridge is now a trader
0:30 The CFTC Frontier Forum explained
1:22 Why AI trading agents matter now
2:00 Know your agent already exists
3:11 Where know your agent breaks
3:47 What banks and builders should do
4:09 My prediction for agent rules

Sources
• CFTC chief poses questions about policing AI but calls it a road to 'autonomous trading' (CoinDesk), 28 Oct 2026: https://www.coindesk.com/policy/2026/10/28/cftc-chief-poses-questions-about-policing-ai-but-calls-it-a-road-to-autonomous-trading
• CFTC's Selig Sees Role for Compute Futures, Rules for AI Trading Agents (PYMNTS), 29 Oct 2026: https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/cftcs-selig-sees-role-for-compute-futures-rules-for-ai-trading-agents/
• CFTC's Selig: Who Is Liable When an AI Agent Trades Crypto? (FinanceFeeds), 29 Oct 2026: https://financefeeds.com/cftc-chair-floats-a-future-where-ai-agents-trade/
• CFTC Chair Proposes 'Know Your Agent' Framework (Phemex News), 28 Oct 2026: https://phemex.com/news/article/cftc-chair-proposes-know-your-agent-framework-as-aidriven-autonomous-trading-raises-regulatory-questions-101610
• MiFID II: Transaction reporting (Dechert), Oct 2017: https://www.dechert.com/content/dam/dechert%20files/knowledge/hot-topics/mifid-ii/MiFID%20II%20-%20Transaction%20reporting.pdf
• MiFID II Article 17 algorithmic trading notification (Presencis), n.d.: https://presencis.com/regulations/mifid2/article-notification/

Should the developer of an AI trading agent have to register, or only the person who uses it? Tell me in the comments. Subscribe for daily takes on AI in regulated industries.

Narration: AI voice (Kokoro, open source). This video is AI-generated and human-curated.

segments.text: America's derivatives regulator just
asked a question that sounds like a
joke. What happens when your fridge
starts trading? It isn't a joke. It's
the first draft of a rulebook for AI
agents in markets.
The phrase to remember is know your
agent. My take, it's the right question,
but most of the answer already exists,
and it's been sitting in Europe for
years.
On the 28th of October, Mike Selig,
chairman of the Commodity Futures
Trading Commission, the CFTC, opened the
agency's first frontier forum. He said
super intelligence, crypto, and modern
market infrastructure could lead to
autonomous trading.
Then he asked three questions. If an AI
agent trades for you, does its developer
have to register? Who is liable if it
goes rogue? And who is it acting for?
His idea was a know your agent check
next to know your customer.
To be fair, nothing was proposed, and he
said the views were his own. But when a
regulator asks questions in public, a
rulebook usually follows.
Why now? Because the tools are here.
Brett Harrison, chief executive of the
trading firm Architect, told the forum
that AI coding tools let far more people
trade with black box algorithms. Crypto
platforms already offer wallets that let
AI agents trade within limits the user
sets.
Selig named the risks himself. Agents
can react unexpectedly. Similar models
can make correlated trades, and fast
transactions make surveillance harder.
Here's where I push back. Know your
agent sounds new. It isn't. Europe has
run a version of it for years under my
MiFID II, its main markets rulebook.
Firms' transaction reports must identify
who decided to trade and who executed
it. That can be a person, a committee,
or an algorithm with a code unique to
each strategy.
Algorithmic traders must also notify
their regulator and the trading venue
and be ready to describe their
strategies, limits, controls, and kill
switches. That's know your agent in
everything but name.
So, my answer to Selig's first question
is no. Don't register the developer.
Register the principal, the firm or
person the agent works for. And tag
every order with an agent ID that points
back to them. Selig hinted at this
himself. The approach must be grounded
in the functions performed and the
control exercised.
Now the catch. Europe's model works
because a regulated firm sits in the
middle of every trade. In crypto and
with agents people run for themselves,
there often isn't one. Your fridge
doesn't have a compliance officer.
A second catch. An ID tells you who an
agent works for, not what it will do.
Thousands of similar agents can all be
identified and still stampede together,
but you can't fix herding if you can't
see who's moving.
If you build trading agents, start now.
Give every agent and strategy its own ID
and a named human owner. Set hard
limits, log every mandate, and test the
kill switch. And banks and brokers,
decide now what proof you'll ask for
when clients' agents turn up.
My prediction, within 2 years a major
American markets regulator will require
orders from AI agents to carry an
identifier linked to an accountable
principal, with crypto venues first.
Watch the CFTC round table on
round-the-clock trading on the 15th of
December for early clues.
Over to you. Should the developer of an
AI trading agent have to register or
only the person using it? Tell me in the
comments and subscribe for daily takes
on AI in regulated industries.

**Are You Betting Live... or Betting Behind?**
Most live sports bettors don’t realize they’re playing a delayed game—and not just mentally, but *technologically*. In this eye-opening deep dive, we break down the shocking latency gap between what *you* see on screen and what *bookmakers* know in real-time. It’s not a glitch—it’s built-in. And it could be costing you money with every live bet you place.

In this episode, we expose the hidden disadvantage in live sports betting. While you think you're watching the game in real time, there's a crucial delay between your screen and the bookmaker's ultra-fast data feed. This lag—sometimes up to 30 seconds—can mean you’re betting on an event that already happened, giving the house a massive, invisible edge.

We unpack the technical infrastructure behind this edge—private satellite links, zero-latency stadium feeds, exclusive league data contracts—and show how latency arbitrage strategies take full advantage of delayed streams. But it's not all doom and gloom. You’ll also learn how to adjust your strategy to minimize this gap and possibly outsmart the system.

This is essential knowledge for anyone placing live bets. Because once you understand the latency game, you’ll never watch—or wager—the same way again.

---

**🎓 What You’ll Learn:**

* The hidden tech gap in live sports betting
* How bookmakers get near-instant data from games
* Why your “live” stream is often 10–30 seconds behind
* What latency arbitrage is—and how it affects your odds
* How algorithms might exploit your betting decisions
* Actionable strategies to level the playing field
* Platforms that offer lower latency betting alternatives
* How to use odds movements as real-time indicators

---

**🕒 Timestamps Breakdown:**

00:00 – Intro: The illusion of live sports betting
00:36 – How stream delays really work
01:04 – Devices and streaming platforms that increase latency
01:36 – What bookmakers use instead: zero-latency feeds

04:02 – Key advice: Know your delay and adjust strategy
04:32 – Avoid reaction-based betting
05:00 – Low-latency exchanges as an alternative
05:29 – Final takeaway: Awareness is your best defense

---

**👍 If you found this eye-opening or helpful, give it a thumbs up, leave a comment sharing your betting experience, and don’t forget to subscribe for more deep dives into the unseen world of online money, tech, and strategy. Your support fuels our hustle!**
